summary: Added the first real week of school words as a JSON file and wired the game to load it, so the kid now plays ten actual homework words instead of the test list.
body:
The word list used to be a hard-coded array of three test words in main.ts. I moved it into public/words/week-01.json with the shape {"week": 1, "words": [...]} and added a small loader that fetches it at startup. If the fetch fails, the page shows a plain message instead of a blank screen.

I typed in the ten words from the school sheet and checked each one against the sheet twice, because a typo in the list would teach the kid a wrong spelling. The game picks them in the order of the file for now. Shuffling is a later step. Dev server and a production build both load the file correctly.

Next is the voice: the default one sounds too fast for the younger kid.

summary: Tuned the speech settings: rate 0.8 and an English voice picked by name with a fallback, because the default voice on the tablet read words too fast and sometimes in the wrong accent.
body:
The first run on the tablet showed two problems. The default voice spoke at a speed the younger kid could not follow, and on the tablet it was not the same voice as on the laptop. I set utterance.rate to 0.8 and tested 0.7 and 0.9 as well; 0.8 was the one the kids liked.

Voice choice now goes through speechSynthesis.getVoices(). The list is empty on first call in Chrome, so I wait for the voiceschanged event before picking. The code looks for a preferred en-GB voice by name, then any voice whose lang starts with en, then the browser default.

I added a repeat button that reads the word again, and a slower repeat at rate 0.6 on a second press. The slow repeat helps with long words like 'necessary'.

Open question: the voice names differ per device, so the preference list is a guess. I will log the voice list on the tablet and adjust.

Nothing is saved yet, so the chosen voice resets on reload, which is fine until the settings exist.

summary: Built the first score board: each finished week stores correct count and tries per word in local storage, and the end screen shows it as a simple table.
body:
The game now records, for every word, whether it was right on the first try and how many attempts it took. At the end of a round it writes one record to local storage under the key spellbee.scores, as a list of {week, date-less round counter, results}. I avoided real timestamps in the display; a round number is enough for the kids.

The end screen shows a table with the word, a tick or a cross, and the attempts. Top line: '7 of 10 right first time'. The younger kid asked right away whether she could beat her own best, so I added a small 'best so far' line for the same week.

A problem came up while testing: parsing a broken or empty value from local storage threw and killed the page. I wrapped the read in a try/catch that falls back to an empty list, and I wrote a tiny test for it.

Limits: the data lives per browser, so the laptop and the tablet have separate scores. That is acceptable for now.

Still to do: styling of the table, which is plain, and a reset button for scores.

summary: Added right and wrong sound effects, and fixed the tablet blocking audio until the first tap by creating the audio context inside the start button handler.
body:
I made two short sounds with a tone generator: a rising two-note chime for right and a low single buzz for wrong. Both are small mp3 files under 10 KB in public/sounds. The wrong sound is quiet on purpose, because the older kid said a loud buzz felt like being told off.

On the tablet nothing played at first. The browser blocks audio until a user gesture, and I had created the Audio objects at page load. Moving the creation and a silent first play into the click handler of the start button solved it.

The speech API had the same kind of problem on iOS-like browsers: the first utterance only worked after a tap. Since the start button is now the first tap, both are covered.

I also added a mute toggle in the corner, stored in local storage. Checked: with mute on, speech still works, only effects are silent.

Remaining: the sound plays slightly late on the tablet, about 200 ms. I will look at preloading next time.

summary: Preloaded the sound effects and cut the tablet's delay on right and wrong sounds from about 200 ms to barely noticeable.
body:
The delay came from creating a new Audio element on each answer and letting the browser load the file then. I now create both elements once at start, call load(), and on each answer reset currentTime to 0 and call play().

I timed it with performance.now() between the submit and the play promise resolving. Before: roughly 180 to 220 ms on the tablet. After: under 30 ms. The laptop was always fast.

One side effect: a quick double answer cut the first sound off. That is fine for the game, the second answer is what matters.

No other changes today.

summary: Made the game usable on the tablet: bigger input, no zoom on focus, and the on-screen keyboard no longer hides the word area.
body:
Three things were wrong on the tablet. Focusing the input zoomed the page, because the font size was 14px; setting it to 18px or more stops that. The keyboard covered the buttons, so I put the layout in a column with the input near the top and used 100dvh instead of 100vh.

I also turned off autocorrect, autocapitalize and spellcheck on the input. Without that the tablet fixed the kid's wrong spelling before the game could mark it, which defeated the point. That one took a while to find, because the answers seemed to be right when they were not.

The buttons got a minimum size of 48px so small fingers hit them. I tested in both orientations. Landscape is cramped but works.

Next: a proper look at the week selection.

summary: Added a week picker and a manifest of word lists, so the kids can choose a week and the game defaults to the newest one.
body:
Until now the game loaded week-01.json only. I added public/words/index.json listing the weeks available, for example {"weeks": [1, 2, 3]}, and the loader reads it first. The default is the highest number.

The picker is a plain select on the start screen. Choosing a week reloads the word list and the best-so-far line for that week. I kept the select native because it works well with touch.

I typed in weeks 2 and 3 from the sheets the kids brought home. While typing I noticed that the sheet for week 3 had 'separate' and the kid had been writing 'seperate', a good sign that the game is useful.

I made the shuffle: each round uses a Fisher-Yates shuffle of the words, so the order differs. The end screen still lists the words in the original order, which is easier to compare to the sheet.

Edge cases tested: a week with fewer than 10 words works, an empty list shows a message, a missing file shows an error text.

A small cleanup: the loader code moved to src/words.ts, with types for the JSON shape. The build is clean and the bundle is around 6 KB gzipped.

To do: the parent has to edit JSON by hand to add a week. That will get a page later, but not yet.

summary: Gave each wrong answer a second chance with a short pause, and counted the word as wrong only after two misses, which the kids found much less stressful.
body:
The old rule marked a word wrong at the first miss and moved on. The younger kid got upset after two words in a row. New rule: after a first miss, the game says 'try again', replays the word slowly and lets her type again. After the second miss it shows the correct spelling for three seconds and moves on.

The score keeps both facts: right first time, right second time, or missed. The end screen shows a tick, a small 2 for second try, or a cross. The summary line counts only first-time answers.

I had a bug where the input was not cleared after a miss, so the kid had to delete the old text. The field now clears and refocuses.

The timing of the three-second reveal feels long for the older kid. I may make it depend on the word length later.

summary: Fixed the score history growing without limit and a bug where best-so-far compared rounds from different weeks.
body:
Looking at local storage after two weeks of play, the scores list already had over 60 records. It will only grow. I now keep the last 30 rounds per week and drop older ones when writing.

The best-so-far bug was in my filter: it compared week as a string on one side and a number on the other, so the strict equality never matched and the line always showed the overall best. I made the week a number everywhere in the types and added a test with two weeks of data.

While in there I also added a version field to the stored object, {version: 1, rounds: [...]}, and a migration for the old plain list. The old data of the kids kept working after the change; I checked it by loading the page with the old format in storage.

All tests pass. No UI changes.

summary: Reworked the look of the game with larger type, friendlier colours and a progress bar, after the kids said the page felt like a form.
body:
The kids' comment was blunt: it looked like homework. I changed the look to something calmer and more playful without adding a framework, only CSS in src/style.css.

What changed: a rounded card in the middle of the page, a 28px speaker button that pulses while the word is read, a progress bar showing word 4 of 10, and colours from a small set of CSS variables. The right answer flashes green for half a second, the wrong one shakes the input once.

The pulse is a CSS animation that I switch on from the speech 'start' and 'end' events. On the tablet the 'end' event did not fire reliably for short words, so I added a timeout fallback of 3 seconds that removes the class.

I checked contrast: the grey on the card was too light, so I darkened it until it passes at a normal reading size. I did not run a full accessibility audit.

I also reduced motion when prefers-reduced-motion is set, because the shake is a bit much.

The bundle did not grow in JavaScript, only about 1 KB of CSS.

The older kid asked for a dark mode. Noted, but not planned.

summary: Found why the voice sometimes read nothing on the laptop: speechSynthesis stayed paused after a cancel, so I call resume and cancel in the right order before each word.
body:
The symptom was random: now and then the word button did nothing, and a reload fixed it. I reproduced it by pressing repeat quickly several times. After a speak() right after cancel(), the queue was stuck.

The cause, as far as I could tell, is that cancel() followed at once by speak() can leave the engine in a paused or pending state in Chrome. My fix is a small function speakWord(text) that does cancel(), then resume(), then waits one animation frame before speak(). With this order I could not reproduce the problem in 200 quick presses.

I also guard against overlapping speech by ignoring a repeat press while an utterance is pending for less than 300 ms. That felt natural in testing.

The tablet browser did not show the bug at all, so the fix is mainly for the laptop.

I wrote down the repro in a comment above the function, because the code looks odd without it. A real test is not possible, since the speech API is not available in the test runner; I mocked it only to check the call order.

Next: settings for voice and speed, saved in local storage.

summary: Added a settings panel for speech speed and voice choice, stored in local storage, so the older kid can use a faster voice than the younger one.
body:
The panel is a small dialog opened from a gear icon. It has a slider for rate from 0.5 to 1.2, a select with the English voices found on the device, and a test button that says a sample word.

Settings are saved under spellbee.settings with a version field like the scores. Missing values fall back to the defaults from earlier: rate 0.8 and the preferred voice list.

A catch: a saved voice name may not exist on another device or after an update. If the saved voice is not found, the code falls back to the automatic choice and does not overwrite the saved name, so it comes back if the voice returns.

The slow repeat is now rate times 0.75 instead of a fixed 0.6.

Tested on laptop and tablet. Both keep their own settings, as expected with local storage.

summary: Added a confetti burst and a short message for a perfect round, and a quieter encouragement line for low scores.
body:
The end screen now looks at the first-time score. Ten of ten starts a canvas confetti animation for two seconds and the text 'Perfect round'. Seven to nine shows 'Nearly there', and below seven shows 'Good practice, try again tomorrow'.

I wrote the confetti myself in about 40 lines instead of adding a package: coloured rectangles with gravity and a random spin, cleared when the time is up. It stops immediately if reduced motion is requested.

The canvas sat on top of the buttons and blocked taps, which I noticed on the tablet. I set pointer-events: none on it.

The younger kid played three rounds just to see the confetti again, so I think it works.

summary: Wrote a test setup with Vitest for the scoring and word loading code, and found two real bugs: an off-by-one in the progress bar and a crash on a duplicate word.
body:
There were no tests apart from the single storage test. I added Vitest to the dev dependencies and a vitest config that uses the jsdom environment, since the code touches local storage and the DOM a little.

I first pulled the game rules out of main.ts into src/game.ts, a pure state machine: start(words), answer(text), next(). It has no DOM or speech in it. main.ts only calls it and renders.

Tests written so far, 18 in total:
- first-time right, second-time right, missed after two tries
- case and surrounding spaces ignored in answers
- the shuffle keeps all words and does not repeat any
- summary counts
- storage read of broken data, old version and trimming to 30 rounds

The tests found two bugs. The progress bar showed 'word 11 of 10' at the end, because the index was incremented before the render of the last screen. And a week list with the same word twice, which I had actually typed by mistake in week 3, made the results table collapse the two rows, as I keyed them by word. I now key by position, and the loader warns in the console about duplicates.

I fixed the duplicate in week-03.json: 'receive' was typed twice, and 'believe' was missing. The sheet confirms it.

Running npm test takes under 2 seconds. I added it to the README as the one command to run before a deploy.

No features today, but the code is easier to change now. The hint button is on the list for the next block of work.

summary: Deployed the site to the static host with a build script and checked that the speech and the word files work from the real address on the tablet.
body:
Until now the kids played on a local dev server, which only works when the laptop is on. I set up the static host with the dist folder of npm run build. The deploy is a single command in package.json that builds and copies to the host.

Two things broke at first. The word files returned 404 because the Vite base path was wrong; setting base to './' made all asset links relative, and then everything loaded. And the host served the JSON files with a long cache time, so a new week did not show up on the tablet. I set a short cache header for the words folder in the host's config.

The speech API needs a secure context in some browsers, and the host serves over https, so that is fine.

Tested on the tablet from a home screen shortcut: it opens full screen, speech works, scores are saved. Scores from the dev server are not carried over, since the origin differs. The kids started fresh, which they did not mind.

Next time: a proper way to add a week.

summary: Added a small keyboard shortcut set and fixed Enter submitting an empty answer, which counted as a miss and upset the younger kid.
body:
An empty field plus Enter was counted as a wrong try. The younger kid pressed Enter by habit and lost her second chance. Now an empty answer is ignored and the game just replays the word.

I added two shortcuts for the laptop: Ctrl+Space repeats the word and Escape closes the settings panel. They are listed in a small hint under the input, which the kids can ignore.

I also trimmed the answer before comparing and removed double spaces inside. Words with a hyphen or an apostrophe were not in any list yet, but I wrote tests for them so they work when they arrive.

Tests: 22 pass.

summary: Looked into dark mode on request and decided on a CSS variables approach that follows the system setting, but did not ship it yet.
body:
The older kid asked again for dark mode. I checked how much it would take: the colours are already in CSS variables, so it is mostly a second set under prefers-color-scheme: dark.

I drafted the dark set and tried it on the laptop. The card, text and bars look fine. The confetti colours and the wrong-answer red need a change, since they look harsh on a dark background.

I did not merge it. The draft is in a local stash, and I want the kids to look at it first and say if they really want it. If yes, it is about an hour of work.

summary: Shipped dark mode that follows the system setting, with adjusted feedback colours and a manual toggle in settings saved in local storage.
body:
The kids looked at the draft and the older one liked it, so I finished it. The variables in :root hold the light set, and a second set applies under prefers-color-scheme: dark. A data-theme attribute on the html element overrides both, which is what the manual toggle sets.

The settings panel has a select with three options: automatic, light, dark. The value is saved in spellbee.settings along with the voice and rate. Old saved settings without the field are read as automatic.

Colour changes: the wrong-answer red became a softer coral, the green got a bit lighter, and the confetti uses a palette that works on both backgrounds. The sound mute icon had a fixed dark fill, so it disappeared in dark mode; it now uses currentColor.

I applied the theme in a small inline script in the head before the CSS loads, to avoid a white flash when the page opens in dark mode. This is the only inline script, and it is 6 lines.

Tested: system light, system dark, manual override both ways, on laptop and tablet. A test for the settings reader covers the missing field.

One cosmetic thing left: the select on the tablet uses its own dark style, which differs a bit from the page. It is fine.

The next block of work is the hint button, which the younger kid has asked for several times.

summary: Added the hint button that shows the first letter of the word, and made a used hint count in the score as a separate mark.
body:
The hint button sits beside the repeat button. Pressing it fills the first letter of the current word into a faded placeholder above the input, so the kid still has to type the whole word. It can be used once per word.

The game state got a hintUsed flag per word. The result of a word with a hint is still right or wrong as before, but the end table shows a small 'h' next to it, and the headline count of 'right first time' does not include words where a hint was used. I wanted the score to stay honest without punishing the younger kid for asking.

The tests cover: hint only once, hint reset on the next word, and the scoring rules with a hint plus a second try. 27 tests pass.

One question was whether the hint should also reveal the length of the word. I tried showing underscores, one per letter, and the older kid said it made it too easy. I kept only the first letter. This can be a setting later if the kids ask.

On the tablet the hint placeholder was hidden behind the keyboard in landscape. I moved it directly above the input, inside the same container, which fixed it.

Stored scores from before have no hint info; they are read as no hint used.

I deployed it and the kids tried it in the evening. The younger kid used the hint on nearly every word on the first night, which I expect to drop.

summary: Started the parent page at /parent.html where the words of the week are typed into a textarea, previewed and exported as a JSON file, with no password yet.
body:
Adding a week meant editing JSON by hand, which is error-prone. The parent page is a second HTML entry in Vite, with its own small script, parent.ts.

The parent types or pastes the words, one per line, and chooses the week number. The page shows a preview list with a count, trims spaces, lowercases nothing (some words may need capitals), and warns about duplicates and about a count other than 10. Then a button downloads week-NN.json in the right shape.

Because the site is static, the page cannot write to the host. The flow is: download the file, put it in public/words, update index.json, deploy. That is still manual, but the risky part, typing JSON syntax, is gone. The page also builds the new index.json content from a list of existing weeks that it reads from the current index.

I shared the validation code with the game loader in src/words.ts, so both agree on what a valid list is. Tests added for the validator: empty lines, duplicates, very long words, characters that are not letters, hyphens or apostrophes. 34 tests pass.

Open: the page is public at its address and anyone who knows the path can open it. It cannot change anything, so the risk is small, but the kids may find it and mess with the preview. A simple gate is the next step.

summary: Put a simple arithmetic gate in front of the parent page and linked it from the settings, so the kids do not wander into it by accident.
body:
The gate is a small question like 'What is 7 x 8?' with random numbers between 6 and 9. A correct answer shows the parent tools; a wrong one gives a new question. It is not security, only a speed bump for a seven-year-old, and I wrote that in a comment so nobody expects more.

The unlock state is kept in sessionStorage, so it lasts until the tab closes. The settings panel in the game got a 'For parents' link that opens parent.html. I did not put the link on the main screen.

While testing I found that the parent page ignored the dark mode choice. It uses the same CSS file, but not the inline head script. I added the same six lines there, and now both pages follow the theme.

I also changed the preview so the words are shown in the same font and size as in the game, in order to catch things like a letter l that looks like a capital I.

A second small thing: the download file name used the week number without a leading zero for weeks 1 to 9, which broke the sort order in the folder. It uses two digits now, and I renamed the existing files week-01 to week-09 to match. The loader builds names the same way, so nothing else changed.

Tests: the gate logic is tested for the range of numbers and for the answer check. 37 pass.

Next I want to look at streaks, since the older kid wants a reason to play each day.

summary: Implemented daily streaks: a day counts when at least one round is finished, the streak shows on the start screen, and one missed day is handled by a gentle reset.
body:
Streaks need a notion of days, and so far the scores had no dates. I added a day number, counted as whole days since the first use of the browser profile, stored with each round as dayIndex. That avoids storing calendar dates and any time zone trouble in the display.

The rule: finishing a round marks that day as played. The current streak is the count of consecutive played days ending today or yesterday. If nothing was played yesterday, the streak shows as 0 and starts again with the next round. I thought about a grace day, but the older kid said that would be cheating, so there is none.

The start screen shows a small flame icon with the number. At 0 it shows nothing, so a new kid does not see a sad zero.

Edge cases in tests: two rounds on one day count once, a gap of two days resets, a clock set backwards does not give a negative streak, and old rounds without dayIndex are ignored. 45 tests pass.

One issue: the day index is derived from the local time of the device, and the tablet's time was off by an hour at one point, which could put a round on the wrong day around midnight. It is rare and the kids play in the afternoon, so I left it.

The older kid has a streak of 4 already, and checks it before dinner.

summary: Fixed the streak flame showing the old number after a round until the page reload, by recomputing it when the end screen opens.
body:
The streak was computed once at page load and kept in a variable. After finishing the first round of a day, the start screen still showed yesterday's number until a reload, which confused the older kid.

I changed the start screen to compute the streak each time it is shown, from the stored rounds. The cost is tiny with at most 30 rounds per week kept. I also made the flame pop with a short animation when the number goes up.

A test now checks that finishing a round on a new day raises the computed value. All 46 tests pass and the fix is deployed.

summary: Added a second kid profile with its own scores, settings and streak, chosen on a profile screen at the start, and migrated the existing data to the first profile.
body:
The younger kid wanted her own scores because the older one's numbers were always higher. Storage is now keyed by profile: spellbee.profiles holds a list of {id, name}, and scores and settings live under spellbee.<id>.scores and spellbee.<id>.settings.

The migration runs once at startup. If the old keys exist and no profiles are stored, it creates a first profile named 'Player 1', moves the data to the new keys and removes the old ones. The parent can rename profiles from the parent page. I tested the migration with a copy of the real storage from the tablet, and the scores and streak survived.

The profile screen shows big buttons with the names. The last used profile is remembered, and a small 'switch' link on the start screen returns to the screen. The kids pick the same profile every time, so the screen will mostly be a speed bump, but it avoids mixing scores.

Word lists are shared. The hint rule and the voice speed stay per profile, which is what we wanted: the younger kid has a slower voice and more hints.

A bug found on the way: the best-so-far line read the scores of the previous profile after switching, because it was cached in a module variable. I removed the cache and read from storage each time.

Tests: migration, two profiles not leaking into each other, and renaming. 56 tests pass.

Still to do: deleting a profile, which I left out on purpose to avoid an accidental loss of scores. An export of the scores to a file could come with it.

summary: Wrote a plan for the offline mode: a service worker that precaches the app shell and word lists, with a version bump to refresh, before starting the work.
body:
The tablet sometimes has no network at the places where the kids practise, like the car, and the page then fails to load. A service worker is the fix, and I wrote the plan down before touching the code.

Plan:
- Use a hand-written sw.js in public, not a plugin, since the site is small and I want to understand every line.
- On install, precache the app shell: index.html, parent.html, the built JS and CSS, the sounds and the icon. Vite hashes asset names, so the list has to come from the build output; I will generate it with a small script after the build.
- Word lists are fetched network-first with a cache fallback, so a new week shows up when online and still works when not.
- The cache name carries a version string; on activate the worker deletes older caches.
- The page shows a small notice when a new version waits, with a reload button, so a game round is never reloaded in the middle.

Risks I see: a stale service worker keeping an old build alive on the tablet, which is the classic trap. To limit it, sw.js itself is served with no-cache, and I will add a way to unregister it from the settings panel.

Speech synthesis works offline only if the device voice is local. On the tablet the chosen voice is a local one, but some network voices exist, so the voice picker should prefer entries with localService set to true. I will add that to the preference order.

Order of work: first the build script for the file list, then sw.js, then the update notice, then tests on the tablet in flight mode. Nothing is changed in the code yet.

summary: Wrote the service worker that precaches the app shell and word lists, and the game now starts with the network off, though updates still need a version bump by hand.
body:
Started the offline work planned a few days ago with a hand-written service worker at public/sw.js. On install it opens a cache named spellbee-v1 and adds index.html, the built JS and CSS, the sound effects and the word list manifest. The word files listed in the manifest are added in the same step, so every week the kids can pick is available offline.

The fetch handler answers from the cache first and falls back to the network. I left out any runtime caching on purpose, because the plan said to keep the first version small. Registration happens in main.ts after the load event, so it does not slow down the first paint on the tablet.

The first run failed. The hashed file names Vite writes into dist are not known when I write sw.js by hand, so the cache list pointed to files that did not exist and addAll rejected the whole install. The console showed 'Failed to execute addAll on Cache: Request failed'. For now I fixed it by reading the file names from dist/index.html in a small script that runs after the build and writes them into the worker. It is crude, but it works for this step.

I tested on the laptop with the network panel set to offline. The page loaded, the voice read the word, the sound effects played and the score was saved to local storage. Switching weeks worked too, since all the lists were in the cache.

The activate handler deletes caches whose name differs from the current one. That keeps old files from piling up after a version bump. The bump itself is still manual: I have to edit the cache name by hand before each deploy, and I will certainly forget it at some point.

I have not tried it on the tablet yet, and that is the device that matters. Safari-like browsers can treat service workers differently, so I want to see it with airplane mode on. Next I will deploy it and check there. After that I will look at how a new version reaches a device that already has the old one cached, and how the kids learn about it.

summary: Verified the service worker on the tablet: the game starts in airplane mode, but a newly built version did not show up until the tab was closed twice.
body:
I put the tablet in airplane mode and opened the site. The start screen, the week picker and a full round with sounds all worked, so the precache covers the week JSON files as hoped.

Then I deployed a build with a visible text change and reopened the page online. The old text stayed. The new worker installed but sat in the waiting state, because the old page still controlled the clients. Only after closing the tab and opening it again, twice, did the change appear.

That is too confusing for the kids and for me. I will add an update step: when a waiting worker is found, show a small banner that says a new version is ready, and a tap on it sends a skipWaiting message and reloads. I wrote down the message names but did not code it yet.

Side finding: the tablet browser refuses to register the worker over plain http on the local network, so I can only test it on the real address.

summary: Added the update banner: a waiting service worker triggers a small 'new version' bar, and tapping it activates the worker and reloads the page.
body:
I implemented the plan from this morning. In register-sw.ts I keep the registration, listen for updatefound, and when the new worker reaches the installed state while a controller exists, I show the banner element that I added to index.html.

A tap posts {type: 'SKIP_WAITING'} to the waiting worker. In sw.js a message handler calls self.skipWaiting(). The page listens for controllerchange once and reloads, with a guard flag so that it cannot loop into several reloads, which happened in my first version.

I also made the page check for an update when it becomes visible again, with registration.update(), since the kids leave the tab open for days on the tablet. Without that, the check only happened at navigation.

Testing: I deployed v2 with a changed title and saw the banner on the laptop within a few seconds of focusing the tab. Tapping it reloaded with the new title. On the tablet it worked the same way.

One rough edge remains. If a kid is in the middle of a round when the banner shows, a tap would lose the round. The banner is small and easy to ignore, but I want it to wait until the end screen. That is for tomorrow.

I also bumped the cache name by hand for this test. I would like the build to derive the version from the file hashes, so I do not forget it.

summary: Made the cache version come from a hash of the built files and held back the update banner during a round, so nothing is lost mid-game.
body:
Two small things from yesterday's list. First, the cache version. The post-build step now computes a short sha1 over the sorted list of file names and contents and writes spellbee-<hash> as CACHE_NAME. A build with no changes gives the same name, so an unchanged redeploy does not trigger a banner. I checked this by building twice and comparing the output of sw.js with diff, and it was identical.

Second, the banner during a round. The game now exposes a small state flag, roundActive, set when the first word is read and cleared on the end screen. The banner code checks it; if a round is active it stores the pending update and shows the banner only when the end screen opens. The tap handler is unchanged.

I tested the flow by hand: start a round, deploy a new build, play through, and the bar showed up on the score table screen. I also tried leaving the page on the start screen, where the bar showed up at once as before.

A bug I found on the way: the hash included the sw.js placeholder itself in one ordering, which made the hash depend on whether the file was already patched. I now compute the hash before the replacement and exclude sw.js from the list.

Not done: what happens when a word file is fetched that is not in the precache, for instance a new week added by the parent page. That is the next topic.

summary: Switched word lists to stale-while-revalidate so a newly added week appears online without a full version bump, while old weeks stay available offline.
body:
The problem was clear: the precache holds the week files that existed at build time, but the parent exports a new JSON file each week and I copy it into public/words. With cache first, a changed manifest.json stays stale until the next version.

I changed the fetch handler to treat requests under /words/ differently. It answers from the cache at once if there is an entry, and in parallel fetches from the network and updates the cache. If neither has the file, it returns a plain 404 response so the game shows its usual error message instead of hanging.

The manifest has one catch. The page reads it on start, so a stale answer means the new week appears only on the second visit. To lessen that, I made manifest.json network first with a timeout of two seconds, falling back to the cache. Offline it still works, and online it is always fresh.

I wrote the test list for this by hand: online with a new week, offline after that week was seen, offline with a week never seen, and a slow network faked with the devtools throttle at slow 3G. All four behaved as intended. The slow case waited the two seconds and then used the cached manifest.

I did not add a Vitest test because the worker is hard to run there. I put the logic of choosing a strategy into a pure function in src/sw-routes.ts, which I can test, and added three cases for it.

Left to do: a short note for myself about how to publish a new week, and a check of what the storage limits mean for the tablet.

summary: Wrote a short publishing note in the README for adding a weekly word list and what the offline mode does with it.
body:
Added a section to README.md called how to add a week. The steps: use the parent page to export the JSON, copy it into public/words, add the entry to manifest.json, build and deploy.

I also described the offline behaviour in plain words: the shell is cached by version, the word lists are refreshed in the background, and the manifest is fetched with a two second timeout. A table lists which file uses which strategy.

While writing I noticed that the manifest entry order matters, since the game defaults to the newest week, which is the last entry. I wrote that down. No code changed today.

summary: Found that the tablet kept scores through a browser cleanup but lost the profile choice, and fixed it by requesting persistent storage and storing the profile id with the scores.
body:
The younger kid reported that the game asked who is playing again after a few days of not using it. The scores were still there, so it was not a full wipe. I looked at where the active profile id is stored: it was in sessionStorage by an old shortcut from the profile work, so closing the tab lost it.

I moved the active profile id to localStorage under the key spellbee.activeProfile. A small migration reads the old session value if present and copies it. The profile screen still shows at first start, when no value exists, and it can be opened from settings.

While I was there I looked at the offline side of storage. The service worker caches use the same quota as local storage, and the browser may clear them under pressure. I added a call to navigator.storage.persist() after the first finished round, with a check that the function exists. On the laptop, Chrome granted it without a prompt; on the tablet browser it returned false, so it may still be cleared in theory.

To see how large the cache is, I logged navigator.storage.estimate(). The app uses about 1.4 MB, most of it sounds, so the pressure risk is low.

I wrote two Vitest cases for the profile id: reading the old session key and the new key, and the empty case. Both pass, and the whole suite of 31 tests is green.

One more thing: the scores for each profile are stored in separate keys with the profile id in the name, so a lost profile id would show empty scores for a new profile. I added a short line on the profile screen listing existing profiles, which already existed, and made sure it reads the list from storage, not from memory.

I will watch whether the kids see the question again over the next weeks. If so, the tablet is wiping more than I think.

summary: Fixed the new-version bar appearing on the very first visit, when there was no old worker, so a fresh tablet no longer asks to reload for nothing.
body:
The kid noticed a 'new version' bar on the tablet right after I cleared the site data. That should not happen, because there was nothing to update. The cause was in the registration code in main.ts. It showed the banner whenever a worker reached the installed state, and on a first visit the very first worker does that too.

The fix is to show the banner only when navigator.serviceWorker.controller already exists. If there is no controller, the page is running without a worker, and the new one is simply the first. I added that check in the updatefound handler and again for the case where a worker is already waiting when the page loads.

I also found a second small problem while testing. After the first install the page was not controlled until the next load, so the first offline start of a fresh install still failed. I added clients.claim() to the activate handler. That makes the first install work offline right away, without a second visit.

I tested three cases: cleared data, an ordinary reload with the same version, and a reload after a new build. Only the last one shows the bar now. The update bar button still activates the waiting worker and reloads, and that behaved as before. I did not add an automated test, because the logic depends on the browser's worker lifecycle and the check is a single condition. A note in the code explains why the controller check is there. Left to do is deciding when the bar may appear, since it should not interrupt a round.

summary: Fixed the service worker serving the cached index.html for the parent page, which made /parent.html open the game instead.
body:
After the offline work I opened /parent.html and got the game. The fetch handler had a navigation fallback that returns index.html for every navigation request not found in the cache, and parent.html had not been added to the precache list, because it is a second entry in the Vite config.

Two fixes. The post-build step now takes all html files in dist, not only index.html. And the navigation fallback only applies to requests whose path is the root or index.html; other paths go to the network and fail normally when offline.

I confirmed that the built file list now contains parent.html and its script. With the network off, the parent page opens and the arithmetic gate works. The preview and the export button also work offline, because the export is a Blob download with no server.

I added a case to the sw-routes tests for the parent path. It failed before the change and passes now.

summary: Reviewed the offline mode as a whole, listed three remaining risks and decided that none needs more work right now.
body:
I went through the service worker code and the build step once more with fresh eyes, since it is the most fragile part of the project so far.

Risk one: the hash-based version depends on the file list, so adding a sound file without a rebuild would not update clients. That cannot happen because the list is built from dist.

Risk two: if the install step fails halfway because one file is missing, the whole worker fails to install and the old one stays. That is the safe behaviour, though silent. I added a console.error in the install catch so I can see it in devtools.

Risk three: users who have an old cache from my first test, named spellbee-v1, keep it until activate runs. The activate handler deletes everything with a different name, so it is handled.

I also timed a cold load with a primed cache on the tablet: the start screen is interactive in roughly 0.4 seconds against about 1.1 seconds before. The kids will not notice, but I do.

I decided to leave it here and move to streak and score topics next.

summary: Fixed a streak miscount after the clocks change by comparing calendar days instead of dividing milliseconds by 86400000.
body:
The older kid had a streak that reset although she played on two consecutive days. I traced it to the function that computes the gap between days: it subtracted two timestamps and divided by the milliseconds of a day. When the clocks changed, one day was 23 hours long and Math.floor gave a gap of 0 for the next morning's round in one case.

I rewrote the gap using local date parts: build a Date at local midnight for each day and use Math.round on the difference divided by a day, which absorbs the one hour. Even better is to compare a day number computed from year, month and day, which I did in toDayNumber with Date.UTC of the local parts.

I added four Vitest cases for the boundary: a normal next day, same day, a gap of two days, and the case with a 23 hour day built by feeding fixed local dates. The last one failed with the old code, as expected.

The stored streak data does not need a migration, because it keeps the last played date string and the count. The kids' current streaks are intact, and hers goes on tomorrow.

summary: Added a printable weekly report to the parent page that lists each word with tries and hints for the chosen kid, to see which words need more practice.
body:
The parent asked for something to see which words keep going wrong. I added a report section to parent.html, behind the same arithmetic gate.

The data already exists in the score history: for each finished week, each word has the number of tries and a hint flag. The report reads the profile's history, picks a week from a select box, and shows a table with word, tries and hint. Words with two misses are marked in a strong colour, and a line at the top counts them.

I also added an all weeks view that aggregates by word, because a word can come back in later weeks. This one sorts by the number of misses, so the hardest words are at the top. It handles a word written in different cases by lowercasing the key.

The print stylesheet hides the navigation and the export controls and uses black text on white, even in dark mode. I checked it with the print preview, and the table fits one page for up to about 40 rows.

The aggregate code lives in src/report.ts as a pure function, so I wrote six Vitest tests: empty history, one week, repeated words, case differences, hints counted separately, and a profile with no history. All pass.

One bug during testing: a week that was started but not finished is stored with a partial list, which made a word appear with zero tries. I now skip entries without a finished flag.

The profile picker on the parent page lists both kids and defaults to the one last active on the device. I tested with data from both kids from the real tablet, copied by the export.

The next step might be to let the parent mark difficult words so they repeat in the next week's round, but I will ask first whether this is wanted.

summary: Built an optional practice round that mixes the words missed most often from earlier weeks into the new week, after the parent said yes to the idea.
body:
The parent answered that repeating the hard words would be good, so I built it as an option, not a default. In settings a toggle called practice mix is saved per profile. When it is on, a round of 10 words becomes 8 new words plus up to 2 hard words from earlier weeks.

The selection uses the report code from last week. It aggregates misses per word over the profile's history and takes the words with at least 2 total misses, highest first. To avoid always showing the same two, I choose randomly among the top 6, and I never pick a word already in the current week.

The progress bar and the score need care. The score table stores tries per word for a week, and a mixed-in word is not part of the week. I added a field extra: true to those entries, and the table shows them in a separate small section under the week. The best-so-far comparison ignores them, so the fix from long ago about comparing different weeks is not broken.

The end screen has a line such as 'Two old words came back, one was right'. I wrote it in the same friendly style as the other messages, and it only shows when extra words were played.

Tests: I added nine cases covering few misses, no history, a word in the current week, the random choice with a seeded generator, and the extra flag. A first version crashed when the history had fewer than 2 candidates because I used slice with a negative index. Fixed and tested.

I tried it myself with copied data from the tablet: the older kid's top missed words were 'necessary' with five misses and 'separate' with three, and both came back in the first rounds.

The settings toggle is off by default, and the existing scores need no migration. I will ask the kids to try it this week.

summary: Fixed the practice mix repeating one old word twice in a round when it had been missed in several weeks.
body:
The older kid saw 'necessary' twice in one round. The aggregate key was lowercase, but the word list stored it with a capital letter in one week, and I compared the candidate to the picked ones with the raw spelling in the dedupe step.

I made the pick function lowercase for all comparisons and keep the original spelling from the most recent week for display. A test with the same word in two cases now yields one entry.

I also noticed the random choice could select the same index twice in the top six. I replaced it with a shuffle of the candidates and a take of two. That removed the need for a retry loop.

Suite is at 49 tests, all green. Deployed, and the service worker banner showed up on the tablet as designed.

summary: Looked at why the sound effects stopped on the laptop after a long idle time and found the audio context suspended, which now resumes on the next tap.
body:
The younger kid said the right sound was missing on the laptop in the evening, after the page had been open since the afternoon. The speech still worked, only the sound effects were quiet.

In devtools the AudioContext state was suspended. The browser suspends it after inactivity or when the tab is in the background for a long time. My earlier fix created the context in the start handler, but nothing resumed it afterwards.

I added a small ensureAudio function that calls context.resume() if the state is not running, and I call it on each submit of an answer, before the sound plays. Resume returns a promise, and I await it with a short guard, so the sound is not lost.

I reproduced it by leaving the tab in the background for about 15 minutes and then playing a word. Before the change it was quiet, and after the change it played at once.

No test, because the audio context is not in the Vitest setup. I noted it in the code with a comment about the browser's behaviour.

summary: Answered the user's question about how much data a kid's profile stores and added a size check in settings, since both profiles and history live in local storage.
body:
The user asked whether the scores could ever fill local storage. I measured it. A finished week takes about 600 bytes per profile, and history is capped at 52 weeks since the fix for unlimited growth, so the maximum is around 32 KB per profile. With settings and streak it is about 40 KB, against a limit of about 5 MB.

So the answer is no, not in any realistic case. The only larger item would be the practice mix, which adds a few extra entries, still small.

To make this visible I added a line at the bottom of the settings panel that shows how much space the app uses, computed by summing key and value lengths of keys that start with spellbee. It reads for example 'Stored data: 71 KB'. It is aimed at me when something looks wrong, so I kept it small and grey.

I also added an export of all data as a JSON file and an import with a file input, on the parent page behind the gate. This is a backup for the case that the tablet is reset. The import validates that the version field exists and that profile ids are strings, then asks for a confirmation before it replaces anything.

I tested the export and import round trip with data from both profiles: after importing into an empty browser profile, the scores, streak and settings were the same, checked by comparing the two exports with diff. A bad file with a missing version field showed the error message and changed nothing.

Eight new Vitest cases cover the validation function. The import itself is manual to test since it touches the file input.

summary: Replaced the hand-written service worker precache step with a cleaner build script and added a test that checks the generated file list against dist.
body:
The post-build step had grown in pieces: a Vite plugin hook, a regex replace and the hash code. I moved all of it into scripts/make-sw.ts, which runs after vite build through the npm script, and removed the plugin from vite.config.ts.

The script does five things in order: read all files in dist except sw.js and source maps, sort them, compute the hash from names and contents, write the list and the cache name into sw.js using the placeholders, and print a one line summary with the number of files and the total size. The last one is useful: the current build lists 23 files and 1.5 MB.

It fails with a clear message when a placeholder is missing, and when the file list is empty, which would otherwise create a worker that caches nothing.

I wrote a Vitest test that runs the script against a small fixture folder in a temp directory and checks three things: the list contains every fixture file, the hash is stable across two runs, and the hash changes when the content of one file changes. All three pass.

There was one surprise. On the first run, the script included .DS_Store from my machine in the precache list, so a request for that file would have been cached. I added an ignore list for dot files, and a test case for it. It is a good example of why the list should be checked and not trusted.

I built and deployed the new version and checked on the tablet that the update banner showed once and that the offline start still worked. I compared the file list in the deployed sw.js with the list on the host, and they matched.

The README section about the build now describes the script instead of the plugin. The old regex code is deleted.

Nothing is open on the offline topic now, apart from keeping an eye on the storage persistence on the tablet, which still returns false.

summary: Fixed the hint button staying active after the first letter was shown, which let a kid press it repeatedly and register several hint marks.
body:
The younger kid discovered that tapping the hint button many times added more and more hint marks to the score table. The click handler set the hint flag, but the count was incremented in the same place and the button was not disabled.

The fix has two parts. The hint is now a boolean per word, not a counter, and the button is disabled after the first use until the next word. I also made the button show 'hint used' in a lighter style so it is clear why it is dead.

A data question: old scores may hold counts above 1. The table code now treats any number greater than zero as one hint when it shows the mark. No migration is needed.

I added two tests: the word state after two hint calls, and the display of an old count of 3. Both pass. The kid's scores from last week still show a few extra marks in the aggregated report, which I will leave as they are.

summary: Wrote a plan for a second word source with sentences, so the game can read the word inside a sentence like the school tests do, and listed the open questions first.
body:
The user said the school tests give the word in a sentence, 'Please spell: separate. The two teams sat in separate rooms.' and the kids do better when they hear that. I did not code anything today but wrote the plan down.

Data: each word in the week JSON would get an optional sentence field. If it is missing, the game behaves as now. This keeps all existing weeks valid. The parent page needs a second field per word, so I think the textarea format changes to one word per line with an optional sentence after a pipe character.

Speech: the game would read the word, then the sentence, then the word again, with pauses of about 600 ms. The speech rate setting would apply to the sentence as well. I want a replay button that repeats the whole sequence, and a second one for only the word, since the younger kid gets confused by long sentences.

The open questions are these. Who writes the sentences? The school list has only words, so the parent would need to type ten sentences every week, which may be too much work. An option is a sentence template for the case that none was written, but a generic sentence would be odd for many words.

Another question is the hint: should the first letter be shown with the sentence? I think nothing changes there.

I also considered the score effect. It should not change, but the practice mix should reuse the sentence if the old week had one.

The plan has five steps: the data type and loader, the parent page format, the speech sequence, the replay buttons, and tests. I estimate two sessions for the first three.

I will ask the user about the effort of the sentences before starting. If the answer is that it is too much, I can do it only for the words that the parent chooses, which the optional field already allows.

summary: Added the optional sentence field to the word type and loader, validated it, and kept every older week file working unchanged.
body:
The user replied that sentences are fine for a few hard words each week, so the optional field is the right design. I started with step one of the plan.

In types.ts the Word type now has sentence?: string. The loader accepts both forms of an entry, a plain string as before and an object with word and sentence, and normalises them to the object. A sentence that is not a string or is longer than 200 characters is dropped with a console warning, not an error.

I added seven Vitest cases: old files, mixed entries, an empty sentence, a number as sentence and the long one. All pass, and the earlier loader tests did not need a change, which was the aim.

The game itself does not use the field yet.

summary: Changed the parent page to accept one word per line with an optional sentence after a pipe, and to export the new object form only when a sentence exists.
body:
Step two of the sentence plan. The textarea parser splits each line at the first pipe, trims both parts and ignores empty lines. A line such as 'separate | The two teams sat in separate rooms.' gives a word with a sentence, and a line with just a word stays a plain word.

The preview table got a second column showing the sentence, and a small warning if a sentence does not contain its word, which is probably a typo. I did not make it an error, because forms like 'separated' may be intended.

The export writes a plain string for words without a sentence and an object for the others, so the JSON of old weeks is unchanged and the files stay small.

I added a test file for the parser with eight cases, including a pipe inside a sentence, which stays in the sentence because only the first pipe splits. Tests pass.

Next is the speech sequence.

summary: Built the speech sequence for words with a sentence, with pauses and two replay buttons, and found that cancel between utterances broke the chain on the laptop.
body:
Step three and four of the plan. A new function speakWord in src/speech.ts builds a list of parts: the word, the sentence if there is one, and the word again. Each part is an utterance, and they are chained through the onend event with a pause of 600 ms between them using a timer.

My first version called speechSynthesis.cancel() before each part to be safe, following the fix of the paused state from a while ago. That broke the chain on the laptop: cancel fires the end event of the previous utterance in some cases, which started the next part twice and the word was read twice in a row. I moved the cancel to the start of the sequence only, and gave each sequence a token number. Callbacks from an old token are ignored, so a replay in the middle of a sequence works cleanly.

The rate setting applies to all parts. For the sentence I use the same voice, because switching voices in one sequence sounded odd and on the tablet it also caused a delay of about a second.

There are now two buttons: replay all, and word only. The word-only button cancels the running sequence and speaks the single word. Both are disabled while the first sequence plays for the first time, so a kid cannot cut it off by accident. I styled them with the existing button classes and put them on one row for the tablet, with large touch targets.

The tests cover the building of the part list with fakes: with and without a sentence, an empty sentence, and the token logic, using a fake speechSynthesis object that records calls. Eleven cases, all green, bringing the suite to 83.

I tried a real round on the laptop and on the tablet with three words that had sentences. The order was right and the pauses felt natural. On the tablet the pause before the second reading of the word seemed slightly long, so I lowered it to 450 ms for that one only.

Left: I need the parent to write real sentences for a week and watch the kids use it, then adjust the pauses if needed. The practice mix reuse of sentences from old weeks is not done yet and goes on the list.

summary: Made the practice mix reuse the stored sentence of an old word, so a hard word from an earlier week is read in its sentence again.
body:
The last item of the sentence plan. The history stores tries and hints per word, not the sentence, so the practice mix could not know it. I did not want to store text in the scores, so the lookup goes back to the week files instead.

When the mix picks an old word, it now loads the manifest entry of the week where the word was last seen and finds the word object there. If the file is cached or reachable it takes the sentence, and if not it simply plays the word alone. Loads run together with Promise.all before the round starts, and a failure of one file only drops its sentence.

I added four tests with fake loaders: a sentence found, a missing week, a failing load and a word that exists in two weeks, where the most recent one wins. All pass.

I tried it with the offline setting on the laptop and the old sentences were read as expected, since the week files are cached. This closes the sentence feature for now.

summary: Fixed the sentence speech chain on the laptop by dropping the cancel call between utterances and letting each utterance end by itself before the next starts.
body:
The chain of word, pause, sentence, pause, word had been breaking on the laptop since the sequence was built. The cause was the speechSynthesis.cancel() call that ran before each new utterance to be safe. On the laptop voice, cancel also fired the pending onend of the next item, so the chain stopped after the first word.

I removed the cancel between utterances. It is now called only when the kid taps replay or leaves the round. Each step waits for the onend of the one before it, with a 600 ms timer for the pause.

I also added a guard that ignores an onend from an utterance that is no longer the current one. This is a small counter in speech.ts. Without it, a quick double tap on replay started two chains that talked over each other.

Tested on the laptop with five words with sentences and five without. All ten played in the right order. Repeated replay taps ended with a single chain.

The tablet is still to be checked, since its voice behaves differently with pending utterances.

summary: Checked the new sentence speech sequence on the tablet and found that the sentence is read faster than the word, so the sentence now has its own rate setting.
body:
I ran the sequence on the tablet with the same ten words as on the laptop. The order was right and the chain did not break, so the fix of this morning holds there as well.

The problem was speed. The kid-friendly rate of 0.8 suits a single word, but a full sentence at 0.8 sounded rushed and the kid could not follow it. The tablet voice seems to scale rate differently for longer text.

I added a sentenceRate to the voice settings, which defaults to the word rate minus 0.1. It is stored per profile like the other settings. The settings screen got a second slider labelled 'Sentence speed'.

Tried 0.7 with the older kid and it was fine. The younger kid said it was too slow, but only because it was not a game yet. I left the default as it is.

No change was needed for words without a sentence.

summary: Wrote tests for the speech sequence with a fake speechSynthesis, covering order, pauses, replay and the stale onend case that caused the broken chain.
body:
The sequence bugs of this week were all found by hand on devices, so I wanted tests that catch them without a laptop voice. I wrote a small fake speechSynthesis in test/fakeSpeech.ts. It keeps a queue of utterances and lets the test fire onend by hand, or fire it late.

The tests cover these cases:
- a word without a sentence speaks once and finishes
- a word with a sentence speaks word, sentence, word in order
- the pause between steps uses the timer, checked with fake timers
- replay of the word does not repeat the sentence
- replay of the sentence does not repeat the word
- a double tap on replay yields one chain
- a late onend from an old utterance is ignored

The last one failed first. The guard counter was incremented after the utterance was created instead of before, so the old onend could still match. I moved the increment up and the test passed.

I also found that leaving the round while speech was running did not stop the pending timer. The next step would then fire on the end screen and speak. That is fixed with a clearTimeout in the stop function, and there is a test for it.

There are now 14 tests in total for the speech module, and they run in under a second. The fake does not model the real cancel behavior of the laptop, so the original bug itself is not covered. I added a comment in the file saying that, so nobody trusts it too much.

Next is the display side: the end screen should show the sentence with the word hidden.

summary: The end screen now shows the sentence with the word blanked out while the kid types, and the full sentence after the answer, so the kid sees the word in context.
body:
The game now has the sentence in its data, so the screen can use it. While a kid types, a line under the input shows the sentence with the word replaced by a row of underscores of the same length. After the answer is checked, the line shows the full sentence with the word in bold.

The blanking is a function in sentence.ts that does a case-insensitive match on the word. The first version used a plain replace, which broke on words that appear inside another word. In 'The cat sat on the mat' for 'at', it blanked the 'at' in 'cat'. I switched to a word-boundary regex, with the word escaped first.

Two edge cases came up. A sentence may contain the word in a different form, such as 'jumped' for 'jump'. Then there is no match and the sentence is shown without blanking. I decided that is acceptable and logged a console warning so the parent page can later flag it. A sentence that has the word twice blanks both.

There was also a layout problem. Long sentences pushed the input below the fold on the tablet in portrait. I made the sentence line smaller and limited it to three lines with a scroll.

I tested with the week of ten words, of which six have sentences. Everything showed correctly. The blank length gives a small hint of the word length, which I think is fine since the hint button exists for letters.

Still open: whether the blanked line should be shown at all for a kid who has the sentence audio. The parent will decide after trying it for a week.

summary: Added a check on the parent page that warns when a sentence does not contain its word, using the same matcher as the game, so blanking never silently fails.
body:
Following the console warning from the end screen, I moved the problem to where it can be fixed: the parent page. When the words are typed, the preview now marks each line with a sentence that does not contain the word as a whole word.

The warning is a small yellow note in the preview row: 'sentence does not contain the word'. It does not block the export, because the parent may want 'jumped' for 'jump' on purpose. The matcher is imported from sentence.ts, so the page and the game agree.

I tried it with the current week and found one real case. The sentence for 'beautiful' had a typo, 'beutiful', which would have blanked nothing. That would have shown the answer to the kid in the sentence line. The parent corrected it.

The preview has a count at the top now, such as '2 warnings'. Tests cover a clean list, a missing word, a word in another case and a word inside a longer word.

summary: Planned the next step, a spelling-by-letter mode where tiles are tapped, after the younger kid struggled with the keyboard, and listed the choices before writing code.
body:
The younger kid has trouble with the tablet keyboard: it covers half the screen and the typing is slow, which makes the game feel like a typing test instead of a spelling one. The user asked whether a tile mode would be possible. I wrote this plan before starting.

Idea: the word is shown as empty slots, and below are the letters of the word plus a few extra ones, shuffled. The kid taps a letter, it fills the next slot, and a back button removes the last one. Checking happens when all slots are full.

Open questions I listed first:
- How many extra letters? Probably 3, fewer for short words.
- Should this be a setting per profile? Yes, since the older kid wants the keyboard.
- How does it count in the scores? As the same right or wrong, but marked as tile mode, so the report can show it.
- Does the hint button still work? It would fill the first slot and take that letter from the tiles.
- What about words with a space or a hyphen? Show these characters fixed in the slots.
- Does the answer logic change? It should not. The tiles produce a string and the same checker gets it.

The last point matters most. The checker, the retry rules and the score marks should stay untouched, so the new mode is only another input component. The game currently reads the input element directly in several places, so I looked at where. It is in game.ts at four places, plus the focus code.

Plan of steps: first an Input interface with getValue, clear, focus and an onSubmit callback. Then the keyboard input behind it with no change of behavior. Then the tile input. Then the setting, then the report mark.

I estimated two sessions. No code was written in this entry, only the plan in docs/tiles-plan.md.

The user agreed with the plan and the extra letter count, and asked that the older kid's profile stay on the keyboard by default.

summary: Pulled the answer input behind a small Input interface in game.ts with no change of behavior, so the tile mode can plug in next.
body:
This is the first step of the tile plan. I defined an interface in input/types.ts with getValue, clear, focus, setDisabled and onSubmit.

The existing text field became KeyboardInput in input/keyboard.ts. It holds the element and wires the Enter key to onSubmit. game.ts now takes an Input in its constructor and no longer touches the element by id.

There were four direct uses and one hidden one: the focus after the hint, which used document.getElementById. That one I would have missed if I had not searched for the id in the whole source. It now goes through focus().

The tests that existed for the round still pass without change, which was the goal. I added two for KeyboardInput itself: Enter calls onSubmit once, and disabled ignores Enter.

I played a full week on the laptop and on the tablet and saw no difference.

summary: Built the tile input with shuffled letters, extra letters, slots and a back button, and checked it against the same answer checker as the keyboard.
body:
TileInput in input/tiles.ts shows one slot per character and a row of letter tiles. The tiles are the letters of the word plus three random extras, or two for words under four letters. The shuffle is seeded by the word and round number, so a re-render does not reorder the tiles under the kid's finger.

Tapping a tile moves it into the next free slot and greys it in the row. Back removes the last letter and frees its tile. When all slots are filled, onSubmit fires by itself. Fixed characters like hyphens are pre-filled and skipped.

Two bugs showed up while testing. A word with a double letter, such as 'letter', used the tile id of the first 't' for both, so one tile was freed twice. Tiles now have unique ids. The tiles also were too small for a thumb, so I set a minimum size of 56 px.

The checker is unchanged and receives the string. I did not yet wire the setting, so for now a query flag turns the tiles on. The tests cover double letters, back at the start and fixed characters.

summary: Added a per-profile input setting for keyboard or tiles, and made the hint button fill the first slot in tile mode and remove that letter from the tiles.
body:
The settings screen has a new choice, 'Answer with: keyboard or tiles', stored in the profile like the other settings. The existing profiles migrate with the keyboard, as the user wanted, and the younger kid's profile was switched to tiles by hand.

The hint button needed work. In keyboard mode it shows the first letter in a label. In tile mode the first slot should be filled and locked, and the matching tile greyed out. I added a lockFirst method to the Input interface. KeyboardInput implements it as a no-op, because its hint label remains.

One bug: with the hint used, back removed the locked letter too. The back button now stops at the locked slot. A test covers that.

I watched the younger kid play a week of ten words in tile mode. They finished it in less time than the week before, and no word was entered wrong by a mis-tap, as far as I could see. They did ask for the tiles to make a click sound, which I will consider with the sound effects.

The score mark for tile mode is not done yet, so the report cannot tell the modes apart.

summary: Marked each stored result with its input mode and showed it in the weekly report, with older results treated as keyboard so no history had to be rewritten.
body:
The results in local storage have tries, hints and correctness per word. I added an optional field, mode, with the value 'keys' or 'tiles', written when a word is finished. Old results have no field, and the reader treats a missing mode as 'keys', which is true for all of them, since tiles did not exist before.

The weekly report on the parent page got a small column with a K or a T for each word. When a kid used both modes in a week, the report shows both letters for the words that were tried twice.

I also thought about the practice mix, which counts the words missed most often. Should a miss in tile mode count the same as a miss with the keyboard? Tiles give the letters away, so a miss there is arguably more telling. I decided against a weighting for now, since there is too little data, and wrote the question in the plan file for later.

The size check in settings was affected a bit: each result grows by about 15 bytes. For the history of one profile, which is about 900 results, that is 13 kB, not a worry.

Tests: the writer includes the mode, the reader defaults to keys, and the report renders both letters. One test failed at first because the report sorted by word and the order of the two entries was not stable; I added the try number as a second key.

I checked the migration by loading an exported copy of the real data from the tablet into the laptop. The old results showed K everywhere and the new ones the right letters.

summary: Added a soft click sound for each tile tap, reusing the audio context resume fix, with a mute that follows the existing sound setting.
body:
The younger kid wanted the tiles to click. I added a short sound to the sound effects module, generated with a 40 ms oscillator burst at a higher pitch than the right-answer tone, so no audio file is needed.

It uses the shared audio context, so the resume-on-tap fix from earlier covers it. A tile tap is a user gesture anyway.

The click follows the existing sound on/off setting. I checked that a muted profile stays silent in tile mode. On the tablet the click was a bit loud against the speech, so I reduced the gain to 0.15.

No new tests, apart from one that checks the setting is read.

summary: Found that the tile shuffle gave the same order for the same word every week, which let a kid memorize positions, and mixed the profile and week into the seed.
body:
While watching the older kid test the tiles for a few words, I noticed that a repeated word, in the practice mix, had its tiles in exactly the same order as the last time. The seed used only the word and the round number. A kid who sees the same layout can learn the positions instead of the spelling.

I changed the seed to include the profile id and the week id, plus the day number of the round. The order stays stable while the page is open and a re-render happens, which was the reason for the seed, but it differs between sessions.

The day number is computed from calendar days, as in the streak fix, not from milliseconds. I reused that helper after reading its test once more.

Checking this took longer than the change. I wrote a test that builds the tiles for the same word with seeds from two different days and asserts that the orders differ for words of six letters or more. For short words, a collision is likely by chance, so the test does not apply there. A test that was flaky from the start would have been worse than none.

The extra letters are also drawn from the seeded generator now, so they change with the order. Before, the same three extras always came with the same word.

I also looked at the extra letters themselves. A random draw can add a letter that makes a second valid spelling, like an extra 'e' in a word that ends in 'e'. It does not cause a wrong accept, since the checker compares strings, but it could confuse a kid. I left it as is.

The tiles were checked once more on the tablet. Nothing visible changed, which is the idea.

summary: Looked at why the first word of a round sometimes spoke before the tiles appeared on the tablet, and moved the speech start after the first render.
body:
The younger kid reported that the game sometimes talks first and shows the tiles a moment later. I could reproduce it on the tablet only when the round started right after the profile screen.

The cause was ordering in game.ts. The round start called speak() and then created the input component. With the keyboard this was invisible, because the field already existed. The tile component builds many elements, and the tablet needs a few hundred milliseconds for that.

I changed the start to build the input first and call speak inside requestAnimationFrame twice, which is a known way to wait for the paint. I also made the tiles render with a fixed number of elements so the cost is small.

On the tablet, I ran 20 round starts and the tiles were visible before the speech each time. Before the change it happened 6 times out of 20.

A test is not practical for a paint, so I wrote a note in the code and a line in the plan file.

There is a small extra delay now of about 30 ms, which no one will notice.

summary: Wrote a plan for a progress view that shows how each word improves across weeks, after the user asked whether the kids are actually getting better.
body:
The user asked a plain question: are the kids getting better, or just getting used to the game? The weekly report shows one week, which cannot answer it. Before building anything I wrote down what the data can say.

What is stored: for each word, each try, with hints, mode and the week. Since the practice mix brings old words back, some words have several weeks of data. That makes a first useful number: for words that appeared in at least two weeks, how many were right on the first try the second time, compared with the first time.

I ran a quick script over the exported data of both profiles. For the older kid, 31 words appeared more than once, and 24 were right the second time when only 15 had been the first time. For the younger kid, there were 18 such words, going from 6 to 11. These are small numbers but they point the right way.

A second number is the share of first-try-correct words per week. It is noisy because the weeks differ in difficulty. The word lists are from the school, so I cannot control it.

Proposed view on the parent page:
- a line per week with the share of first-try-correct
- a list of words improved and words still missed
- a note that hints and tile mode are shown separately, so help does not look like skill
