Things I would not do: no ranking between the kids, and no score that mixes tiles and keyboard.

Open question: whether the kids should ever see it. The user said not for now. It is a parent tool.

The plan is in docs/progress-plan.md. The code comes in the next sessions.

summary: Built the progress calculations as a pure module with tests, covering first-try share per week and words that improved or are still missed.
body:
I wrote src/progress.ts with no DOM or storage code, so it is easy to test. The input is the list of results, and the functions are weekShare, improvedWords and stuckWords.

weekShare returns for each week the number of words and how many were right on the first try without a hint. A word with a hint does not count as clean, which follows the earlier decision of a hint being a separate mark.

improvedWords takes the words that appear in two or more weeks and compares the first and the latest appearance. A word is improved if it was not clean before and is clean now. stuckWords are words that were not clean in the latest two appearances.

The tests used small fixtures:
- a word seen once is neither improved nor stuck
- a word that goes from missed to clean is improved
- a word missed twice in a row is stuck
- a hint counts as not clean
- results without a week field are skipped

The last case came from the real data. A few results from the first weeks, before the weeks had ids, have no week, and the first version of the code crashed on them. I now skip them and count them in a separate skipped value so the page can say so.

I ran the module on the exported data again and the numbers matched my script from before: 24 of 31 and 11 of 18. That check was worth doing, because my quick script had treated hints differently and gave 26 at first. The difference was 2 words that were right with a hint. The module is the one to trust.

Sorting is by week order, not by timestamp, because a week can be played late. I used the week id for ordering, which is an ISO-like string and sorts correctly.

Nothing is shown on the page yet. That is next.

summary: Added the progress section to the parent page with a week table and lists of improved and stuck words, and kept tile and keyboard results apart as planned.
body:
The parent page has a new block under the report, with a kid chooser that is shared with the existing one. It renders from the progress module.

The week table shows the week id, the number of words, and the clean first-try share as a number and a simple bar made of a div. I used no chart library, since the page is meant to stay small and offline.

The lists of improved and stuck words are plain text, with the weeks in which each was missed. A skipped note appears when old results had no week.

To keep the modes apart, the table has a switch, 'all / keys / tiles'. For the younger kid, who changed to tiles in the middle, the keys-only view shows the early weeks and the tiles-only view the later ones. Seeing both next to each other is the honest way to read it, and I wrote one line of help text under the switch.

The layout was checked on the laptop only, because the parent uses it there. A table with 40 weeks scrolls inside its box. I did not test with that many weeks, only with a synthetic fixture of 60, and it was fine.

summary: Fixed the progress table counting a week twice when a profile had played it in both modes, by grouping on the week id before the mode filter.
body:
The parent saw a week listed two times for the younger kid, once with 10 words and once with 4. The cause was in the table code, which grouped on week plus mode in the all view. The all view should group only on the week.

I changed the group key and applied the mode filter before grouping only for the keys and tiles views. A test now has a fixture with one week played in both modes and asserts that the all view has a single row with 14 tries counted properly.

While there, I noticed the share was computed per word, but a word played in both modes in one week appeared twice. I now take the last result of a word within a week for the share. This matches how the report prints it.

I checked the numbers again by hand for one week: 10 words, 7 clean, which is 70 percent, and the page showed the same.

summary: Reviewed the tile and progress work from the last two weeks, found two small gaps in the offline cache and the export, and fixed both.
body:
After this much new code, I read through the diff since the sentence work began to look for things that only show up later.

First, the offline cache. The build script generates the file list for the service worker, and the new modules are bundled, so nothing was missed there. But the tiles use no new assets, and the sound is generated, so the offline mode is fine. I ran the test that compares the list with dist and it passed. I also loaded the game with the network off on the tablet and played a tile round. It worked.

Second, the data export in settings. It lists the profile data for backup, and it did not include the new mode field in its documented format, because the format note in the README was written before. The export itself does include it, since it dumps the objects, but the README was wrong. I corrected the README.

Third, a real gap: the import of a backup validated results and rejected unknown fields. A backup made now could not be imported on an older build, which is expected, but a backup with the mode field could not be imported on the current one either, since the validator was strict. I loosened the validator to accept mode as keys or tiles and nothing else, and added a test for a backup with both old and new results.

I also looked at the size check in settings. With the mode field it grows slightly, but nothing near the limits of local storage.

No other findings. I decided that the review does not need a plan for more work.

summary: Looked into a report that the game read a word wrong on the tablet after an update, found the voice list loading late, and made the voice choice wait for it.
body:
The user said the younger kid's tablet read a word with a very different voice after the browser updated, deeper and slower. I checked the settings and the voice name stored in the profile was still the same one as before.

The cause: the browser fills speechSynthesis.getVoices() asynchronously. After the update it took longer, and on a fresh start the list was empty when the game picked the voice. The code then fell back to the default voice without telling anyone, and it did not try again.

How I found it: I logged the list length at game start on the tablet. It printed 0 on the first call and 23 after the voiceschanged event. The previous code read the list once.

The fix in voice.ts:
- a function whenVoicesReady returns a promise that resolves when the list is non-empty or the voiceschanged event fires
- a timeout of 1500 ms resolves anyway, so the game never hangs on a device with no voices
- the stored voice is looked up after that, by name first and then by language
- if the name is not found, the settings screen shows a small note that the voice changed

The round start waits for the promise only the first time. Later rounds use the loaded list.

I wrote tests with the fake speech object from before. It now has a voice list that can be filled late. The cases are an immediate list, a late list, no list at all with the timeout, and a stored name that does not exist anymore.

One more thing I noticed is that matching by language alone could choose a different voice than the one the kid knows. I made the language fallback prefer a voice from the same language and region, such as en-GB over en-US, when the stored voice had that region.

On the tablet, I restarted the browser ten times and the right voice was used each time. Before the fix, it was wrong in 4 of 10.

The settings note for a changed voice was checked by renaming the stored voice in the profile by hand, and it appeared. Nothing is left from this report, but I will keep an eye on it after the next browser update.

summary: Added a small voice preview button in settings so a parent can hear the chosen voice and speed, since a changed voice is easy to miss.
body:
After the voice bug I wanted the settings to make a voice problem obvious. Next to the voice choice there is now a play button that says a sample word and a sample sentence with the current word speed and sentence speed.

It uses the same speak function as the game, with the stored settings of the chosen profile, so it also proves that the whole path works. The sample is 'Listen carefully. The weather is lovely today.'

I tested it with both profiles, whose speeds differ, and each one sounded as expected. The button is disabled until the voice list is ready, using the same promise as in the game.

A test checks that the button calls speak with the profile's rates. The preview does not count in any score or stat.

summary: Found that the tile mode on the small tablet put the tiles in two rows that pushed the slots off screen, and fixed the layout so both stay visible without scrolling.
body:
The younger kid reported that after four or five letters she could not see the slots any more. I reproduced it on the tablet in portrait: words of eight letters plus the extra letters made two rows of tiles, and the slot row scrolled out of view above them. The cause was a fixed tile size of 64px in the stylesheet that did not account for the extra letters.

The tile size now comes from the available width divided by the number of tiles in a row, with a minimum of 44px so a finger can still hit them. Slots and tiles share the same size variable, so they line up. The tile area wraps into at most two rows, and the slot row is pinned above it with position sticky.

I checked words of 4, 8 and 12 letters in portrait and landscape on the tablet and on the laptop at a narrow window. The 12-letter word is the tightest case, and it fits with tiles of 46px. The back button and the hint button stayed reachable in every case. What is left is a long word with many extra letters on a very small phone screen, which the kids do not use, so I left it alone.

summary: Answered the user's question on whether the tiles should be the default for new profiles and decided to keep the keyboard default, with a short setup choice instead.
body:
The user asked whether new profiles should start in tile mode, since the younger kid likes it. I looked at what a new profile does today: it gets the keyboard, because that was the default for migration.

The argument for tiles is that a young child without keyboard skill gets a better first experience. The argument against is that tiles show the letters, so a new profile would never see the real task unless the parent changes the setting.

I did not change the default. Instead, the profile creation screen now has one extra question, 'How does this kid like to answer?', with two big buttons for keyboard and tiles, and it stores the choice. The parent can still change it later in the settings.

The screen uses the same strings as the settings choice. A test creates a profile with each button and reads the stored mode.

I mentioned to the user that the progress page keeps the modes apart, so a choice of tiles at the start does not hide anything.

summary: Fixed tile mode accepting a double tap on one tile as two letters, which filled two slots with a single letter and marked correct words wrong.
body:
The older kid noticed that some words came out wrong even though he had tapped the right tiles. I found the cause by logging the tap events on the tablet: a fast double tap fired two touch events on the same tile before the re-render removed it from the tray. The second event placed the same letter again, so a word like 'letter' ended up as 'lletter' or a slot got an empty duplicate.

The fix marks a tile as used the moment it is tapped, before any state update, and ignores further taps on a used tile. The tile model keeps an id per tile instead of finding it by its letter. Words with repeated letters would otherwise have been ambiguous, since two identical letters looked the same to the old lookup.

I added three tests to the tile input tests. One is a double tap on the same tile, one is a word with repeated letters tapped in turn, and one is the back button after a double tap. All three failed before the change and pass now. I also tried them by hand on the tablet with fast tapping, and the slots stayed correct. Results that were already stored with a wrong mark stay as they are, because there is no reliable way to tell which ones were caused by the bug, and I noted that in the weekly report notes for the parent.

summary: Updated dependencies for Vite and TypeScript, fixed two type errors that appeared with the newer compiler, and checked that the build and the offline cache list stayed identical.
body:
A patch-level update of Vite and a minor one of TypeScript were waiting. I did them together since the project is small, and ran the build and the tests after each.

Vite built without a change. TypeScript reported two new errors, both in the speech code. The fake speech object in the tests did not fully implement the SpeechSynthesisVoice type that the newer compiler checks more strictly, and one callback in voice.ts had an implicit any. I added the missing fields to the fake and typed the callback.

The cache list test compared the generated file list with dist and passed, but the hashed file names changed, as expected with a new bundler. The cache version hash changed, so the update banner will show once on the tablets, which is the intended behavior.

I built, served the site and played a round with the keyboard and one with tiles. Both worked. The bundle size went from 61.2 kB to 60.8 kB, gzipped.

summary: Planned the streak feature before writing code: what counts as a played day, how skips work, where the count is stored, and which cases the tests must cover.
body:
The user asked yesterday for a streak, a count of days in a row on which a kid played a round, to get the kids to play on the days without school words. Before writing anything I wrote the plan and listed the open questions first, because a streak is easy to build and easy to make unfair.

The first question was what counts as a played day. I decided that one finished round is enough, and that a round left half-way does not count. The hook therefore belongs after the end screen is reached, not at the start of a round.

The second question was the day boundary. The tablet clock is the only clock available, so a day is the local calendar day as the browser reports it, stored as a plain day string and not as a timestamp. That avoids trouble with time zones and with rounds played just after midnight.

The third question was what happens when a day is missed. A hard reset after one missed day is harsh for a seven-year-old, so the plan gives one free skip: a single missed day does not break the streak, but two in a row do. The free skip comes back after the next seven days of play. I noted that this rule is the part the user should confirm, and wrote it down as the default.

The fourth question was a clock that jumps backwards, which happens when a kid fiddles with the tablet settings. The plan says that a last-played day in the future is ignored and the streak is neither raised nor reset in that case.

For the structure I chose three steps. First a pure module that takes the stored state and today's day string and returns the new state, with no access to storage or to the clock, so it can be tested with plain values. Second, storage per profile under its own key, with safe reading of missing or broken data. Third, the display on the start screen and the best streak on the parent page.

The tests to write first are: two rounds on the same day, a skipped day, a free skip used and then not available, a missed pair of days, a clock set backwards, and a first ever round. I also decided that the streak shows no message when it resets, since a sad message does not help a kid.

Nothing was changed in the code today. The next entry is the pure module with its tests, and the user's answer on the free skip rule can still change the numbers there.

summary: Wrote the streak day logic as a pure module with tests for same-day play, a skipped day, a free skip and a clock set backwards.
body:
Added src/streak.ts with one function, updateStreak(state, today), returning a new state and no side effects. The state holds lastDay, current, best and a skipUsedWeek id. Days are compared as local date strings converted to whole day numbers, so month ends need no special case.

The rules follow the plan. Playing twice in one day changes nothing. Playing the day after lastDay adds one. A gap of exactly two days uses the free skip if it was not used in this week, and then adds one. Any larger gap, or a second skip in the same week, resets current to one.

I decided the free skip is per school week id, the same id the word lists use, which means no new calendar logic. That was the one choice from the plan I settled here, and the user had already agreed to it.

The tests cover eleven cases. The interesting one is the clock set backwards: today is earlier than lastDay. The function returns the state unchanged, so a wrong tablet clock cannot break the best value. Another case checks that best never drops when current resets.

All eleven pass under the existing test runner. I also ran a short random sequence of 500 play days against a simple reference loop to check there was no drift, and both gave the same result. Storage is next, and the start screen after it.

summary: Stored the streak per profile under its own local storage key, with safe handling of missing or broken data and a hook after each finished round.
body:
Added src/streakStore.ts with load and save functions keyed by the profile id. The key is separate from the results, so the export and the weekly report stay as they were. If the stored text is missing or does not parse, the loader returns a fresh state instead of throwing, because a thrown error at start would leave the page blank on the tablet.

I also validate the shape: numbers must be finite and non-negative, otherwise the state is reset. I tested this by writing a broken value by hand in the browser console and reloading, and the game started normally with a zero streak.

The update is called from the round-finished handler in game.ts, after the result is saved. Putting it after the save means a failure in the streak code cannot lose a score. I wrapped the call in a try and log a warning only.

One detail: a round counts as finished only when all words are answered. A kid who quits halfway gets nothing, which matches the plan. I checked this by quitting through the back button on the laptop and the counter did not move.

No display yet. The next step is the start screen with the count next to the name.

summary: Showed the streak on the start screen as a small flame count per profile, plus the best streak on the parent page, with no message when it resets.
body:
The start screen now shows a flame and the current count beside each profile name. When the count is zero the flame is hidden, so a reset shows nothing sad, which is what the user wanted for the younger kid.

The current value shown must account for time passing. If the last play was three days ago the stored current is stale, but it only resets on the next play. So the display uses a small helper that returns zero when the gap is above the allowed skip, without saving. Otherwise a kid would see a streak that is already dead.

On the parent page I added one line per profile with current and best. The text is plain: Best streak: 9 days. I reused the existing table styles and added no new CSS file.

I checked both screens on the tablet in portrait and landscape. The flame fits next to long names, but one test name of 20 characters wrapped, so I added an ellipsis rule with a max width. Offline cache list is unchanged because no new asset was added, only code that gets bundled.

The streaks feature is now complete apart from a short note in the parent page help text, which I left for later.

summary: Planned the second kid profile work as a review of what is already per profile, and found the settings and the practice mix still use shared keys.
body:
The profile code exists in part, since the tile input and the streak already use a profile id. Before building the full second profile feature I grepped for every local storage key to see what is shared. The list had eleven keys.

Three were still global: the sound mute, the voice choice, and the practice mix history. Sound mute can stay global because it is a device preference. The voice and speed should be per profile, because the older kid wants a faster voice and the younger one wants it slow. The practice mix history must be per profile or one kid's hard words show up in the other's rounds.

I wrote the migration idea down: on first load after the change, copy the global voice and history values into the first profile's keys and leave the old keys alone. That way nothing is lost if I need to roll back. The first profile is the one that existed before, so that is safe.

Open questions for the user: whether the profile switch needs a pin (I suggested no, the kids are honest enough), and whether both profiles share the weekly word list (yes, same school class level for now). The user answered both in chat during the session.

Steps: per-profile voice and speed, per-profile mix history with migration, a profile picker on the start screen, then add and rename on the parent page.

summary: Made voice and speed per profile with a one-time copy of the old global values into the first profile, leaving the old keys untouched.
body:
Moved the voice name and rate into the profile settings object. The loader now reads profile.voice first and falls back to the old global key, so a profile without values still works.

The migration runs once at start. It checks a flag key, and if not set, copies the global voice, rate and sentence rate into the first profile and sets the flag. The old keys stay, as planned, in case of a rollback.

I tested with a fake local storage holding only the old keys, and the first profile got the values while a second test profile got defaults. A second run did nothing because of the flag.

summary: Made the practice mix history per profile and found the hard-word list was written under the old key from two places, so both now use one accessor.
body:
The practice mix reads a history of missed words to choose hard words from earlier weeks. I moved it to a per-profile key with the same copy-once migration as the voice settings, run by the same flag.

While searching for writers I found the old key was written from two places: the round-finished handler and the import code on the parent page. The import path would have kept writing to the global key and the second profile would never have seen it. I replaced both with one accessor, historyFor(profileId), in src/history.ts.

The import case matters because the user restores a backup after a tablet reset. I ran an import of a backup from the older format and checked that the words land in the first profile's history only.

Tests: five new ones for the accessor covering empty, migrated, and two profiles that stay apart. All pass, and the earlier mix tests needed only a profile id argument.

I also looked at the weekly report. It reads results by profile already, so nothing changed there. Next is the picker on the start screen.

summary: Built the profile picker on the start screen with big name buttons, remembered the last profile, and fixed a crash when the stored profile had been deleted.
body:
The start screen now opens with a picker when more than one profile exists, with one large button per kid and the streak flame beside each name. With only one profile the picker is skipped, so the game starts as before.

The last chosen profile id is stored and preselected on the next start. A tap on the name button starts the game for that profile directly, because a second confirm step was too slow for the younger kid in a trial on the tablet.

I tested deleting a profile by hand in the stored data and found a crash: the stored last id pointed to nothing, and the code read name of undefined. The fix checks that the id exists in the list and otherwise falls back to the first profile. I added a test for it.

A second issue showed up on the small tablet. With three test profiles, the buttons ran under the bottom bar. I switched the layout to a wrapped flex row with a max height and scroll only in the picker area. Two real profiles fit without scroll.

The back-to-picker button in the game header had no accessible label, so I added one while I was there. Switching profile mid-round discards the unfinished round, which I confirmed matches the quit behavior from the streak work.

Next step is add and rename on the parent page.

summary: Added create, rename and delete for profiles on the parent page, with delete asking for a typed name so a kid cannot erase the other's scores by accident.
body:
The parent page has a new Profiles section listing each profile with a rename field and a delete button. Create takes a name and gives the new profile defaults: keyboard input, the shared voice, an empty history and no streak.

Names are trimmed, limited to 20 characters, and must be unique ignoring case. Duplicates show an inline message instead of an alert. I tested with names that differ only by a trailing space, and the trim catches it.

Delete was the careful part. The button opens a small panel asking the parent to type the profile name. Only then are the profile's keys removed: results, history, streak and settings. I wrote a function, removeProfileData(id), which lists those keys in one place, and a test checks that no key containing the id is left after it runs.

I also made it impossible to delete the last remaining profile, since the game needs one. The button is disabled with a short hint.

While testing I noticed that renaming kept the id stable, as designed, so the scores follow the kid. Before this I had worried the id might be derived from the name. It is not, it is a random short string from creation.

The export now includes the profile list. I checked a round trip: export, clear storage, import, and both profiles came back with their scores and streaks. The streak keys were not in the export yet, so I added them and the round trip then matched exactly.

Cache list unchanged. The second kid profile work is complete apart from a pass on the report page.

summary: Checked the weekly report with two profiles and fixed it showing the other kid's results in the progress lists when switching profiles quickly.
body:
I played a full week as each profile on the laptop, then opened the report and the progress section. The weekly table was right, but the improved and stuck word lists showed words of the other profile after I switched profiles twice without a reload.

The cause was a module level cache in the progress code that held the result list from the first call. It was keyed by nothing. I keyed it by profile id and, since the calculation is cheap with a few hundred results, then removed the cache altogether.

I added a test that computes progress for profile A, then B, then A again, with different data, and checks that each result matches a fresh computation.

The report heading now includes the profile name so a parent can tell which kid they are looking at. That was a small gap noticed during the check. Everything else in the report matched the expected counts from my notes. The user will try it with both kids this weekend.

summary: Planned the offline mode with a service worker, listing what must be cached, how updates reach the kids, and the risk of stale files being served for weeks.
body:
The user wants the game to work on the tablet at the grandparents, where there is no wifi. This session was the plan only, with notes from reading how the site is built.

What must be cached: the HTML page, the bundled JS and CSS with their hashed names, the sound files, the icons, and the word list JSON files. The speech comes from the browser and the device voices, so nothing is needed there, but I noted that some browsers use network voices that would fail offline. The voice choice should prefer a local voice when offline, which I will check later.

The main risk is stale code. A service worker that serves old files forever means a fixed bug never reaches the tablet. Two options: cache first with a version name that changes on each build, or network first with cache fallback. For a game that is mostly opened at home with wifi, network first with a short timeout and cache fallback is simpler and keeps updates fast. I chose that for the page and the word lists, and cache first for hashed assets, which never change under the same name.

The word lists matter most. A new week's file must arrive when online, so the list file names are not hashed and go through the network first path.

The cache list needs generating at build time. Vite writes a manifest, and a small build step can turn it into the file list the worker uses. Doing it by hand would drift.

Open questions: how the kid knows the game is offline (a small badge, probably), and how to clean up old caches on a new version (delete every cache name not equal to the current one in the activate step).

Steps: the build step that writes the file list, the worker with the two strategies, registering it, a test in airplane mode on the tablet, and the offline badge. Starting with the build step next.

summary: Added a build step that turns the Vite manifest into a precache list file, so the service worker never relies on a hand-written list of files.
body:
Wrote scripts/make-precache.ts, run after vite build. It reads dist/.vite/manifest.json, collects every emitted file, adds the sound files, icons and the word list files found in dist/words, and writes dist/precache.json with a build id from a hash of the file names and sizes.

The build id changes only when content changes, so an unchanged rebuild gives the same id. I ran the build twice and the ids matched. Then I changed one word and the id changed.

The list has 34 files. The package script now chains the build and this step. The worker itself comes next.

summary: Wrote the service worker with cache-first for hashed assets, network-first with a three second timeout for the page and word lists, and cleanup of old caches.
body:
public/sw.js reads precache.json on install and stores every file in a cache named with the build id. Hashed assets are answered from the cache first. The page and the word lists try the network for three seconds, then fall back to the cache.

The activate step deletes every cache whose name differs from the current one. I used skipWaiting and clients.claim so a new version takes over at the next open, not one open later.

On the laptop I loaded the page, switched the browser to offline in the dev tools and reloaded, and the game worked with its sounds. One gap: the precache.json fetch itself is not cached when the first install happens offline, which is acceptable since install needs a network anyway. Registration and the real tablet test are next.

summary: Registered the service worker only in production builds and tested airplane mode on the tablet, where the game ran but the first word spoke with a network voice that failed.
body:
Registration now happens after the load event and only when the build is a production build, so the dev server is not affected by cached files.

On the tablet I opened the game with wifi, closed it, turned on airplane mode and reopened it. The page, the tiles and the sounds all worked, and the word lists loaded from the cache.

The problem was the speech. The default voice on this tablet is a network one, and offline the first word was silent with no error shown to the kid. The speech event gave an error of network. I changed the voice selection to prefer a voice whose localService flag is true when navigator.onLine is false, and to listen for the error event and retry once with a local voice.

After that the words were read offline in the local voice, a little less pleasant but clear. I did not yet add the offline badge, which is the next step. I also want to check that a score saved offline survives, but that is plain local storage and should be fine.

summary: Registered the service worker only for production builds and found the first word spoke with a network voice that failed in airplane mode on the tablet.
body: The service worker is now registered from a small function in main.ts that runs only when the build is a production build, so the Vite dev server never gets a worker that caches stale files while I edit. The function waits for the load event, so registration does not compete with the first render. A failed registration is caught and logged once and does not stop the game. I built the site, served the output locally, and checked in the browser tools that the worker installed and the precache list was filled. Then I put the site on the tablet and turned on airplane mode. The page, the word list and the scores all loaded from the cache, and a round could be played to the end. The first word, however, was spoken in silence, and the console showed a speech error. The default voice on that tablet is a network voice, and it cannot work without a connection. The other words in the round were read by a local voice, which means the voice choice falls back, but only after the first failure. I did not fix this today. The likely fix is to prefer a voice marked as local when the browser reports no connection, and I wrote that down as the next step together with a test on the tablet.

summary: Found that a new week's word list did not appear on the tablet after an update because the network-first timeout fired on slow wifi, and made the list refresh in the background.
body:
The user reported that this week's words were missing on the tablet, which still showed last week's list, although the parent page had the new ones. The tablet was on weak wifi in the kitchen.

I reproduced it by throttling the network to slow 3G in the dev tools. The worker waited three seconds, the timeout won, and the cached old list was returned. The fetch kept running but its result was dropped, so nothing updated until the next open.

The fix is a stale-while-revalidate step for the word lists. The worker answers with the network result if it comes within the timeout, otherwise with the cache, but in either case lets the fetch finish and writes the response into the cache. I used event.waitUntil on the fetch promise so the worker is not stopped early.

That helps the next open, but the kid would still see the old list in this session. So I added a message from the worker to the page when a word list cache entry changes, and the page reloads the list if no round is running. During a round it waits until the round ends.

I tested with the throttle: first load showed the old list, and about eight seconds later the start screen updated to the new week without a reload. During a round nothing changed until the end.

One more check was that a failed fetch, for example a 404 on a week that does not exist yet, must not overwrite a good cache entry. I added a response.ok check before writing.

I also added a test for the cache write logic by pulling the decision into a small function, shouldStore(response). The user will check the tablet in the kitchen tomorrow.

summary: Confirmed on the kitchen tablet that the new week list now arrives after a slow start, and noted the reload waits correctly until a round ends.
body:
The user tried the tablet in the kitchen with the weak wifi. The first open showed last week's list, as expected under the timeout, and around ten seconds later the start screen showed the new words without any touch.

I then started a round and, from the laptop, published a small change to a list file to see what happens during a round. The round continued with its words and nothing flickered. After the last word the end screen appeared, and when the kid went back to the start screen, the changed list was loaded.

One thing I noticed is that the weekly report counts results by week id and not by list content, so a list changed mid-week does not split the results. That is the behavior I wanted.

No code change this session. The offline mode is considered complete: cache, worker, update path, badge and local voice. I wrote a short note in the repository readme about how the precache list and the two strategies work, since I will forget it.

summary: Reviewed the profile and offline work of the last weeks and fixed three gaps: the old caches stayed after a rename of the cache prefix, a missing export key, and a stale label.
body:
The user asked for a review pass over the second profile and offline changes before moving on. I read through the diffs of the last two weeks and ran the build and the tests, which all passed.

Gap one: when I renamed the cache prefix to include the build id format, caches from the first test version, with a different prefix, were not matched by the cleanup. The activate step deleted only names starting with the new prefix. I changed it to delete any cache that is not the current name, which is what the plan said. On the tablet I found one leftover cache of about 1.2 MB and it was gone after the next open.

Gap two: the export included profiles and streaks but not the per-profile voice settings, so a restore after a reset gave default voices. I added the voice key and the sentence rate to the export list and the import, and checked a full round trip with two profiles that have different voices.

Gap three: the settings page still said Voice for the whole game, although the voice is per profile now. I changed the label to include the profile name.

I also looked for places that could throw in private browsing, where local storage may be unavailable. The loaders all use a try block, except the new offline badge preference, which did not exist, so nothing to fix there. The streak store has a try already.

Two things I did not change. The picker does not sort profiles, it uses creation order, which is fine for two kids. And the worker does not limit the cache size, which is fine with 34 files and a few word lists.

The tests number 71 now and the build output is the same size as before apart from the added lines. The next work will be small polish items, and the user mentioned the sound effects for a streak milestone.

summary: Added a short happy sound for reaching a streak of 5 and 10 days, played once on the end screen and covered by the existing mute.
body:
The user wanted a small reward when a streak reaches a milestone. I made one short sound by layering the existing right-answer sound at two pitches, saved as a small file, because I did not want to add a larger asset.

The end screen checks whether the streak value changed this round and now equals 5 or 10. If so, it plays the sound once. The check uses the old and new state returned by the update function, so a replay on the same day does not trigger it again.

The sound follows the mute setting and the audio context resume fix. The file is in the precache list through the build step, which I confirmed in precache.json. A test covers the milestone check.

summary: Answered the user's question of whether the kids' data could be lost when the browser clears storage, and added a reminder on the parent page to export a backup after each month of use.
body:
The user asked what happens to the scores if the tablet clears site data. The honest answer is that everything is lost, since scores, streaks, profiles and settings are all in local storage and there is no server. I checked whether the storage persist API is available: navigator.storage.persist exists in the tablet browser, and it returned false at first, meaning the data is not protected from clearing under storage pressure.

I added a call to persist on the first start, which some browsers grant silently for installed or often used sites. On the tablet it was granted after the site was added to the home screen, and on the laptop it was not. So it helps but cannot be counted on.

The second measure is the backup. The export already exists on the parent page, but nobody remembers it. I added a line that shows the days since the last export and turns a warning color after 30 days. The export time is saved in its own key when the file is created.

I considered an automatic download of a backup, but browsers block repeated downloads without a tap, so a reminder is the realistic choice.

A test checks the days-since helper, including the case with no export yet, which shows a message to make the first one. I also checked that the import does not overwrite the last export time with an older value from the file.

The user exported a backup right away and saved it in the family cloud folder. Nothing else changed this session, and the cache list is the same.

summary: Fixed the backup reminder showing a huge number of days on a fresh install because the missing export time was read as zero.
body:
The user opened the parent page on the laptop with a clean profile and saw a warning that the last backup was 19,000 days ago. The missing key was converted with Number(), which gave 0, and zero is the start of the clock count.

I changed the loader to return null when the key is missing or not a positive finite number, and the display to show Make your first backup in that case. The existing test covered no export, but it called the helper with null directly, so it did not catch the loader.

I added a test for the loader with an empty storage and one with a broken value like abc. Both give null now. The warning color applies only when a real time is more than 30 days old.

I also read the import path again, where the export time is compared as numbers, and made sure a null value in the file is ignored. All tests pass.

summary: Looked into a slow start on the old tablet and found the sound files were decoded all at once on load, so decoding now happens on the first tap and in sequence.
body:
The user said the old tablet takes about six seconds before the start screen reacts. I profiled it with the remote dev tools and saw a long task of about 4 seconds right after load.

The cause was the audio setup. All eight sound files were fetched and decoded in one Promise.all, and decoding on that device is slow and blocks the main thread. The start screen was drawn, but taps were not handled until it finished.

I moved the decoding to the first user tap, which is needed anyway for the audio context to resume, and decode the files one after another, with the right and wrong answer sounds first because they are needed soonest. Files not yet decoded when needed are skipped for that play instead of waiting.

After the change the start screen reacted within about one second on the tablet, and the first round had both answer sounds ready. The tile click sound was ready after the second word. That is acceptable.

The tests for the sound module needed a fake audio context with a decode counter, and I added one for the order of decoding.

summary: Planned a small redesign pass after the user said the game looks plain, listing what to change in colors, fonts and the end screen, and what to leave as it is for the kids.
body:
The user said the older kid finds the game boring to look at and the younger one likes it as is. So this session was a plan, with a look at every screen on the laptop and the tablet, and notes on what to change.

The start screen has a plain white background with default buttons. I proposed a soft background color per profile, chosen by the kid from six colors in the settings, so each feels the game is theirs. The color would be stored in the profile settings with a default.

The font is the system font. A rounded font would be friendlier, but a web font adds a file and a loading flash, and has to go in the offline cache. I suggested a system rounded stack first (ui-rounded and a fallback) which costs nothing, and only adding a font file if that looks poor on the tablet.

The round screen should stay calm. The word area, the input and the slots must not move, because the younger kid depends on the places of things. I listed what must not change: the position of the replay buttons, the size of the tiles and the hint button location.

The end screen is the one with room for change. It shows the result, the sentence and a button. I proposed a row of stars for the first-try share, one to three, and a short line that names the best word of the round. No text that says the kid failed.

The contrast needs a check. Several colors in the six-color choice might make the white text hard to read, so each needs a ratio test of at least 4.5. I wrote the idea of a small script that computes the ratio at build time and fails if one color is below it.

Open questions for the user: whether the colors should affect the buttons too, or only the background, and whether the stars may use animation. The user wanted the background and buttons both, and no animation on the start screen but a short one at the end.

Steps: the color setting with its contrast check, the font stack, the end screen stars, and a check on both devices. The color setting comes first.

summary: Added a per-profile color choice of six colors with a contrast check script that fails the build when white text on a color is below the 4.5 ratio.
body:
Added a color field to the profile settings with six named values and a default of the current light blue. The settings page shows six round swatches, and a tap sets the color at once and stores it. The start screen and the round screen read it into a CSS custom property on the root element, so the buttons and the background follow the same value.

The contrast script, scripts/check-contrast.ts, computes the relative luminance of each color against white text using the standard formula and exits with an error if any ratio is under 4.5. The first run failed for two colors: the yellow gave 1.9 and the light green gave 2.4. I darkened the yellow to an amber and the green to a deeper tone, and they came out at 4.9 and 4.6.

The script is part of the build chain after the precache step. I also added a test for the luminance function with known values, black on white at 21 and white on white at 1.

The older profile loads without a color and gets the default, so no migration is needed. The export includes the color key now, and I checked a round trip with two different colors.

On the tablet, the colors looked fine in daylight, and the younger kid immediately picked the amber. The font stack and the end screen stars are next.

summary: Built the end screen redesign with one to three stars from the first-try share, a line naming the best word, and a short animation that respects reduced motion, then checked it on both devices.
body:
The end screen now shows a row of stars. One star is for finishing, two for a first-try share of at least 60 percent, and three for at least 90 percent. The share comes from the round result that the progress module already computes, so I added no new counting. A test covers the edges: 59, 60, 89 and 90 percent, and a round with zero words, which cannot happen but should not divide by zero.

Under the stars is one line that names a word the kid got right on the first try, chosen as the longest such word. For a round with no first-try words, the line says Every word counted and no word is named. I wrote the text to avoid any mention of mistakes, as agreed in the plan.

The animation is a short pop of the stars, 400 ms each in a row, using CSS only. It is disabled inside a prefers-reduced-motion query, where the stars appear at once. I tested this by switching the setting in the dev tools. The start screen has no animation, as the user asked.

The font stack went in first: ui-rounded, then a rounded system font name list, then the system default. On the laptop the rounded font showed, and on the tablet the browser fell back to the default, which looks the same as before, so no gain there. I decided not to add a font file because the load flash and the cache size are not worth it for this device, and noted it as a decision.

The sentence display on the end screen kept its place and size. I compared screenshots before and after for the blanked sentence and the full sentence, and the positions are the same within a pixel. The hint button and the replay buttons were not touched.

On the tablet the older kid played a full round and said it looked better, mostly the color. The younger kid got two stars and wanted to play again for three. The contrast check passes in the build, the tests number 88, and the offline cache list gained no files.

What is left is only polish: the help text for the streaks on the parent page, which I still have not written, and a look at the layout on the very small tablet in landscape.

summary: Finished the redesign pass with new fonts and a calmer start screen, keeping big tap targets and the plain word display the kids already know.
body:
The redesign plan from a few days ago listed colors, fonts and the end screen. The colors and the end screen are done, so this session covered fonts and the start screen. I replaced the system font stack with one rounded font file, served from the same host, so nothing is fetched from a third party and the offline cache stays complete.

The font file is a subset with only Latin letters, digits and basic punctuation, which brought it down to about 18 KB. I added it to the precache list through the existing build step, and checked that the list file now contains it. The word being spelled stays in the large plain size, because the user said the kids read it to check their typing.

On the start screen I made the profile buttons a little rounder and gave each one the profile color chosen last week. The flame count moved under the name instead of beside it, which fixed a wrap on the narrow tablet. I left the button sizes untouched, since the minimum tap target is 56 px and the new padding keeps it there.

I looked at both devices. On the old tablet the font loads late on the first visit and the text jumps once, so I set font-display to swap and preloaded the file. After that the jump was not visible in three reloads. The contrast script still passes for all six colors.

Not done: the settings page still looks plain, but the user said parents do not care. Next I want to ask the user whether the kids like the new look before touching anything else.

summary: Wrote down the user's feedback that the new fonts are fine but the star animation distracts one kid, and added a setting to turn it off per profile.
body:
The user passed on a comment from one of the kids: the stars on the end screen bounce for so long that they cannot see the score. The animation already respects the system reduced-motion setting, but the tablet does not have that turned on, so it played in full.

I added a per-profile flag called calmEnd, stored with the other profile settings. When it is on, the stars appear at once with no bounce and the best-word line shows immediately. The flag is a checkbox on the parent page next to the color choice.

The animation code now reads one function, shouldAnimate(profile), which returns false if either the system setting or the profile flag asks for calm. Before this, the media query was checked in two places, and I merged them. I added a test for the four combinations.

Old profiles have no flag stored, so a missing value means the animation stays on, as before. I checked this by loading a profile saved before the change. The export file now includes the flag, and import of an older backup still works.

On the tablet I switched the flag on for the second profile and played one round. The stars showed at once, and the first profile still got the bounce. Left to do: nothing for this, unless the kid wants a shorter animation instead of none.

summary: Fixed the end screen showing 0 stars after a round where every word was wrong on the first try but right on the second, which should still give one star.
body:
The user noticed that a round with ten words, all fixed on the second try, gave no stars at all. That felt harsh to a kid who finished the round correctly. The star rule from the redesign used only the first-try share, and gave one star from 40 percent.

I changed the rule so a finished round always gives at least one star. Two stars still need 70 percent first try and three stars need 90 percent. I wrote this in a small table in the scoring module so the thresholds sit in one place instead of in the end screen code.

I wrote tests for 0, 40, 70, 90 and 100 percent, and for a round where a kid skipped words. Skipped words count as not first try, but a round with every word skipped still gives zero stars, since nothing was played. That case made me add a check on the number of answered words.

While in there I found the best-word line picked the first word of the list when all words were equal in tries. It now prefers the longest word among the ones with the fewest tries, which reads better on the screen.

I ran the round on the tablet with deliberate mistakes and saw one star appear. Old saved rounds are not recalculated, because only the end screen uses the rule and nothing is stored from it.

summary: Planned the word of the week import from a pasted school list, covering the formats the user receives, how to clean them, and what the parent page should show before saving.
body:
Typing ten words every week is the part the user likes least, so I looked at what the school actually sends. The user showed me three recent messages: a numbered list, a comma separated line, and a list with a sentence after each word. The import should accept all three.

The plan is a pure function parseWordList(text) that returns words and a list of warnings. It splits on line breaks and commas, removes leading numbers like "3." or "3)", and removes bullet characters. If a line has a dash or colon followed by a sentence, the part before it is the word and the sentence is dropped. Later the sentence may be useful as an example, but that is not part of this step.

Cleaning rules: trim, lowercase for the stored form but keep the original case for a note, remove duplicates, and flag any word with characters other than letters, apostrophes and hyphens. Flagged words stay in the preview with a warning mark, and the parent can fix them before saving.

The parent page gets a text box and a Preview button. The preview shows the cleaned words in a list with a count. Saving stays disabled unless the count is exactly ten, but a checkbox allows another count, because some weeks have eight or twelve words.

Tests to write: each of the three formats, windows line breaks, a word with an apostrophe, a pasted word with a trailing space, a duplicate, an empty text, and a list with 11 words. I also want a test with a typographic apostrophe, because phones often produce one, and it should be turned into the plain one.

Open question for the user: whether the sentence after the word should be kept. I will suggest to drop it for now. Next session I will write the parser and its tests.

summary: Wrote the word list parser as a pure module with tests for the three school formats, fixing curly apostrophes and Windows line breaks along the way.
body:
Following the plan from this morning, I wrote src/parseWordList.ts. It takes the pasted text and returns an object with words and warnings. Both are plain arrays, so it needs no browser API.

The steps are: normalize line breaks, turn curly apostrophes into the plain one, split on line breaks and commas, strip leading numbers and bullets, cut at a dash or colon followed by text, trim, and drop empty entries. Duplicates are removed after lowercasing, keeping the first position. A warning is added for each duplicate and for each word with other characters.

The tests cover the numbered list, the comma line, the list with sentences, a pasted block with Windows line breaks, a curly apostrophe in "don't", and a duplicate. All passed except one at first: a hyphenated word like "well-known" was cut at the hyphen because I treated every dash as a separator. I changed the rule so only a dash with spaces around it, or a colon, counts as a separator.

Another failure came from a number rule that also removed the 4 in a word list like "4th". I tightened the pattern to digits followed by a dot or closing bracket and a space. That kept the test for "4th" green.

The module is not yet connected to the parent page. That is the next piece. The whole test file runs in under a second.

summary: Connected the parser to the parent page with a preview list and a save button that stays disabled unless the word count is ten or confirmed otherwise.
body:
I added the text box and the Preview button to the parent page, calling parseWordList on click. The preview shows each cleaned word on its own row, with a warning mark and a short reason for flagged words.

Each row has an edit field, so a parent can correct a typo before saving. Editing a row runs the same checks again, and the warning goes away when the word is clean. A small remove button deletes a row.

Save is enabled when there are ten words and no warnings. A checkbox, "This week has a different number of words", enables Save for other counts. Saving writes the list to the same place the manual entry form used, so the game does not need any change.

I tried it on the tablet with the numbered list the user pasted from a message. It produced ten words, one flagged because of a stray full stop, which I fixed in the preview. The page works in airplane mode, since nothing here uses the network.

The old manual form is still on the page below the import. I will leave it for a few weeks and remove it if the user does not need it.

summary: Looked into why the tablet showed the previous week's words after the user saved a new list, and found the page kept a copy of the list in memory from before.
body:
The user saved a new list from the import on the tablet, went back to the game and got last week's words. A reload fixed it, which pointed to a stale copy rather than to the service worker.

I first suspected the cache, since the service worker handles word lists network-first. But the saved list lives in local storage, not in a fetched file, so the worker was not involved. I confirmed this by disabling the worker in the browser tools and getting the same result.

The cause was in the game module: it loaded the word list once at module start and kept it in a variable. The parent page and the game are the same page in one session, so switching views did not reload the module. The list changed in storage, but the variable did not.

I replaced the variable with a function getCurrentWords() that reads storage on each round start. Reading costs almost nothing for ten words. I also removed a second place that held a copy, in the hint logic, which took the first letters from the stale list. That one would have shown hints for the wrong words.

I added a test that saves a list, starts a round, saves a second list and starts another round, expecting the second words. It failed before the change and passes now. I then did the same steps on the tablet, and the new words came at once.

What I did not touch: the weekly report still reads words by week key, so it was not affected. Nothing else is open on this topic.

summary: Answered the user's question on keeping the example sentence after each school word and advised against it, since reading it aloud would give the answer away.
body:
The user asked whether the import should keep the sentence that follows each word in the school message, because some are quite nice. I thought about what the game would do with it.

The game reads the word aloud. A sentence containing the word would be useful for words that sound like others, such as "their" and "there". But if the sentence were shown on screen, it would show the answer. Reading it aloud through the voice is fine, though it makes each word take longer.

My advice was to drop the sentences for now, as planned, and add an optional field later only for homophones. The user agreed and said that only two or three words a term need it. No code changed. If the case comes up again, the word list file would need a second field and the voice code would need a way to read it after the word.

summary: Added a hint for homophones: an optional sentence per word that the voice reads after the word, with a Hear it in a sentence button.
body:
Since the user said a few words each term need a sentence, I added a small optional field. The parent can write the sentence in the preview row, and the stored word becomes an object with text and an optional sentence. Older saved lists with plain strings still load, through a normalizing function.

In the game, a button appears only when a sentence exists. It reads the sentence with the same voice and speed as the profile. The sentence is never printed on screen, so it does not give away the spelling.

I wrote tests for loading old and new list formats and for the export, which now includes the sentence. The backup import accepts both. I checked it on the tablet with the word "their", and the sentence played clearly.

summary: Fixed the parent page losing a half-typed word list when the tablet screen locked, by saving the draft text to local storage as it is typed.
body:
The user pasted a long list into the import box, got interrupted, and found the box empty when the tablet woke up. The browser had reloaded the page after the lock, a common thing on this old tablet when memory is low.

I added a draft: while the user types in the import box, the text is saved to a local storage key after a short pause of 400 ms. When the parent page opens, the draft is put back in the box if one exists. After a successful save of the list, the draft is deleted.

The draft key is global, not per profile, because the week list is shared by both kids. I checked this against the profile review of the last weeks, and the word list indeed has no per-profile copy. I wrote that down so nobody changes it by accident.

I tested three cases. First, type, reload, and see the text again. Second, save and reload, and see an empty box. Third, a draft with 20 000 characters, which stored without trouble. A quota error from storage is caught and ignored, since losing a draft is better than a crash.

The backup export does not include the draft, as it is temporary. I also made the Preview button clear old warnings first, because I saw an old warning mark stay after a second preview in one test.

On the tablet I locked the screen with a half-typed list for five minutes. The text was there after waking. Nothing is open on this.

summary: Planned the hint button as a small feature: first letter shown on request, a cost in stars, and what the tests must check, before writing any code.
body:
The user wants a hint button that shows the first letter of the word. Before coding I wrote down the questions, because a hint touches the scoring, the end screen and the keyboard and tile modes.

First, what the hint does. It shows the first letter in the first slot, filled in gray, and the cursor moves to the second slot. In tile mode the matching tile is highlighted instead of being placed. The kid still types the rest.

Second, the cost. A word with a hint does not count as first try, even when typed right. I chose this over taking away points because the end screen has only the first-try share, and a second system would be harder to explain to kids. The best-word line must not pick a word that used a hint.

Third, limits. Each word allows one hint. A round allows three hints in total, so the button cannot be used on every word. When the limit is reached the button is disabled and shows a small zero count. The user said three is fine for ten words.

Fourth, storage. The hint use per word is saved with the round result, in a field hinted, so the weekly report can show which words needed help. Old results have no field, which reads as false.

Fifth, the voice. The hint does not make the voice repeat the word, because there is already a repeat button.

Tests to write: a hint on a word marks it as not first try, the limit of three, the best word skipping hinted words, a word where the first letter has a capital in the list but is typed lower case, an apostrophe as the first character if there is any, and old results without the field.

The order of work is: the round logic with tests, then the keyboard mode, then the tile mode, then the report. I will start with the logic and not touch the screens until it passes. One open point is whether a hint should be possible after a wrong try, and I will allow it, since that is when a kid is stuck.

summary: Built the hint logic in the round module with a per-word flag and a limit of three per round, and covered it with tests including the best-word rule.
body:
I implemented the hint in the round module, as planned. The round state got two additions: hintsUsed for the round, and a hinted flag on each word result.

The function requestHint(state) returns a new state. It does nothing when the limit of three is reached or when the current word already has a hint. Otherwise it sets the flag, adds one to the count and returns the revealed letter and its position. Position is always zero for now, but I kept it in the result so a later change to reveal more would not need an API change.

First-try calculation now reads the flag: a hinted word is never first try. I changed one place in the scoring module for this, and the star table from the other day did not need to change.

The best word logic now filters out hinted words before picking the one with the fewest tries. If every word had a hint, the line is left out. Before, it would have shown an empty name, so I made the end screen skip the line.

The tests:
- a hint sets the flag and counts once
- a second hint on the same word does nothing
- the fourth hint of a round is refused
- a hinted word typed right at once is not first try
- the best word skips hinted words
- all words hinted gives no best word
- an old result without the field loads as not hinted

One test failed at first. The hint count was kept in a place that reset when the next word started, so the limit never reached three. I moved it up to the round level, and the test passed.

No screen changed yet. The button and the highlighting come next, first in keyboard mode. I also want to ask the user later whether the third hint should warn the kid that it is the last one.

summary: Added the hint button to the keyboard mode with the first letter shown in gray and the remaining hints counted on the button.
body:
Using the round logic from this morning, I put a Hint button next to the repeat button in keyboard mode. It shows a small number for the hints left in the round. At zero it is disabled and looks faded.

Pressing it shows the first letter in the first slot in gray. The input field starts with that letter already counted, so the kid types from the second letter on. I first tried to put the letter into the text field itself, but then backspace could delete it. I kept the letter in a separate span and joined it with the typed text when checking the answer.

Focus was a problem. Pressing the button took the focus away from the field, so the kid had to tap the field again. On the tablet this closes the on-screen keyboard. I fixed it by preventing the focus change on pointer down and refocusing the field after the click. The keyboard now stays open.

The check of the answer compares the joined string with the word, ignoring case. I tested a word with a capital first letter in the list and typed the rest in lower case, and it was accepted.

On the tablet, hint on the first word, then wrong, then right worked as expected. The word was not counted as first try on the end screen. With three hints used, the button turned gray and tapping did nothing.

Tile mode is not done yet. It needs a different treatment, since the tiles are what the kid taps.

summary: Made the hint work in tile mode by highlighting the correct first tile with a soft pulse instead of placing it, and fixed a duplicate letter case.
body:
In tile mode the hint should show which tile to tap first. I added a highlight class on the tile for the first letter, with a slow pulse that stops when the kid taps it. The pulse uses an outline rather than motion in size, so it works with reduced motion too.

The tricky part was words with repeated letters, such as "letter" with two t. Tiles are shuffled, and any tile with that letter would do. I decided to highlight the first matching tile in the visual order, and accept either one when tapped, since the letters are equal. The check compares letters, not tile ids, so this is safe.

The first version highlighted a tile that had already been placed in a slot. This happened after a wrong try, when the kid had put letters in and then used the hint. I changed it so that the hint first clears the slots, as the first letter belongs in the first slot, then marks the tile. A clear on hint might surprise a kid, but the alternative would have been confusing.

There was also the double tap guard from a few weeks ago. The highlight must not break it. I tested double tapping the highlighted tile, and only one letter was placed.

I wrote tests for the tile logic with "letter", "banana" and a one-letter word "I". For the last, the hint reveals the whole word, which seems silly but harmless; I made the button disabled for words of one letter.

On the small tablet the highlighted tile was visible in both rows of tiles. The layout fix of the earlier weeks still holds, and the slots stay on screen.

What remains: the weekly report column for hinted words and the end screen note. I also want to check the hint count shows correctly after switching profile mid-round, which should not be possible but might be.

summary: Added hinted words to the weekly report and a small note on the end screen, and checked that a profile switch mid-round resets the hint count.
body:
The weekly report shows per word the tries and whether it was right. I added a small marker for words where a hint was used, and a line at the top with the number of hinted words in the week. Old results have no flag, so they show no marker.

With two profiles, the report reads only the chosen profile's results. I checked this after the earlier mix-up of progress lists, and the hint markers follow the profile correctly, also when switching quickly.

The end screen now has a short line when hints were used, such as "2 hints used". It stays quiet if none were used. The user wanted nothing that makes a kid feel bad, so the text is neutral and has no color of warning.

I then looked at the profile switch. The profile picker is on the start screen, and a round cannot be started while another runs. But the browser back button can return to the start screen in the middle of a round. I tried it, and the round state stayed, so the next round for another profile would have started with the old hint count. I made the round state reset whenever a round starts, not only when it ends. A test covers back button, other profile, new round.

The backup export includes the hinted flag through the round results, and import of an older backup works. I tested with a file from before the hint work.

I ran the whole test suite, which has grown to about 90 tests, and all pass. The build size grew by 1.2 KB. The offline cache list is still generated and identical in structure.

The hint topic is now complete. The user will try it with the kids this week and tell me what they think.

summary: Recorded the user's report that the kids overuse the hint on the first word, and added a short delay of five seconds before the hint button becomes active.
body:
The user watched the kids play. One used the hint on the first word of every round before even trying. That uses up the three hints early and also lowers the first-try share without need.

I considered three choices: fewer hints, a delay, or asking the kid to try first. Fewer hints would hurt the kid who really needs them. A delay is simple and does not change the rules. I chose a delay of five seconds after the word is spoken, during which the button looks faded, then it becomes active.

The timer starts when the voice ends, not when the word starts, because a slow voice would otherwise eat the delay. The speech API has an end event, but it is unreliable on the old tablet, so I added a fallback of ten seconds after start. A repeat of the word restarts the delay, which seemed fair.

The delay is a constant in one file, so the user can change it. I did not add a setting, since it is not worth a parent screen. A test with fake timers checks that the button is disabled at four seconds and active at five.

An important detail was reduced motion: the fading is only a style change, with no movement, so it needed no special case.

On the tablet I counted about five seconds on the first word and found the end event firing correctly. On the second profile, with the slower voice setting, the delay started late as expected.

The user will watch whether the kids still tap early. If so, a gentle label like "try first" may help.

summary: Reviewed the hint feature after a week of use and found that a hinted word still counted as a perfect word in the streak message on the start screen.
body:
After the week of use, I went through the places that read round results to see if any ignored the hinted flag. Most were fine: scoring, stars, best word and the report.

The one I found is the small line on the start screen that says how many words the kid got right without a mistake in the last round. It counted words with zero wrong tries, and a hinted word with no wrong tries counted as perfect. This was a small inconsistency with the stars, where the same word is not first try.

I changed it to use the same function as the stars, isFirstTry(result), instead of its own check. That also removes the risk that the two drift again. I searched the source for other direct reads of the tries field and found one more, in the export summary, which only counts totals and is fine.

I added a test for the start screen line: ten words, three hinted without mistakes, expecting seven. It failed before and passes now.

The user reported that the kids use the hint less with the delay. One kid still takes it on most first words, but the other rarely. I left the rules as they are.

I also checked storage size of results with the new field. For 40 rounds it grew by under 2 KB, nothing to worry about.

Nothing is open, except the optional "try first" label, which the user does not want for now.

summary: Planned the work for a new browser version warning: the user saw the speech voices list come back empty on first load, so the plan is to wait for the voiceschanged event.
body:
The user said the game was silent for the first word on the kitchen tablet after the browser updated itself. The word showed but nothing was read. Tapping repeat made it work. This looks like the known behavior of the speech API, where the list of voices is empty until an event fires.

Before changing code, I read how voices are chosen now. The module calls getVoices() when a round starts and looks for the voice name saved in the profile. If the list is empty, it falls back to the default voice, which on this tablet is the network voice that fails offline. That fits what was seen, since the first word was silent while the kids were offline.

The plan has four parts. First, a function whenVoicesReady() that returns a promise: it resolves at once if the list has entries, otherwise waits for voiceschanged, with a timeout of two seconds. Second, the round start waits for this promise before speaking the first word. Third, if the timeout passes, speak with the default and remember to retry the voice choice on the next word. Fourth, log a short message in the console on the timeout, so I can see it on the tablet.

The tests need a fake speech object with a controllable voice list and event. Cases to cover: voices ready at once, voices arrive after 300 ms, voices never arrive, and the event fires twice. The last matters because some browsers fire it repeatedly, and the promise must resolve once.

A risk is that the wait delays the first word by up to two seconds on a slow start. That is acceptable, but the kid may think the game is stuck. A small "getting ready" text in the word area for that time would help.

I will not change the voice preview in settings in this step, since it runs after a tap, when the list is normally filled. Next session: write whenVoicesReady with the tests.

summary: Wrote whenVoicesReady with a two second timeout and used it before the first word of a round, which fixed the silent first word on the kitchen tablet.
body:
I implemented the plan from the last session. The new function in the speech module returns a promise. It checks getVoices() first. If the list has entries it resolves immediately. Otherwise it adds a voiceschanged listener and a timer of two seconds, and resolves with whatever is there when either comes first. The listener is removed afterward, so a second event does nothing.

The round start now awaits this before speaking the first word. A "getting ready" text shows in the word area only if the wait lasts longer than 400 ms, so a normal start shows no flicker. After the first word the voices are known, so later words do not wait.

For the voice choice, I changed the lookup to run after the wait. Before, it ran at module start and kept the result, which was the fallback voice when the list was empty. Now it runs per round and picks the saved voice by name, falling back to a voice with the same language, and then to the default.

Tests with a fake speech object:
- list filled at once: resolves without waiting
- list arrives after 300 ms: resolves with it
- list never arrives: resolves after two seconds, empty
- event fires twice: resolves once

All four passed. A fifth test for the saved voice missing from the list, which can happen after an update, checks the same-language fallback, and it passed too.

On the kitchen tablet I closed the browser fully, switched on airplane mode and started a round. The first word was spoken with the saved local voice after about a second, where it had been silent before. The "getting ready" text appeared briefly. The second kid's profile with a different voice also worked.

The console message for the timeout did not appear in five starts, so the event arrives in time on this device. The old tablet is the next place to check, and the user will do that this week.

summary: Planned the second kid profile: separate scores, streaks and settings per profile, a picker on the start screen, and a one-time move of the existing single-kid data.
body:
The user asked for a second kid to have their own scores, since the two siblings were overwriting each other's streak on the kitchen tablet. Before writing code I went through how the storage looks today: one key, spellbee.scores, holds a flat object with best scores, the streak counter and the mute flag. Nothing in it says whose it is.

The plan is to introduce a profiles key holding a list of objects with an id, a name and a color slot, plus one key per profile for scores, named spellbee.scores.<id>.
