The mute flag stays global because it belongs to the device and not to the kid. The word lists stay shared, since both kids get the same ten words from school, though the older one may get a different list later.

The start screen gets a picker with big buttons showing the names, remembered from the last session. Switching in the middle of a round must be blocked or must reset the round, and I leaned toward reset because it is simpler and a kid will rarely do it.

Migration is the risky part. On first load after the update, if the old key exists and no profiles exist, create one profile called Kid 1, copy the old data under its id, and keep the old key for one release as a fallback. The parent page gets a rename field so the user can type the real name.

The tests to write are: migration from the old shape, migration run twice does not duplicate, a missing or corrupt old value gives an empty profile, and two profiles keep independent streaks. I also noted that the weekly report must say which profile it shows.

Nothing was built in this session. The first step next is the storage module with the migration and its tests, before any screen changes. The picker UI follows after that, and the parent page rename last.

summary: Wrote the profile storage module with a one-time migration from the single-kid scores key, with tests for a repeated run and a corrupt old value.
body:
Built src/profiles.ts as a small module that owns every read and write of profile data, so the rest of the code no longer touches local storage keys for scores directly. It exposes listProfiles, getActive, setActive, createProfile and loadScores(id) and saveScores(id, data).

The migration runs once at startup. If the profiles key is missing and the old spellbee.scores key exists, it creates profile p1 named Kid 1, writes the old data under spellbee.scores.p1 and sets p1 as active. The old key is left in place on purpose, so a rollback of the site would still find the data.

I wrote tests for four cases: a fresh install makes one empty profile, an old key is moved, running the migration twice leaves one profile, and a corrupt old value such as the text undefined produces an empty profile instead of throwing. The last one failed at first, because JSON.parse threw inside the migration and the page stayed blank. A try and catch around the parse fixed it, and the corrupt text is ignored with a console warning.

All 31 tests pass. The round module still calls the old load function, so the app is not switched over yet. That is the next step, together with the picker.

summary: Switched the round, streak and score board code to the active profile and added the picker on the start screen with big name buttons.
body:
Replaced the remaining direct reads of the old scores key in the round module, the streak message and the score board with calls into profiles.ts. It was five places, found by searching for the key string, and one more in the weekly report that I had forgotten at first.

The start screen now shows one large button per profile above the play button. The active one has a thick outline and the name in bold, and the choice is stored, so the tablet opens on whoever played last. Tap targets are 64 pixels high as before. With only one profile the picker is hidden, so nothing changes for a household with a single kid.

Switching profiles while a round is running resets the round and returns to the start screen. I tried keeping the round but the typed letters then belonged to the wrong kid, so reset it is.

I checked on the kitchen tablet with the migrated data: the old streak of 4 showed under Kid 1, and a newly created second profile began at 0. Playing a round as the second kid did not change the first kid's score. One small glitch: the score board title still said My scores, now changed to the profile name.

Still open: the parent page needs a way to add and rename profiles, since for now a second profile can only be made from the console. That comes next.

summary: Added profile management to the parent page, with add, rename and delete, and found that deleting the active profile left the game pointing at a missing id.
body:
The parent page now has a Profiles section with a list of the profiles, a rename field for each, an Add kid button and a Delete button. Delete asks for confirmation with the kid's name in the text, because the scores cannot be recovered afterwards.

While testing I deleted the active profile and the start screen then showed an empty picker and the play button threw an error in the console: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'streak'). The active id still pointed at the deleted profile. Cause: deleteProfile removed the entry and its scores key but never touched the active setting.

The fix is in deleteProfile: if the removed id was active, set the first remaining profile as active. If none remain, create a fresh Kid 1, so the game never has zero profiles. I added tests for both cases and for deleting a profile that is not active, which must leave the active one alone.

I also limited the name to 20 characters and trimmed spaces, and refused an empty name by keeping the old one. Two profiles with the same name are allowed, since twins or a typo should not block anything, but the picker would then be confusing, so I added the color dot next to the name as a second cue.

A run through on the tablet: add Mia, rename Kid 1 to Leo, play as each, delete Mia, and the game falls back to Leo. All fine. The next task is how the weekly report should show two kids, since it currently prints one table.

summary: Made the weekly report show one section per profile and fixed the hinted word counts landing in the wrong kid's table.
body:
The weekly report on the parent page printed a single table of words with first-try and hinted marks. With two profiles it needs a section for each kid, so I changed it to loop over the profiles and call the same table builder with that profile's scores.

The first version showed the hint counts of the active profile in both tables. The report read the hints from the round module's in-memory state, which only exists for the kid currently playing. The saved scores did hold the per-word hint flag, so the table builder now reads only saved data and no longer touches the live round. After that, both tables were right.

A kid who has not played this week shows a line No rounds this week instead of an empty table, which looked like a bug before. The sections are ordered as in the picker, and each has the color dot and the name as a heading.

I added three tests for the report builder: two profiles with different data, a profile without rounds, and a hinted word that stays marked in its own table only. The count is 36 tests now.

The print layout puts both sections on one page, and that fits for ten words each. The user may print it for the fridge, so I checked the print preview and it fits on one sheet.

summary: Planned the offline mode with a service worker, choosing what to cache, how updates reach the tablet and what must work with no network at all.
body:
The user wants the game to work on the tablet when the wifi is off, for the car and the grandparents' house. I wrote the plan before touching code.

What must work offline: the page, the script, the styles, the sounds and the current word list. The speech itself is the open question. The browser speech API may use a local voice or a network voice depending on the device, and a network voice fails with no connection. The plan is to prefer a voice whose localService flag is true, and fall back to the default with a visible note if there is none.

Cache strategy: precache the built files with a hash list generated at build time, and use network-first with a short timeout for the word list JSON, so a new week appears when there is a connection and the cached one is used otherwise. Static files use cache-first because their names include hashes.

Updates: a new service worker should wait, and the page should reload only between rounds so a kid does not lose a half-typed word. I want a small cache name with a prefix and a version, so old caches can be deleted on activation.

Risks I listed: the dev server must not register the worker, because stale caches make debugging painful; the tablet may keep an old worker for a long time; and local storage is separate from the cache, so scores are not touched.

First step next is a hand-written worker with a precache list, tested in a production preview.

summary: Wrote the first service worker with a precache of the built files and cache-first for hashed assets, and verified the page loads with the network off.
body:
Added public/sw.js and a Vite plugin step that writes the list of built file names into it after the build. The worker precaches those files on install and answers fetches for them from the cache, falling back to the network.

In the browser devtools I switched the network to offline after one load and reloaded the production preview. The page, styles and script came from the cache, and the word list was still missing because it is not part of the precache yet. That is the next piece, with the network-first rule.

One mistake along the way: the precache list included the sw.js file itself, which made the worker cache its own old copy and delayed updates. I excluded it. The cache is named spellbee-v1 for now.

The worker is registered from main.ts, still in all builds including dev, which I noted to fix next because stale files are confusing while developing.

summary: Added the network-first rule for the word list JSON with a three second timeout, and stopped registering the worker in the dev server.
body:
The weekly word list files are fetched at runtime, so they are not in the precache. I added a fetch handler for URLs under /words/ that tries the network first, and if no answer comes within three seconds, or the request fails, serves the cached copy. A successful network answer is stored in the cache for next time.

Testing offline: with the network off, the list loaded from the cache in about 20 ms. With the network on and a changed list file, the new words showed after one reload. With devtools throttled to slow 3G, the cached list showed after the three seconds, which felt long but is acceptable for a kid's start screen.

I also fixed the registration. main.ts now registers the worker only when import.meta.env.PROD is true, and in dev it unregisters any existing worker, so my earlier registrations in localhost stop serving old files.

One open point: the first visit offline for a new week has nothing cached, and the game shows the empty list message. I made the message friendlier, saying that the list needs one visit with the internet. The cache name is still without a prefix scheme, and I will handle that with the update flow.

summary: Wrote the update flow so a new service worker waits and the page reloads only after a round ends, never in the middle of a word.
body:
Until now a new worker took over at once with skipWaiting, and the page could reload while a kid was typing. I removed skipWaiting from install and made the worker wait instead.

The page listens for the updatefound event and checks whether a worker is in the waiting state. If so, it sets a flag. When a round ends and the end screen shows, the page sends a SKIP_WAITING message to the waiting worker, and a controllerchange handler reloads once. A guard variable prevents a reload loop, which happened in my first test because controllerchange fired twice.

I built two versions and tested on the desktop preview: loading the old one, building the new one, reloading, and then playing a round. The new version appeared only after the end screen, as wanted. If a kid never finishes a round, the update simply waits, and that is fine.

Cache names now use the prefix spellbee- and a version taken from the build hash. On activation, the worker deletes all caches that start with the prefix but do not match the current one. This will clear old caches after future updates.

Still to check on the real tablet, where the worker behavior can differ.

summary: Tested the offline mode on the kitchen tablet and found that the first word used a network voice and failed in airplane mode, so the voice choice now prefers local voices.
body:
I took the production build to the kitchen tablet, loaded it once on wifi, then switched on airplane mode and reopened the page. The page, styles and sounds worked, and so did the cached word list.

The first word of the round was silent, though. The voice list on this tablet has several English voices, and the default choice was a network voice, which cannot speak without a connection. No error appeared in the interface, only the silence, and the kid would think the game was broken.

The voice picker now sorts candidates: first the saved voice from the settings if it is local, then any voice with localService true that matches the language, then the default. If only a network voice exists, the game shows a small note saying that the voice needs internet.

There was a side effect: the local voice is a bit more robotic and a little slower than the network one. I left the speed setting alone, and the user can still choose a voice in the settings, with network voices marked by a cloud label in the list.

After the change I repeated the airplane mode test. All ten words were read aloud, and typing, scores and the end screen worked. Back on wifi, the game still chose the local voice, which is consistent.

A question to watch: the label for a network voice depends on the localService flag being right, and some browsers report it wrongly. I will see if the user notices anything.

summary: Looked at why the game showed last week's words on the tablet after an update and found that the update flow reloaded before the background fetch had finished.
body:
The user said the tablet still showed the old list on the first round after he pasted the new one. I reproduced it on the preview by changing the list file and reloading once.

The cause was the order of events. The network-first handler returned the cached copy when the network took more than the timeout, but it did not continue the fetch to update the cache, so the new list only arrived at the next visit. On a slow connection this happened every time.

I changed the handler to keep the network request alive with event.waitUntil after the timeout fires, and to put the answer in the cache when it comes. The next load then has the new list. For the current round the old list is still used, which is acceptable.

I checked with slow 3G throttling: first reload shows the old words, second reload shows the new ones. Offline still works as before.

A better fix would let the page know that a new list has arrived and refresh it after the round, which I may do later.

summary: Made the page learn when a fresher word list lands in the cache and apply it between rounds, so a slow start no longer needs a second reload.
body:
After the last fix, the new list arrived in the background but the kids still saw the old words until the next reload. That is confusing on a slow network, so I made the worker tell the page.

When the background fetch finishes and the content differs from the cached copy, the worker posts a message of type LIST_UPDATED to all clients, with the file name. The page keeps a flag, and on the end screen it reloads the list into memory so the next round uses it. It never replaces the list in the middle of a round.

To compare the contents I store a small hash of the text in the cache entry headers. Comparing the full text would also work, but the files are tiny, so I used the simple string comparison in the end and dropped the header idea, which was needless complexity.

There was a bug on the first try: the message was sent even when the content was equal, because I compared the Response objects. Comparing the text fixed it, and the page then ignored the identical lists.

I wrote a test for the pure part, a function that decides whether to notify. The worker itself I tested by hand in the preview with changed files. Three cases worked: a changed list, an unchanged list, and a network failure, where nothing is sent.

Another detail: the parent page saves a typed list to local storage, and the worker does not know about that. The two sources of a list are separate, and the page prefers the saved one when its week number is newer. I added a short comment in the loader about this priority, since I had forgotten it myself while debugging.

The tablet check is planned for tomorrow, when the next school list comes in. The end screen flow stays the same, and no new strings are shown to the kids.

summary: Confirmed on the tablet that a new school list arrives after a slow start and that the reload waits for the end screen as intended.
body:
The user pasted the new list in the morning, and I watched the tablet on the home wifi, which is slow in the kitchen. The first round started with last week's words, as predicted.

After the round, the end screen appeared and the page refreshed the list. The second round used the new words, and the order of the words matched the list on the parent page. No reload flash was seen during the round.

I also tried airplane mode after that, and the game kept the new list, so the cache entry had been updated properly.

One small oddity: the very first round after an update used the old list for kids who play right away. The user said that is fine, since they usually play after school, not at the moment of pasting. I will leave it.

summary: Reviewed the profile and offline work of the last weeks and fixed three gaps: old caches that stayed, a missing export key and a stale label.
body:
I went through the code of the profiles and the service worker with fresh eyes, reading the diffs of the last weeks in order. Three real problems came out.

First, caches from the earlier naming scheme. The first service worker used the name spellbee-v1, and the later scheme uses the prefix spellbee- with a build hash. The cleanup deletes every cache that starts with the prefix and is not current, but I had renamed the prefix at one point, so the first version's cache did not match and stayed on the tablet. I checked in devtools and found a leftover cache of about 1.4 MB. The activation step now also deletes the known old names, listed in an array.

Second, the export of data for backup. The parent page has an Export button that writes a JSON file with the profiles and scores. It listed the scores per profile but forgot the active profile id, so an import would pick the first profile. I added the activeProfile key and a test that exports and imports a two-profile setup and expects the same active one.

Third, a label. The score board heading still said Best streak for the old single profile design, and the mute switch label on the parent page said Sound for Leo, taken from a test name I had left in. Both were corrected to use the active profile name and Sound.

I also read through the profile switching code for races. If the kid taps a profile button twice quickly, setActive runs twice with the same id, which is harmless. I added a test for it anyway.

Things I checked and left alone: the migration keeps the old scores key, and I decided to delete it in a later release, once the user confirms that everything is fine. The worker's precache list is generated, so nothing manual needs to change.

Tests: 41 pass, up from 38. The build output size is unchanged, roughly 96 KB including the sounds.

Next is the streak feature for the kids, with a plain rule for what counts as a day played.

summary: Planned streaks as days in a row with at least one finished round, keeping the day boundary in local time and handling a missed day without punishing kids harshly.
body:
The user asked for streaks to motivate the kids, with a number of days in a row. I wrote down the rules before coding.

A day counts when the profile finishes at least one round, regardless of the score. The day boundary is local midnight on the device. The streak is stored per profile as a count plus the last played day, written as a local day string, so no time zone conversion is needed when the clock stays the same.

If the last played day is today, the streak does not change. If it was yesterday, finishing a round makes it one more. Otherwise it resets to one. I considered a free day per week as a grace, since the kids go away for weekends, but the user preferred the simple rule, so no grace for now.

Edge cases: the device clock moving back must not reduce a streak, so if the last day is in the future, treat it as today. Daylight saving changes make days of 23 or 25 hours, so I compute day differences using calendar day numbers and not by dividing milliseconds.

The start screen shows a line such as 3 days in a row. The perfect-word message must not count hinted words, which I noticed in an earlier review.

The pure function takes a streak state and a day string and returns the new state, so the tests need no clock. Next: write it with tests.

summary: Implemented the streak module with calendar-day arithmetic and tests for clock changes, then showed the streak on the start screen per profile.
body:
I wrote src/streak.ts with a function recordRound(state, today) that returns the new state, where today is a day string in the form of year, month and day numbers separated by dashes, produced by a small helper from the local date.

Day differences use a dayNumber function that converts a date into a count of days using Date.UTC from the parts, so daylight saving shifts do not matter. The first version used milliseconds divided by 86400000 and gave a wrong result in a test around a clock change, with a difference of 0 instead of 1. The UTC based version fixed that.

Tests cover: a first ever round gives 1, a second round on the same day stays the same, the next day gives plus one, a gap of two days resets to 1, a last day in the future leaves the streak as it is, and a long streak across the end of a month and a leap day. There are 9 new tests and all pass.

Then I wired it in. The end of a round calls recordRound for the active profile and saves the result with the other scores. The start screen reads the state and shows the line with the count. If the last day is older than yesterday, the count shown is 0, since the streak is already broken even though it is not yet recorded. This display rule uses the same module, with a function currentStreak(state, today).

On the tablet I faked the date using a debug query parameter that overrides today, only enabled outside production. I played a round, moved the date one day forward, played again, and the count went from 1 to 2. Moving two days forward showed 0 on the start screen, and a round made it 1.

The existing migrated profile had a streak value without a last day. I treat a missing last day as no streak, so Leo's old streak of 4 is lost. The user said that is acceptable, but I added a note in the changelog text.

Next: a small celebration for round milestones, maybe a sound, which the user has not yet asked for.

summary: Fixed the streak line showing yesterday's count after midnight while the tablet stayed open on the end screen, by recomputing it on visibility change.
body:
The user said that the streak on the start screen looked too high one morning. The tablet had been left on the page overnight, and the line was rendered the evening before, so it showed 5 although the streak had broken.

The render ran only at page load and after a round. I added a listener for visibilitychange that recomputes the line when the page becomes visible, and a timer at local midnight that does the same. The timer was dropped after I thought about it: tablets sleep and timers are unreliable, so the visibility event is enough.

I tested by changing the debug date and switching tabs. The line updated each time, from 5 to 0 after a gap. A test of the render function with two different days was added.

The round start also reads today again, not a stored value, because the old code kept a day string at page load. That could have recorded a round on the wrong day, which was the more serious part of the same bug. Both are fixed now.

summary: Wrote down the user's wish for a streak message that is kind after a break, and changed the text from Streak lost to a fresh start line.
body:
The user said the kids were sad when the start screen showed a 0 after a week of holiday. They asked for something gentler.

I changed the text. With a streak of 0 and a best streak above 0 the line now says Start a new streak today, and the best streak is shown below in small text. A brand new profile sees Play your first round. A streak of 1 says 1 day, and larger values say N days in a row.

The best streak value is new: the state now keeps a best count, updated whenever the current one exceeds it. Older saved states without it are treated as having the best equal to the current count, in the loader.

Tests were added for the text function with the four cases. I looked at it on the tablet and the font size is the same as before. No sound is involved.

summary: Checked streaks across two profiles on the tablet and found that the second kid's rounds changed the first kid's last played day, due to a shared state object.
body:
I played a few rounds on the tablet with both profiles on faked dates. After Mia played on the second day, Leo's start screen showed a streak of 0, although he had played the day before and not yet today, which should show 1.

I traced it to the loader. When a profile had no streak state, the loader returned a shared default object, and recordRound mutated it, so the next profile that also had no state got the changed object. Mia's first round had set the last day on the shared default, and Leo's later load picked it up.

The fix: the default is now created fresh by a function on each call, and recordRound returns a new object and never changes its input. I added a test that records a round on one default state and checks that a second default is still empty. A frozen object in the test would have caught it earlier, so the tests now use Object.freeze on their inputs.

I repeated the manual check with the fake dates. Leo kept his streak, Mia's counted separately, and the start screen was right for both.

I also cleaned up the export, which had copied the shared object for two profiles in the same way. It writes the real per-profile state now. All 53 tests pass.

summary: Added a second-profile test with a shared device clock and found the settings object was also shared, so the sound mute of one kid muted the other.
body:
After the streak fix for two profiles, I wrote a test that plays rounds for both kids in one session and then compares every stored value. The streak values were fine now, but the mute flag was not: turning the sound off for the first kid also turned it off for the second.

The cause was the same kind of shared object. The settings module returned one default object for every profile that had no saved settings yet, and the mute toggle changed that object in place. The second kid, who had no saved settings, therefore read the first kid's change.

I changed the settings module to return a fresh copy of the defaults on every read, and to write a profile's settings under its own key only when a toggle is used. I added tests for mute, the star animation switch and the color choice, each checking that the other profile keeps its value.

I also searched the other modules for module-level objects that are handed out and mutated. The score board had one cached array, which is now copied before sorting. All 41 tests pass. I still want to check on the tablet that the mute holds after a profile switch and a reload, which is next.

summary: Looked into the old tablet starting slowly and found that all sounds were decoded at once on load, then moved decoding to the first tap, one file at a time.
body:
The user said the old tablet needs several seconds before the start screen reacts. I profiled the page in the desktop browser with 6x CPU throttling to imitate it and saw a long task of about 900 ms right after load.

The long task was the sound setup. Each sound file was fetched and decoded with decodeAudioData in a loop started at load, and there are nine files now, including the new milestone sound. Decoding them in parallel blocked the main thread, and the start screen buttons did not respond in the meantime.

There is a second reason to delay it: browsers only allow an audio context to start after a user gesture, so decoding before the first tap gave a suspended context and warnings in the console.

The new flow creates the context on the first tap on the play button and decodes the sounds one after another with a small await between them, so the main thread has time between files. The sounds needed first, right and wrong, are decoded first and the milestone sound last. If a sound is requested before it is decoded, it is skipped quietly instead of blocking.

Measured under the same throttling, the longest task dropped from 900 ms to about 120 ms, and the start screen responded at once. On the real tablet the user's report of the delay was gone in my test, and the first word was spoken after the tap without a gap.

I added a small test for the decode queue with a fake decoder, checking the order and that a failing file does not stop the others. There are 56 tests now.

A remaining risk is that a kid who taps very fast gets the first right sound missing, which seems minor.

summary: Answered the user's question whether the kids' data could be lost when the browser clears storage, and explained what survives and what does not.
body:
The user asked what happens to the scores if the tablet cleans up its storage. I checked how things are stored and answered from that.

Scores, streaks and profiles are in local storage, and the word lists are in the service worker cache. A browser can clear both when the device is short of space, and the user clears them by hand when deleting website data. On an iPad, a site that is not used for a long time can also lose its data. There is no copy anywhere else, since the game has no server.

What survives is only what the user exported. The parent page has an Export button, which writes a file with all profiles. I suggested exporting after each month, and said I could add a reminder.

I also mentioned navigator.storage.persist(), which asks the browser to keep the data, but the answer depends on the browser and may be silently refused, so it is no replacement for a backup.

summary: Added a reminder on the parent page to export a backup when the last export is more than 30 days old, plus a call to ask the browser for persistent storage.
body:
Following the question this morning, I added a backup reminder. The export now saves the time of the last export in local storage under spellbee.lastExport. The parent page compares it with the current time and shows a yellow note, Export a backup, when more than 30 days have passed.

The note says how many days have passed and has an Export now button next to it. After the export the note disappears. It is only on the parent page and not on the kids' start screen, which must stay plain.

I also call navigator.storage.persist() once when the parent page opens, if it exists, and store the result as a boolean. The parent page shows a small line, Storage is protected or Storage may be cleared by the browser. On the desktop browser the request was granted and on the tablet it was refused, so the second line is what the user will see. I did not hide it, since it explains why the reminder matters.

For the day count I wrote a pure function daysSince(lastExport, now) that returns null for a missing value. Tests cover a missing value, 29 days, 30 days, 31 days and a last export in the future, which counts as 0.

I checked the parent page by setting the stored value to older times in devtools. The note appeared at the right limit and the button reset it. All 60 tests pass.

A gap I know of is the first install, where no export has happened, and what the note should say then. I will check that on a fresh profile next.

summary: Tested the backup reminder and persistent storage request on the kitchen tablet and the laptop, and fixed an import that rejected a valid backup from before the profiles existed.
body:
I went through the backup flow end to end on both devices, since the reminder and the persistent storage request were written only a short while ago. On the laptop browser the request for persistent storage was granted at once. On the kitchen tablet it was denied silently the first time and no message was shown, which is the intended behavior, because a kid should never see a prompt about it.

The reminder itself worked. I set the last export time to 31 days back by hand in local storage, and the note appeared on the parent page. After an export it disappeared and the new time was saved. With 29 days back it stayed hidden, so the boundary is right.

The real problem came when I tried to restore an old backup. I had a file exported before the profile work, with the single-kid format: one scores key and one settings block, and no list of profiles. The import code expected a profiles list and rejected the file with the message Backup is not valid. That would be a bad surprise for the user, who may well have such a file in a mail folder.

I fixed it by running the old format through the same migration that the profile storage module uses on first start. The import now detects the missing profiles key, builds the first profile from the old data, and gives it the name the user already has for the first kid. The new format is untouched.

I added three tests: an old format file, a new format file, and a file with a damaged scores value. The damaged one is refused with a clear message and nothing in storage is changed, because the import first checks the whole file and only then writes. All tests pass.

I also changed the import text on the parent page to say that older backups work too. Left to do: a restore test on the tablet itself, where the file picker behaves differently, and a look at whether the export file name should include the profile count.

summary: Planned a mute and volume control per profile after the shared settings bug, so each kid keeps their own sound choices and the parent page can reset them.
body:
The shared settings object of two weeks ago showed that sound, voice speed and volume all belong to the profile, not the device. The plan is to move these three into the profile record and read them through one getSettings(profileId) function. A volume slider with three steps will sit on the start screen next to the mute button. The parent page gets a reset-to-defaults button per profile.

Open question: whether voice choice should also be per profile. The user said the younger kid likes the slower voice, so it will be. Order of work: storage change with a migration, then the UI, then tests with two profiles.

summary: Built the per-profile mute and volume control: each kid now keeps their own sound choices, and the parent page can reset them to defaults.
body:
This followed the plan from earlier in the day and the shared settings bug found last week. First I moved volume, mute and the choice of wrong-answer sound into the profile record, next to the name and the streak data. The old global settings key stays in place only as a source for the one-time copy. On first load after the update, each existing profile receives a copy of the old values, so nobody's sound suddenly changes.

The volume is a slider with five steps instead of a free range. The user wanted this because small fingers miss exact positions on the tablet. The mute is a separate big toggle with a speaker icon, and it applies to the sound effects only. The spoken word is never muted by it, since a muted word would make the game pointless. I wrote this rule into a comment and into the label, which now reads Effects off.

The sound player now asks the active profile for its gain on every play instead of caching it at startup. That removed the last place where one kid's choice could leak into the other's. I added a test with two profiles that sets one to muted and the other to the lowest volume, then switches back and forth ten times and checks both values each time. It passed.

The parent page got a Reset sounds button per profile, with a confirm step. It restores the default volume, unmutes, and selects the standard wrong-answer sound. The backup export now includes these fields, and the import accepts older backups that lack them by filling in defaults. I checked the import with a backup from before the profiles existed. Remaining work is trying it on the kitchen tablet with both kids tomorrow.

summary: Checked the new per-profile sound settings on the kitchen tablet and laptop, and fixed a slider that kept the old volume after a profile switch.
body:
After the morning work on per-profile sound, I tried it on real devices. On the laptop everything behaved: muting one profile left the other audible, and the values survived a reload. On the kitchen tablet the first run showed a bug. After switching from the first kid to the second, the volume slider still showed the first kid's position, although the sound itself played at the correct level.

The cause was that the settings panel was built once and only read the profile values at that moment. The sound player asked the profile on every play, but the slider never refreshed. I added a profile-changed event that the storage module fires after a switch, and the panel now listens and redraws its controls. The same event also fixed the mute icon, which had the same stale problem and which I had not seen yet because both kids happened to have it off.

I then ran a longer check by hand. I set the first kid to the lowest volume, the second to the highest and muted effects for the first. Then I switched five times, played a round each time and listened. The levels followed the profile every time. I also tested the reset button from the parent page while the game was open in the other tab. The game picked up the reset values after the next visibility change, which is good enough here.

One more thing came up on the tablet. The volume steps are audible only on the effects, and the spoken word has its own loudness from the system. The user asked whether the word could get a slider too. I said it could be added, but the system volume already does that job and a second control would confuse the kids. The user agreed to leave it. I added a test for the profile-changed event and moved on.

summary: Looked into a report that the word list for the week showed a word with a trailing space, found a bad entry in the JSON, and trimmed words on load.
body:
The user said one word, 'because ', could never be typed correctly. The JSON file had a trailing space inside the string, copied from the school sheet.

I fixed the file, and also added trimming and lowercase comparison when the list is loaded, so the same slip cannot block a kid again. A small test covers a word with surrounding spaces.

I also searched all other list files for leading or trailing whitespace and found none.

summary: Added a check script that validates every word list file, catching duplicates, empty strings and odd characters before a build, and wired it into the build command.
body:
After the trailing space problem I wrote scripts/check-words.ts. It reads each JSON file in the lists folder and checks that it is an array of strings, that none is empty, that none has surrounding whitespace, and that there are no duplicates within a week.

It also warns, but does not fail, on characters outside letters, apostrophes and hyphens. That warning found 'ice-cream' and 'don't', both of which are fine, and a word with a curly apostrophe. The curly one would never match what a kid types on the tablet keyboard, so I normalized it to a straight apostrophe in the file and in the loader.

The script runs before vite build through the prebuild npm hook. A failing list stops the build with the file name and the position of the bad word.

I tested it by breaking a copy of a list in three ways. Each was reported with a clear message. Nothing else to do here.

summary: Planned a review of accessibility for the youngest kid: bigger tiles, a read-again button, and clearer feedback for wrong letters, with an order of work.
body:
The user asked for a plan after watching the younger kid struggle. Observations from the user: the repeat button is small and sits far from the input, the wrong-answer sound is startling, and the kid loses track of which letters were typed.

Plan, in order:
- Move the read-again button next to the input and make it at least 64 pixels.
- Replace the harsh wrong sound with a softer one, and keep the old one as an option.
- Show typed letters in large boxes, one per letter of the word, so the length is visible.
- Add a setting per profile for the letter boxes, since the older kid finds them babyish.

I checked how the input is built now. It is a plain text input, and the boxes would be a visual layer over it, so the keyboard and autocorrect behavior stays unchanged. That keeps the risk low.

I also checked the tablet's touch targets in the layout. Three buttons are under 44 pixels. They are listed in the plan.

The soft sound needs a new file. I will generate it from the existing sound with lower pitch and a shorter tail, and compare it with the user.

Nothing was changed in code today. The first step comes next.

summary: Moved the read-again button next to the input, made it 72 pixels, and enlarged the three undersized touch targets found in the plan.
body:
The read-again button now sits directly under the input and is 72 pixels wide. It keeps the focus on the input after a tap, which matters because earlier the keyboard would close and the kid had to tap the field again.

The other undersized targets were the mute toggle, the profile switch link and the parent page link. All are 48 pixels or larger now, with spacing so they are not touched by accident. The parent link stays small on purpose in look but has a longer press area.

On the tablet, the keyboard stayed open after the read-again tap. On the laptop, the button worked with the keyboard as well.

I found that the button was still active during the five second hint delay animation, which pushed the layout by a few pixels. I fixed it by reserving the space in the CSS.

Next: the letter boxes.

summary: Wrote an explanation for the user of why the game's first word sometimes sounds different from the others, and found it was the voice choice falling back on a cold start.
body:
The user said the first word of a round sometimes sounds like another voice than the rest, and asked if something was broken. I looked at how the voice is chosen. The code picks the saved voice by name from the list, and if the name is missing it takes the first local voice for the language. On a cold start the list arrives late on the tablet, so the saved voice is not found at that moment.

The whenVoicesReady wait from earlier covers the empty list, but not a list that is partly filled. On the tablet the local voices sometimes load first and the preferred one a moment later. In that case the fallback was taken for the first word and the saved voice for the rest. I confirmed this by logging the chosen voice name before each word on a cold start. The log showed the fallback name once, then the saved name.

The fix was small. The voice is now resolved again after the voiceschanged event, and the first word waits until either the saved voice appears or the two second timeout ends. Only then does the fallback apply. I ran ten cold starts on the tablet and the first word used the saved voice nine times. The tenth hit the timeout, which is the intended behavior. I told the user this and that a rare fallback voice remains possible when the system is very slow.

summary: Swapped in a softer wrong-answer sound, kept the old one as an option per profile, and the user picked the lower version after hearing three variants.
body:
I made three variants of the soft sound with a script that lowers the pitch and shortens the tail: a mild one, a medium one and a very quiet one. The user and the younger kid listened on the tablet. The kid liked the medium one; the user preferred it because it still tells that something was wrong.

The file is about 9 KB. It is decoded on first tap like the other sounds, so the start time is unchanged.

The sound style is a per-profile setting with the values soft and classic. The older kid asked for classic, and it is set. The default for new profiles is soft.

I checked that the service worker precache picked up the new file through the build output, and that it plays with the network off.

summary: Reviewed the accessibility changes after a few days of use and found that the letter boxes broke on a very long word on the narrow layout, wrapping to a second line.
body:
The user reported that 'extraordinary' showed boxes wrapping onto two lines on the phone, with the second line hidden under the keyboard. Box width was fixed at 44 pixels, so thirteen letters needed more than the screen.

I changed the width to a CSS clamp based on the available width divided by letters, with a minimum of 24 pixels. Twelve-letter words fit in one row on a 360 pixel screen. Beyond that the boxes get thinner but stay in one row.

I checked the longest word in all lists, which is fourteen letters, and it fits. Other review points were fine: touch targets held, and the read-again button works. One small item remains: the focus ring on the boxes is too faint in bright light. I will raise its contrast later.

summary: Planned and started a weekly progress chart on the parent page, choosing a simple bar per week per profile drawn with plain SVG and no library.
body:
The user wants to see whether the kids improve over the weeks. The report page already has counts per profile, so a chart is the next step.

Decisions:
- Draw it as inline SVG made by a small function. A charting library would add more weight than the whole game.
- One bar per week showing percent correct on the first try, with hinted words counted as not perfect, matching the streak fix.
- Show the last twelve weeks, and leave a gap when a week has no rounds.
- One chart per profile, with the same color for the same kid as elsewhere.

I wrote the data function first: it groups finished rounds by the week of the school list and returns an array of week label, words, and perfect words. The week label comes from the list name, not the calendar, because the lists are the unit the kids care about.

Tests cover an empty history, a week with only hinted words, and rounds that spanned a list change. The last case found that a round started under one list and finished under another was counted twice. Rounds now belong to the list they started with.

The SVG part is not drawn yet. The data is ready, and the next session will render it.

summary: Rendered the weekly progress chart as SVG on the parent page, with labels, a gap for missing weeks, and a text fallback for screen readers.
body:
The renderer takes the week array and builds an SVG with a fixed viewBox, so it scales with the page. Bars are rectangles with height from the percent, and each has a title element with the numbers, so a long press or hover shows them.

Missing weeks leave an empty slot with a thin dotted line instead of a zero bar, because zero would look like the kid failed. The user asked for exactly that.

Below each chart there is a visually hidden table with the same numbers. It costs little and the SVG alone would say nothing to a screen reader.

Colors per kid come from the profile record. I found that two profiles created on the parent page could get the same color, because the color was chosen from the count of profiles. After a delete and an add, it collided. The color now picks the first unused one from the palette.

The chart looks fine on the laptop and the tablet. On the phone, the week labels overlap, and I will rotate or thin them out.

summary: Fixed the overlapping week labels on small screens by showing every second label below 480 pixels, and checked the chart with a full twelve weeks of test data.
body:
I generated twelve weeks of fake history for both profiles with a script and loaded it through the import function, which also tested the import once more.

On the phone-sized layout, labels overlapped. Rotating them made them hard to read for the kids, so I show every second one below 480 pixels and keep the bars at the same position. The title text on each bar still carries the full label.

With twelve weeks, the tallest bar touched the top edge, so I added a small margin. The y axis has two guide lines at 50 and 100 percent and no numbers on the lines other than that.

I also tried a profile with only one week of data. One lonely bar was wide and looked odd, so the bar width is now capped at a fixed maximum and centered.

The fake data is removed through the profile delete, which still works with the active profile fix from before.

summary: Answered the user's question why the chart showed a lower score for a week the kid said was easy: hinted words and the slow-start retries explained it.
body:
The user saw 60 percent for a week where the kid felt sure. I went through the stored rounds for that week. Nine rounds were finished, and in four of them the kid used the hint on one or two words. Hinted words count as not perfect, so the bar dropped.

Also, two rounds started during a slow voice load, and the kid typed the first word before it was spoken, which counted as wrong. The voice-ready fix of earlier removed most of that, but these rounds were from before it.

So the number is right for what it measures. I suggested a second, lighter bar or a note showing hinted words separately. The user agreed to try a small dot above the bar for each hinted word. I have not built it yet.

summary: Planned the sound-free quiet mode idea into a real small feature: a per-profile option that shows the word as text for a moment, after the user asked about a noisy classroom.
body:
The user said one kid sometimes plays in a room where the sound disturbs others, and asked if the game could work quietly. First I wrote down what quiet should mean. The word cannot be read aloud, so it has to be shown, and a spelling game that shows the word is only a copy exercise. The compromise we discussed is to show the word for a short time, then hide it, and let the kid type it from memory.

The plan has four parts. One is a per-profile setting called Quiet mode, stored next to the volume and mute values from the recent work. Two is the reveal: the word appears in large letters for a time that depends on its length, about one second per two letters, with a minimum of three seconds. Three is a Show again button that replaces the read-again button in this mode, and counts like a hint in the weekly report. Four is that the sound effects follow the mute setting as before, so quiet mode does not change them.

I looked at the code to see how much work this is. The round code calls a speak function in one place for the word and one place for the repeat. Both can go through a small presenter that either speaks or shows, chosen by the profile setting. That keeps the round logic unchanged. The tile mode also needs a check, because the tiles must not appear before the word is hidden, otherwise the kid could read the letters off them.

There are two open questions for the user. The first is whether a repeat view should count against the perfect word, as a hint does. I suggested yes, because otherwise the streak message would praise looking. The second is whether the reveal time should be adjustable. I suggested a fixed rule first and a setting only if the kids complain. I also noted that the end-of-week summary needs no change, since it shows the same ticks and dots.

The order of work is the presenter, then the setting and the parent page toggle, then the reveal timing, then the report. I will start with the presenter next session and wait for the user's answers on the two questions before the report part.

summary: Planned a small redesign of the start screen: fewer buttons, a larger play button, and the profile picker at the top, based on how the kids actually tap.
body:
The start screen grew with each feature. It now has the play button, picker, streak line, mute, volume, speed, and the parent link. The kids only use the picker and play.

Plan:
- Play becomes the largest element, with the profile name shown on it.
- Volume, speed and sound style move into a settings panel opened by a gear button.
- The streak line stays, directly above play.
- The parent link stays small in the corner, behind a simple hold of one second so the kids do not wander into it.

I looked at the CSS and found that about half of the rules are overrides added over time. I will tidy them while moving the markup, but only in the files touched.

Risks: the service worker caches the old markup; the update flow waits for the end of a round, so tablets pick it up fine. The hold-to-open parent link needs touch and mouse events both.

No code was changed. Next entry: markup and CSS for the new layout.

summary: Rebuilt the start screen markup with a big play button and a settings panel behind a gear, and removed about forty lines of override CSS.
body:
The new layout puts the profile picker on top, the streak line, and a play button that fills most of the width and shows the kid's name. The gear opens a panel with volume, speed and sound style, using the same setSettings calls as before, so no logic changed.

While moving rules, I deleted override CSS that no longer matched anything. I checked with a quick search for each class name before removing it. About forty lines went away.

The panel closes on a tap outside and on Escape. Focus goes to the first control when it opens and back to the gear when it closes.

The parent link is next. For now it is in the corner and still opens with a tap.

summary: Added the one-second hold to open the parent page, with touch and mouse handling and a progress ring, and found that the tablet's long-press menu interfered.
body:
The parent link now needs a hold of one second. A thin ring fills around it while held, and releasing early cancels.

On the tablet, a long press on a link opened the browser's context menu in the middle of the hold. I made it a button instead of an anchor, used pointer events, and prevented the contextmenu event on it. That fixed it. The navigation happens through a script call after the hold.

Pointer events replaced separate touch and mouse code, so there is only one path. I tested pointercancel, which fires when the page scrolls, and the hold stops correctly.

The keyboard route: Enter on the focused button opens right away, since keyboard users cannot hold. The user is the only keyboard user, and said fine.

The kids tried to open it for two minutes and gave up, which was the goal.

summary: Checked the redesigned start screen on the old tablet, the phone and the laptop, and fixed a gear panel that was cut off at the bottom on the small screen.
body:
On the phone-sized layout the settings panel ran below the visible area, because it was positioned with a fixed offset from the top. I changed it to a bottom sheet that scrolls internally and has a maximum height of 80 percent of the viewport.

The old tablet showed the play button at the right size, but the streak line wrapped to two lines for a long kid name. I set the name to truncate with an ellipsis on the button and left the full name in the picker.

The laptop was fine. I also made sure the service worker delivered the new markup: after one round on the tablet, the reload waited for the end screen and the new layout appeared.

Nothing else is open for the redesign.

summary: Looked at the service worker cache after the user asked why the site used more storage on the tablet, and found two old build caches that the cleanup missed.
body:
The user noticed on the tablet that the site was holding more storage than expected and asked whether the offline mode was growing without limit. I opened the storage view in the browser and listed the caches. There were four entries: the current precache, the word list cache, and two older precaches from builds several weeks back. The cleanup that runs on activation should have removed those.

Reading the activate handler, I found that it deleted caches whose name did not match the current version string. The two old ones carried a name from before the version prefix was changed, so the comparison treated them as unrelated caches and left them alone. That prefix change happened during the review fixes a while ago. The old names started with a different word, which the filter never matched.

I changed the filter to delete every cache that belongs to this app by a shared prefix check, plus the legacy prefix, except the two current names. I tested it in a clean profile by first installing an old build, then the new one. After activation only the two current caches remained. On the tablet the storage use dropped by about 3 MB, mostly sound files. I told the user the growth was bounded and that it was a leftover and not a leak.

summary: Investigated a report that the game said a word twice at the start of a round on the laptop and traced it to the voiceschanged handler firing a second speak call.
body:
The user heard the first word twice on the laptop, but not on the tablet. I reproduced it by reloading with the cache empty.

The cause: whenVoicesReady resolves on the first voiceschanged event, but the round code had also registered its own listener to speak the first word if the voices came late, left from before the helper existed. Both fired. On the tablet the list is ready at once, so neither path ran twice.

I removed the old listener, so the first word is spoken only after whenVoicesReady resolves. I added a guard so speakWord ignores a second call for the same word within 500 milliseconds, which protects against similar slips.

Tests: a fake speech object that fires voiceschanged twice now produces one utterance. I checked the laptop again with ten reloads and heard one word each time.

summary: Planned and wrote a small end-of-week summary screen that shows the kid's ten words with a tick, a hint dot or a miss, to make the weekly list feel finished.
body:
The user asked for something that marks the end of a school week, since the kids tend to stop when the list is done and nothing says so. The idea is a screen after the last round of a list showing all ten words.

Design: each word is a row with a tick if it was perfect in the most recent round, a dot if hinted, and a cross if missed. A line on top says how many are perfect. If all ten are perfect, a short celebration plays, using the existing sound set and no new files.

The data comes from the stored rounds for the list. I decided to use the best result per word over the week, not the last, because kids who practice should see progress. The user agreed.

First problem: how to know the list is finished. A list counts as finished when every word has at least one perfect result, or when the kid has played five rounds of it. The second rule keeps a kid from being stuck on a hard word.

I wrote a function weekStatus(profileId, listId) returning words with states and a finished flag. Tests cover no rounds, partial, all perfect, five rounds with misses, and hinted-only words, which must not count as perfect.

The screen itself is built with the same row style as the report page. It is shown once per list per profile, tracked with a field in the profile record, so it does not return on every visit. The migration for the new field uses the same versioned approach as before.

An issue found late: deleting a profile left its seen flags in a separate key. I put the flag inside the profile record, so the delete removes it with the rest.

The next step is to try it with the kids on the new list.

summary: Watched both kids finish a list with the summary screen and fixed a ten-word row layout that needed scrolling on the small tablet.
body:
The older kid finished the list after four rounds and saw eight ticks, one dot and one cross. They immediately wanted to replay the missed word, which is a good sign.

On the small tablet the ten rows did not fit and the continue button was below the fold. I reduced row height and used two columns in landscape. The button is now fixed to the bottom.

The younger kid did not read the top line but liked the ticks. I made the text larger. The celebration sound played for a full list as intended.

summary: Reviewed the last weeks of work, tidied leftovers in storage keys and settings, and wrote down a short list of ideas the user may want before the kids lose interest.
body:
I went through the code touched since the profiles went in. Findings:
- Two old storage keys from the single-kid time were still read by an export function. The migration had moved the data, so the export now ignores them, and the old keys are removed after the migration has run twice without issue.
- The settings module had a default for a sound style value that no longer exists, 'normal'. It maps to 'classic' now.
- The summary screen flag and the profile delete are consistent.
- A test file still used a global clock stub that leaked into other tests. I scoped it to the file.

I also ran the full test suite and the word list check. All 112 tests pass, and the build is about 84 KB gzipped including sounds loaded lazily.

On the use of the game: the user said the kids play about three times a week, mostly before the school test. That matches the report page.

Ideas the user may want, none started:
- A practice mode with only the missed words of the week.
- Reading the word in a sentence, typed by the parent on the parent page.
- A printable list of the week's results.

The user liked the first and will decide about the others after talking to the kids. The first one is the likely next step.

summary: Went through the idea list from the review and picked three for the user: a word-of-the-day replay, a slower voice option, and a printable week sheet.
body:
The review of the last weeks ended with a short list of ideas, so this session turned it into choices the user can answer quickly. Seven ideas were on the list. I cut it to three that fit the time the kids still seem to want the game.

The first is a replay of the words the kid missed in the week, shown as a short extra round on the start screen. The data is already in the summary screen, so the work is small: filter the ten results for misses and hinted words, and feed them to the round loader. I estimated about two hours.

The second is a slower voice option per profile. The speech API takes a rate value, and the settings object per profile already exists since the mute fix. The youngest kid often asks for the word again, which suggests the default speed is too quick for them. I would add a three-step choice: slow, normal, fast. Rates would be 0.7, 0.9 and 1.1.

The third is a printable week sheet on the parent page, with the ten words and the results, for the fridge. It needs only a print stylesheet and a button. I left out the ideas for badges, a leaderboard between the two kids and a word-definition popup. A leaderboard could cause quarrels, and the definitions would need a source for every word.

I wrote the three options with their size into a note for the user and asked which to do first. Nothing was changed in the code today. The next step depends on the answer, and the slower voice looks like the most likely pick.

summary: The user chose the slower voice and the replay round; built the per-profile speech rate with three steps and checked that the voice reads at the new speeds.
body:
The user answered the idea list this evening: the slower voice first, then the replay of missed words. I started with the voice rate.

The profile settings got a new field, speechRate, with the values slow, normal and fast. They map to 0.7, 0.9 and 1.1 on the utterance. Old stored profiles have no such field, so the loader fills in normal when it is missing. I checked this by loading a saved profile from before the change, and it came up with normal and no error.

The settings panel behind the gear got a three-button choice. I used the same big-tile style as the start screen so a small finger can hit it. The selected button has a thick outline and not only a colour, because colour alone was a problem in the accessibility review.

One thing surprised me. On the laptop the rate of 0.7 sounded fine, but on the old tablet the default voice ignored values below 0.8 and read at the same speed. I tested this by logging the utterance rate and listening to the three steps. The fix was to pick 0.8 as the slow value on that voice, but I do not want a per-device table. So I set slow to 0.8 everywhere, which is still clearly slower than 0.9 on the laptop and audible on the tablet.

The parent page reset button now also resets the rate to normal. I added the rate to the export file and made the import accept files without it. Tomorrow I will test with the kids on the tablet and then start the replay round.

summary: Built the missed-words replay round: after finishing a list, a button starts a short round of only the missed and hinted words, and it does not touch the weekly score.
body:
The replay round was built today. The summary screen already knows which of the ten words were missed or needed a hint, so I reused that result list.

A new button, 'Try the tricky ones', appears on the summary screen only when at least one word is marked. It starts a normal round with just those words. The round code did not need changes beyond a flag, practice, that says the result must not be written to the weekly scores. Without the flag the first test wrote the practice results over the real week, and the chart showed a perfect score. I caught that on the second run and added a test that plays a practice round and compares the stored week before and after.

The practice round has no hints at first, but I left the hint button in. The kid can still use it, though a hinted word stays in the tricky list for the next practice.

A question was what to do when a kid gets all tricky words right: I show a short message and a plain tick list, no extra sound. With zero tricky words the button is hidden. With ten tricky words the round is the whole list again, which felt odd, so I capped it at five words, taking the missed ones first.

I tried it with test data for both profiles on the laptop. It still needs a check on the tablet with a kid, planned for the weekend.

summary: Watched the youngest kid use the slow voice and the tricky-words round on the tablet; both worked, but the button label was too long and was shortened.
body:
I sat with the youngest kid on the kitchen tablet for one full list, with the slow speech rate and the new practice round.

The slow voice was picked right away. The kid pressed the read-again button less often than before, three times in ten words instead of what I remember as about six. That is a small sample, so I note it as a good sign only.

The practice round worked. Two words were missed and one hinted, so three words came up. The kid finished them without help. The label 'Try the tricky ones' wrapped to two lines on the tablet and the kid did not read it, just tapped the big button. I changed the label to 'Practice' with a small repeat icon, and the button now fits on one line.

One bug: after the practice round, going back to the summary screen showed the old marks, which is right, but the kid thought the misses had not been fixed. I added a line under the list, 'Practice does not change your score', in simple words. A better answer might be to show a second small tick next to the practiced words, but that would need a new field. I left it for later and noted it.

summary: Printable week sheet on the parent page: a print stylesheet shows the ten words and results for the chosen profile, one page, no buttons.
body:
Started the third idea from the list, the printable week sheet. The parent page now has a Print button next to the weekly chart.

The approach is a print stylesheet and not a separate page. With @media print the stylesheet hides the hold ring, the chart controls, the backup section and all buttons. It shows a block with the profile name, the ten words of the week, and the result of each word as a tick, a dot or a cross. For a printer without colour the marks are letters-shaped symbols, and not only colour.

The data comes from the same function that fills the summary screen. I made it return a plain list so both screens use one source. That removed a copy of about thirty lines.

In the browser print preview the page broke after seven words on the laptop because the chart was still taking space. Hiding it with display none fixed it. The text was too small at first, so I set the word size to 18 points with a line spacing that fits on the fridge sheet.

Not done yet: choosing a past week. For now the sheet prints only the current week. I will look at the week selector tomorrow if the user wants it.

summary: Tested the print sheet with a real printer and the second profile, found the profile name missing when both kids were set up, and fixed the selector.
body:
Today I printed the week sheet on the user's home printer for the first time, with both profiles.

The first print had the right words but the wrong name: it always showed the first profile, even after the second kid was chosen on the parent page. The print function read the active profile of the game, not the one picked in the parent page. After my earlier shared-state bugs I checked this first. The fix was to pass the profile id from the parent page's own picker to the sheet.

The second print was fine. One page, ten words, readable at arm's length. The user said the cross marks looked too harsh for a young child, so I changed them to an empty circle for a miss and kept the tick and the dot. The legend line at the bottom says what each mark means.

I also added a check for a week with fewer than ten results. When a kid played only six words, the missing ones show a dash. Before the change the sheet showed four empty lines that looked like errors.

The week selector for old weeks is still open. The scores store data per week key, so it should be easy, but I want to see first if anyone prints the sheet more than once.

summary: Answered the user's question whether the slow voice setting should become the default for the youngest profile, and advised keeping normal for now.
body:
The user asked if the slow voice should simply be the default for the youngest kid. I looked at what the code does for new profiles and what the settings look like.

New profiles start with normal. Changing the default would only affect profiles created later, since existing ones keep their stored value. The youngest kid's profile already has slow set, so a default change gives nothing today.

I advised against changing the default. A new profile for an older kid would start slow, and the user would have to change it. The setting is one tap in the gear panel. I also noted that the old tablet ignores rates below 0.8, so the difference between steps is small there.

The user agreed to leave it. Nothing was changed in the code.

summary: Added a week selector to the print sheet after the user wanted last week's results for the fridge, using the existing week keys in storage.
body:
The user asked to print last week's sheet, since the kids brought a new list on the same day. So the week selector came earlier than planned.

The scores are stored under a week key per profile, so the selector reads those keys, sorts them from newest to oldest and shows them as a dropdown with a readable label such as 'This week' and 'Last week', then 'Two weeks ago' and so on. I avoided calendar dates in the labels because the weeks of the school do not match calendar weeks, and the key is just a counter of lists.

The print function takes the chosen key. The word list for an old week comes from the stored result, not from the current JSON file, which matters because the list files are replaced by new ones. A first version looked the words up in the JSON and printed blanks for old weeks. The stored results hold the word text, so I used that.

I tested with the twelve weeks of test data from the chart work and with a real profile that had four weeks. Selecting a week with no data shows 'No results for this week' and disables the button.

The dropdown is tall on the small tablet, so I limited it to the last eight weeks. That is enough for a fridge sheet.

summary: Looked into a report that the voice sounded robotic after a browser update on the laptop and found the preferred voice name had changed, so the fallback was used.
body:
The user said that on the laptop the game suddenly sounded flat and robotic. Nothing in the code had changed, so I suspected the browser update from a few days earlier.

I logged the list from speechSynthesis.getVoices(). The voice we preferred by exact name was still there, but its name had a suffix added, so the exact match failed and the code fell back to the first voice of the right language. That is the flat one.

The voice choice in the code was a strict name comparison. I changed it to a ranked search: first an exact name match, then a name that starts with the stored name, then any voice of the language that is marked as local, then the first of the language. The chosen voice name is logged once at the start of a round.

After the change the laptop picked the right voice again. I also checked the tablet, where the name had not changed, and it still picked the same voice as before.

The stored voice name in the profile is kept as the user chose it. I did not rewrite it, so that a future change in the other direction also works. I wrote down that voice names are not stable across updates.

summary: Added a small voice picker in the settings that lists the available voices with a test button, after the voice name problem showed the user could not see which one was in use.
body:
After the name change of the voice, the user wanted to see and choose the voice without asking me. So I added a voice picker to the settings panel on the parent page.

It lists the voices of the right language from getVoices(), with a Play button next to each that says a sample word. The choice is stored per profile as before. The list is filled again on the voiceschanged event, and I made sure this handler does not start a speak call, because of the double-word bug of the earlier weeks.

The lists differ between devices. The laptop shows six voices and the tablet two. On the tablet one voice is marked as network and fails when the tablet is offline. I show a small 'online only' note for voices that are not local, using the localService flag.

I tested by choosing a voice, reloading and checking it stuck. I also tested with a stored voice that no longer exists: the picker shows nothing selected, and the ranked search from the last fix still finds a good voice.

It is a parent-only control, hidden behind the one-second hold. The kids do not see it.

summary: Fixed the picker so the sample word plays at the profile's speech rate and cancels any earlier sample, after quick taps stacked up several voices at once.
body:
While testing the voice picker with the youngest kid watching, a few fast taps on different Play buttons made several voices talk at once. It sounded messy and the kid laughed, but it is a real bug.

The sample function called speak without cancelling the queue. I added speechSynthesis.cancel() before each sample. The same call was missing in one more place, the read-again button, where a double tap queued the word twice. I added it there too, with a short guard so the cancel does not eat the first speak call on the browser that needs a small delay after cancel.

The sample was also read at the default rate, not at the profile's rate. For a parent choosing a voice for the slow profile this was misleading. It now uses the profile's rate.

I checked on the laptop and the tablet by tapping quickly ten times. Only the last sample is heard on both. On the tablet there was a half-second gap before the sample started, which comes from the cancel. I think it is acceptable for a parent page.

No new files; changes in the speech helper and the picker.

summary: Planned a new word list for a school unit about words with silent letters, after the user shared the week lists, and checked the lists against the validation script.
body:
The user brought the next four weekly lists from school and asked me to add them. Two weeks have words with silent letters, such as knight, island and honest, which are harder to hear.

I added four JSON files in the same format as before. The check script that runs in the build found one problem: a word with a typographic apostrophe, which the script flags as an odd character. The school sheet used the curly mark. I replaced it with a straight apostrophe. The game compares the typed answer with the word, and a kid's keyboard types the straight one, so this matches.

I thought about whether silent-letter words need an extra feature. A kid who hears 'nite' cannot know about the k. The hint button shows the first letter, which already helps with knight. For island the silent s is in the middle, so the hint does not help. I considered a second hint level that shows the first two letters, but that changes the score rules for hinted words. I noted it as a question for the user and did not build it.

The lists load by week number. I ran the build and all files passed. The weeks come up in the right order on the start screen.

Next I want to listen to each word with the slow voice to check that the speech engine says them clearly.

summary: Built the first-pass silent-letter word list for the school unit, ran the check script on it, and listened to every word at the slow voice speed to find odd readings.
body: The user shared the list of words from the silent letters unit, and I turned them into a new JSON file with the same ten-per-week layout as the older lists. The check script passed on the first run, with no duplicates, empty strings or odd characters. Then I played each word through the game at all three speech rates. Most words read fine, but "knead" and "wrap" came out ambiguous on the laptop voice, so I noted them as candidates for a say override. I did not add the overrides yet, since the tablet voice read both correctly and the tablet is where the kids play. The next step is to repeat the listening pass on the tablet and then decide whether any override is needed at all.

summary: The user asked whether a second hint level is worth it for silent letters; I wrote down the options and recommended a simple version without score changes.
body:
The user answered my question about silent letters and asked what a second hint level would cost.

I looked at the scoring code. A hinted word counts as half a point, and the summary screen shows a hint dot. A second level that gives more letters could keep the same half point, so no score rules change. The only difference is what the hint shows.

There are two ways. One is a second press of the hint button that shows the first two letters. The other is a hint that shows the word with the silent letters marked, which needs extra data in each word entry.
