The second way is better for the kid, but someone has to mark every word, and the school sends ten new words each week.

I recommended the first way. It needs no data and only about twenty lines of code. A kid who presses hint twice sees the first two letters, and the word still counts as hinted. The chart explanation from before still holds.

The user liked the simple version and said to build it. I will do it this afternoon.

summary: Built the second hint press that reveals the first two letters, keeping the half-point rule, and updated the summary screen and chart tests.
body:
Built the second hint level as agreed this morning.

The hint button now has a counter per word. The first press shows the first letter as before. A second press shows the first two letters. A third press does nothing and the button is disabled for that word. The counter resets with each new word.

Scoring is unchanged: any hint at all makes the word half a point and sets the hinted flag, and pressing twice does not cost more. I added a test for this because the chart explanation depends on it. The test plays a word with two presses and reads back the half point.

In the interface the letter boxes show the revealed letters in a lighter colour so the kid can tell what was given. For a long word on the narrow layout I checked that the revealed boxes do not wrap, since that was a problem in the accessibility review. They stayed on one line.

One problem: the first test showed the second press revealing letters even when the kid had already typed the first letter. The typed text was then overwritten. I changed it so the revealed letters only fill empty boxes, and typed letters are never replaced.

I also updated the print sheet and the summary screen, which both read the hinted flag. They needed no change, but I ran them to be sure. The keyboard handler on the laptop already treated the hint key, so a second press works from the keyboard too.

The kids will try it on the tablet over the weekend.

summary: Watched the older kid use the double hint on a silent-letter list and saw that pressing hint twice quickly was common, so the second reveal got a short pause.
body:
The older kid played the knight and island week on the laptop. The double hint was used on four of ten words, which suggests it fits the list.

The kid often pressed hint twice at once, as a double click, and got both letters before trying to think. That makes the half point cost the same but wastes the idea of a gentle help. I added a short pause of one second before the second press is accepted, with the button looking dimmed in that time.

I tried it and the pause feels fine; it is not long enough to annoy. The kid did not notice it.

summary: Looked at a report that scores were not saved after the tablet went to sleep in the middle of a round, and found the save only happened at the end of the list.
body:
The user said the youngest kid played six words, the tablet went to sleep, and the scores of the round were gone when the game was opened again.

I read the round code. The results of a list are kept in memory and written to local storage only when the tenth word is done. A sleeping tablet can discard the page, and the six answers go with it. In the earlier weeks the kids always finished at once, so this did not show.

The fix is to write after every word. The function that saves the week already merges into the stored object, so calling it after each answer is cheap, ten small writes per list. I added the call and a test that stops a round after three words and reads the stored result.

On load, a list that is partly done is shown on the start screen as 'Continue', and the kid goes on with the next word. The summary screen only appears when all ten are done.

summary: Built the continue-a-list behaviour and tested the sleep case on the tablet, including a kid switching profiles halfway and a new list arriving while one was unfinished.
body:
This follows the fix from earlier today: results are saved after each word, and now the game can pick up where the kid stopped.

The start screen shows a Continue button when the current week has between one and nine results for the active profile. It starts the round at the next word without a result. The order of words in a round is shuffled at the start, so I had to keep the order too. I store the shuffled order of word indexes with the week, and Continue reads it. Without it the game would have asked words that were already done.

Three edge cases I tested.

First, the kid switches profile halfway. Each profile has its own partial week, so the other kid sees their own Continue or a fresh start. This was fine, and I checked it because of the shared state bugs of earlier weeks.

Second, a new list arrives while the old one is unfinished. The week key changes with the new file, so the old partial result stays in storage and the start screen shows the new list as fresh. The old one is not offered to continue, which I think is right, since the school has moved on. The print sheet can still show it by the week selector.

Third, the kid taps Continue and the stored order has an index that no longer exists because the list file was edited. I handle this by dropping the partial result and starting fresh, with a note in the console.

On the tablet I started a round, answered four words, locked the screen for five minutes, and opened the game again. The Continue button was there and the fifth word came. I did the same with the browser closed and it also worked.

The practice round is not saved this way, since it is short and never counts. The export file includes the order field and the import ignores it if missing.

summary: Wrote a short plan for the remaining months: only small fixes and new lists are expected, since the kids use the game less, with three checks to do when a browser update lands.
body:
The kids have been playing less in the last weeks. The youngest plays about twice a week, the older one less, and the school mentioned a new app that may replace the weekly lists.

Given this, I wrote a plan that keeps the work small. New features are not worth the effort now. What matters is that the game keeps working when the user opens it.

Three checks to do after a browser update: first, the voice list and the voice choice, since names changed once already. Second, the service worker cache, to see that old build caches are removed. Third, the local storage export and import, with a backup file from an old version.

I also listed what to do with a new list: put the JSON file in the folder, run the build, listen to each word once at the slow rate, and look for words that need a say override.

The plan is in the notes file in the repository. Nothing in the code changed.

summary: A new browser version broke the on-screen keyboard behaviour on the tablet: the input scrolled out of view, fixed by keeping the letter boxes above the keyboard with a viewport height rule.
body:
After the tablet's browser updated, the user reported that the letter boxes disappeared behind the on-screen keyboard when typing a word.

I reproduced it on the tablet. The page used 100vh for the game area. In the new version, 100vh stays the full height and does not shrink when the keyboard opens, so the boxes sat under the keyboard. Before the update the viewport did shrink.

The fix uses the dynamic viewport unit, 100dvh, with a fallback to 100vh for older browsers. I put both in the CSS in that order. With that, the game area shrinks with the keyboard and the boxes stay visible above it.

A second problem showed up: the read-again button, which sits next to the input, moved under the boxes on the narrow layout when the area got short. I changed the layout so the button stays at the right of the boxes and the boxes wrap their size down for long words. I checked it with the longest word of the lists, 15 letters.

I tested on the tablet in both orientations and on the phone. In landscape the keyboard takes most of the screen and the boxes fit, but the play button is hidden, which is fine during a word.

The laptop was not affected. I also ran the three checks from the plan: the voice picked the same voice, the cache had one build only, and an old backup file imported. All passed.

summary: The preferred voice disappeared from the tablet after a system update, and the ranked fallback chose a worse one; added a warning on the parent page when the stored voice is missing.
body:
The user said the voice on the tablet sounded different again after a system update. I opened the voice picker and the voice the youngest kid's profile had chosen was no longer in the list at all. Not renamed, gone.

The ranked search from earlier found no match by name, so it took the first local voice of the language. That is a usable voice but it speaks quickly and the kid noticed the change.

I cannot bring the voice back, since it belongs to the system. What I can do is make the situation visible. The parent page now shows a small notice under the voice picker when the stored voice name is not found: 'The chosen voice is not available on this device. Using another one.' It also shows which voice is used instead.

I also improved the fallback order. Among the local voices of the language, it now prefers one whose name contains a hint of being a higher quality one, such as 'enhanced' or 'premium', before the first in the list. This is a guess based on the names on the laptop and the tablet, so I keep it as the third step only.

The tablet has two local voices left after the update. I let the user listen to both with the picker and they chose the calmer one for the youngest profile. This is stored by name, and the notice is gone.

I tested the notice by storing a fake voice name in a test profile and checking the text and the fallback voice shown. I also tested a profile with no stored voice, which should not show a notice, and it did not.

The lesson is the same as before: voices change with system updates, so the game must not depend on one. I added a line about this to the plan file.

summary: Added the next two school lists, ran the check script and the slow-voice listening pass, and found no new say overrides were needed.
body:
The user brought two more weekly lists from school. I added them as JSON files in the usual format.

The check script passed on the first run. No duplicates, no odd characters, and no empty strings. One word had a capital letter at the start, a name of a country, and the game compares the typed answer without case, so it is fine.

I listened to all twenty words at the slow rate on the laptop and the tablet. Every word was clear and none read with the wrong sense, so no say override was needed. The words this time are plain ones about weather and animals.

The lists show in order on the start screen.

summary: Small redesign pass on colours and fonts: larger letter boxes font, softer colours, and a dark theme that follows the system, with contrast values checked for each pair.
body:
The user asked for a small refresh of the look, since the kids have seen the same colours for a long time. I kept it to colours and type, with no layout changes.

The palette moved to CSS variables in one place. Before, colours were repeated in many rules, and I removed about twenty duplicates. The new palette has a soft blue for the background, a warm yellow for the play button and a green for right answers. Wrong answers are a muted orange and not red, which fits the softer sound from before.

The letter boxes use a rounder font at a larger size, 36 pixels on the tablet. I checked that the longest word still fits on one line on the narrow layout and it does with the box width reduced a little.

A dark theme was added with prefers-color-scheme. The tablet is used in the evening, and the white screen was bright. The dark values are variables too. I computed the contrast ratio for each text and background pair and the lowest was 4.9, above the 4.5 limit. The wrong-answer orange on the dark background first gave 3.8, so I made it lighter.

The hint dot, tick and circle marks on the summary screen and the print sheet keep their shapes. The print stylesheet forces a white background and black text, so the dark theme does not affect the paper.

I went through every screen: start, round, summary, parent page and the chart. The chart bars use the variables now, and the gap for missing weeks is still visible. A screenshot comparison was not possible, so I looked at them by hand on the laptop and the phone.

Tablet check is planned for tomorrow with the kids.

summary: Checked the refreshed look on the tablet with both kids in the evening; the youngest liked the yellow button, and a low-contrast gear icon was darkened.
body:
Both kids tried the new colours on the kitchen tablet after dinner, in the dark theme because the tablet switches in the evening.

The youngest noticed the change at once and said the play button looked like the sun. That is a good sign for the button. The older kid did not comment, which I take as no problem. Both finished a list without trouble and the letter boxes were easy to read.

One issue: the gear icon in the corner nearly vanished on the dark background. I had checked text contrast but not the icon. It was a thin grey line on dark blue. I made it lighter and thicker, and the ratio is now above 3 for graphics, as the guidance asks.

A second small issue was the progress ring of the one-second hold. On the dark theme it was drawn in the same colour as the background of the button, so it could not be seen. It now uses the yellow accent.

The summary screen looked fine in both themes, and the ten-word row still fits without scrolling on the small tablet. I also printed a sheet again to be sure that the dark theme does not leak into print, and the paper was black on white as before.

Nothing else is open from the redesign. The service worker picked up the new build on the next load. I checked that only one build cache remained after the update.

summary: Checked the word-list validation script against the two newest school lists and found it accepted a duplicate word across weeks, so it now warns about repeats.
body:
The user mentioned that a word seemed to come up twice in a month, so I ran the validation script over every list in the data folder. It checked length, characters and the say override field, but never compared lists with each other.

I added a cross-list pass in scripts/check-words.ts that builds a set of all words from earlier weeks and prints a warning for each repeat with the list file names. It is a warning, not an error, because the school sometimes repeats a tricky word on purpose.

The run found three repeats: 'knight', 'answer' and 'listen'. All three were in the silent-letter lists from the last weeks, so they are expected. I checked that the exit code stays zero with warnings only and non-zero when a word has an invalid character.

I also updated the short note in the README on how to run the check. Nothing changed in the game itself. Next I will wait for the next school list and run the script before listening to it.

summary: Planned and built a small word-of-the-day replay on the start screen that picks one earlier word and reads it, and left it off the score completely.
body:
The user chose the word-of-the-day idea from the earlier list, so this session built it. The start screen now has a small speaker button that reads one word from the lists the profile has already finished. Typing is not required; it is only a warm-up.

The pick has to be stable during one day, otherwise tapping the button twice gives two different words. I used a seeded choice from the local day number and the profile id, so each kid gets their own word that stays the same until the next day. The seed code lives in src/daily.ts and has a unit test for the same-day case and the next-day case.

If a profile has no finished list yet, the button is hidden rather than disabled. That avoided a grey button that the youngest kid would tap and wonder about.

The word is spoken at the profile's speech rate, using the same speak function as the game. I first called the speech API directly and the rate was ignored, which I noticed when listening at the slow setting. Going through speak fixed it and also cancels earlier speech.

I also checked that nothing is written to the score keys. The storage inspector on the laptop showed only the existing keys after five taps.

Tested on the laptop and the tablet. The button size is 48 pixels, which is easy to hit. Left to do is watching a kid use it, and deciding whether the word should also be shown as text after the second tap.

summary: Fixed a case where the end-of-week summary counted a replayed word as missed twice, after the user saw nine ticks and a strange total for the older kid.
body:
The user showed me a screenshot of the summary for the older kid with a total that did not match the rows. Nine rows had ticks and the total said 8.5 points, while the hint dots should have given 9.5 at most.

I reproduced it by finishing a list with one hint, starting the missed-words replay and answering that word wrong once, then right. The replay round was not supposed to touch the weekly score, but the summary read results from a shared array of attempts, and the replay pushed its attempts into the same array. The word then showed two entries, a hint and a miss.

The cause was in src/round.ts, where both the normal round and the replay used the same recordAttempt function without a flag. I added a mode argument, 'weekly' or 'replay', and the replay now writes to a separate in-memory list that is dropped at the end of the round.

I wrote a regression test with exactly this sequence. It failed before the change with 8.5 and passes with 9.5. I also ran the old tests for the half-point hint rule and the double hint, and they passed.

The stored data was not damaged. The array is rebuilt from the saved weekly result, and the replay entries were never saved, only shown in the live summary. So the kid's real score had been right all along, and I did not need a migration.

One more thing I checked was the print sheet, since it reads the same results. It read from storage and showed the right numbers.

I told the user the cause in short words and that a reload would also have shown the right total. No further work is needed for this one.

summary: Checked the tablet's storage use after the user noticed scores resetting for one kid, and found the profile list was read before the migration of old keys finished, so the fix reorders startup.
body:
The user said the older kid's streak showed zero on the tablet this morning, although it had been seven the evening before. I first suspected the continue-a-list change from a few weeks ago, since it also writes to storage, but the saved list state was intact and the streak was the only thing missing.

I opened the tablet's local storage through remote debugging on the laptop and looked at the keys. The streak value was there under the new per-profile key, but the profile list was being read before the small migration that renames old keys had run. On a cold start after the tablet had been off for a while, the streak read came back empty and the screen drew zero. A second load showed the right value, which is why it looked random.

The cause was in main.ts. The profile loader and the migration were both started at load, and the loader sometimes won. I made the migration a function that returns before the loader is called, and removed the second call that a leftover import made. No storage format changed, so nothing in the saved data needed repair.

To check it, I cleared the page, restored a copy of the old key layout by hand, and reloaded ten times on the laptop with the network throttled. The streak was correct every time. Then I did the same on the tablet with both profiles, including one with a half-finished list, and the numbers matched what I had written down before.

I also added a small test that calls the startup sequence with old keys present and expects the streak to read as seven. It failed on the old order and passes now. The score board and the summary screen read through the same loader, so they get the fix too.

Nothing was lost for the kid, since the value had never been overwritten. Still open: the migration code could be deleted, because no device should have old keys left, but I left it in for now in case the second tablet is switched on again. I told the user the streak is safe and asked them to say if it happens once more.

summary: Looked into slow start on the old tablet and found the word lists were all loaded at once; now only the current week and the previous one are fetched.
body:
The user said the game takes a long time to show the start screen on the old tablet. I measured with the remote inspector and found the first paint at about 2.8 seconds, with the browser fetching every JSON list in the data folder before showing anything.

There were 31 lists by then, around 90 KB in total. That is small, but the service worker also pre-cached them, and the first load on a cold cache did all the requests at once. On the old tablet the requests queued behind the font files.

I changed the loader in src/lists.ts to read the index file first, then fetch only the current week and the one before it for the replay and the summary. Older lists are fetched when the print sheet week selector asks for them. The service worker still caches them on demand.

After the change the first paint on the tablet was at about 1.4 seconds. The laptop did not show a real difference. I ran the offline test too: with the network off, the current week still loads from the cache, and an old week that was never opened shows a short message instead of a blank page.

I added that message text and a test for the index loader. A thing to watch is the word-of-the-day, which picks from finished lists, so it now needs the loader for older weeks. It worked in my test because it only uses lists the profile finished and those are cached by then, but I will watch it.

summary: Fixed the word-of-the-day button failing offline for an older list that was not cached, by choosing only from lists that are available in the cache.
body:
After the loader change of a few days ago, I checked the word-of-the-day in offline mode on the tablet, as I had planned. It failed for the older kid: the button did nothing and the console had a rejected fetch for a list from two months back.

The seed picked a finished list, and that list had not been opened since the service worker was installed, so it was not in the cache. My earlier assumption that finished lists are always cached was wrong, because a profile may have finished a list before the cache existed.

I changed src/daily.ts so the candidate lists are filtered by an availability check: the current and previous weeks are always there, and for others the code asks the cache with caches.match. If nothing else is available it falls back to the current week. The seed still gives a stable word during the day, provided the availability stays the same, which is true unless the network changes in the middle of the day. I accepted that small risk.

I wrote tests with a fake cache for three cases: all lists available, only the recent ones available and nothing finished. All of them pass.

On the tablet with the airplane mode on, the button now reads a word each time. I also tried it online after clearing the cache, and the word came from the network as before.

I looked at whether the replay round for missed words has the same problem. It only uses the list of the week just finished, which is always loaded, so it is fine.

I wrote down in the notes file that every new feature that reads old lists must go through the availability check. That is the only follow-up.

summary: Planned the work for a new school unit on plurals and compound words after the user shared the next lists, and found two words where the voice reads them oddly.
body:
The user sent the lists for the next unit, which has plurals like 'knives' and 'mice' and compound words like 'rainbow' and 'sunflower'. I started by planning the steps: add the files, run the check script, listen to every word at normal and slow speed, and add say overrides if needed.

I created the five list files with the week keys in the existing naming scheme and updated the index. The check script passed with one warning for a repeat of 'friend', which is expected.

Then I listened to all 50 words. Two of them were read oddly. 'Lead' in the compound 'leadership' list was read as the metal, and 'wind' in 'windmill' was read like winding a clock on the tablet voice. The laptop voice got both right, so the problem depends on the voice.

For these two I thought about the say override field, which holds a respelling used only for speech. For 'windmill' I tried 'wind mill' and the voice read it with the long vowel, so I wrote 'wihnd mill' and that sounded right. For 'leadership' I used 'leed ership'. The shown word is still the real one.

I did not commit yet because I want to listen to the overrides once more with the second voice from the picker. That is the next session.

summary: Committed the plurals and compound lists with the two say overrides and checked all fifty words with both voices from the picker.
body:
I listened again to the new unit, this time with the second voice that the picker offers on the tablet, to be sure the overrides do not make things worse for the other voice.

The override 'wihnd mill' is read correctly by both voices. 'Leed ership' was fine on the tablet voice but on the laptop voice it sounded like two words with a pause. I changed it to 'leedership', which is read as one word by both. Listening to it at the slow speed also worked.

The rest of the words were fine at all three speech rates. I paid extra attention to 'mice' and 'geese', since short words can be clipped at the fast rate. They were clear.

Then I ran the check script again. It passed, with the same warning for 'friend'. I also ran the unit tests and the build; the bundle size is unchanged, because the lists are loaded as separate files.

I opened the game in the offline mode to make sure the new lists are in the precache list of the service worker. The worker is generated from the index, so the new files appear there without a change. The cache version string changed, so old caches get cleaned up, and I verified there were no leftover caches in the storage panel.

I committed the lists and the overrides together with a short message. Next is to see how the kids do with the first week, and in particular whether the youngest has trouble with the compound words.

summary: Watched the kids do the plurals week and found the youngest got 'sunflower' wrong most often because the letter boxes ran out before the typed word, so box count now follows the word.
body:
I looked at the stored results after the first days of the plurals unit and then watched the youngest kid play on the tablet in the morning. The youngest missed 'sunflower' and 'rainbow' three times, while other long words were fine.

Watching the screen showed the cause. The letter boxes are drawn per word, but the row wraps for words over eight letters on the small screen, and the second row of boxes was hidden under the keyboard after the viewport fix of some weeks ago. The kid kept typing but could not see the boxes, lost the place and added a letter.

I looked at the CSS in the letter box row. The boxes had a fixed size of 44 pixels with a gap, so nine boxes needed more width than the small tablet gives in portrait. I changed the size to a clamp based on the container width, so all boxes stay in one row up to twelve letters, with a minimum of 28 pixels. The font inside shrinks with the box.

I checked the sizes on the small tablet, the phone and the laptop. On the phone with twelve letters the boxes are 28 pixels wide, which is still tappable, although typing is done with the keyboard. I also checked the dark theme and the focus ring, which are not cut off.

Then I ran the tests. The snapshot test for the letter row changed, as expected, and I updated it.

The youngest kid tried 'sunflower' again after the change and got it right on the second try. The first try was an actual spelling mistake, 'sunflowr', which is fine.

One thing I noticed was that the hint reveal for the first two letters still works, because it fills boxes by index. I tested it with a twelve-letter word.

There is no further work for this, but I will check a long word in the next list.

summary: Reviewed a browser update that changed autoplay rules for the speech API on the tablet and found the first word of a round stayed silent until a tap.
body:
The user reported that after a browser update on the tablet the first word of a round was not read aloud, and the kid had to press the repeat button. I ran through the checklist from the plan I wrote for browser updates and the speech check was the one that failed.

I reproduced it on the tablet. When the page loads and the kid taps the start button, the round starts and the first speak call happens. The new version treats it as speech without a user gesture when the call comes after an awaited list fetch, since the gesture is considered used up after a short time. The console showed 'speechSynthesis.speak() blocked, no user activation'.

The start flow was: tap, fetch the list, build the round, speak. The fetch for the current week usually comes from the cache, but on a cold start it takes long enough to lose the gesture.

The fix was to unlock speech inside the tap handler. On the first tap I now call speak with an empty utterance at volume zero, synchronously, and then continue as before. After that the later speak calls work, also after the fetch. I put it in src/speech.ts as unlockSpeech and call it once per page load.

I tested on the tablet with a cold cache, a warm cache and airplane mode. The first word was read in all three. I also checked the laptop, where the old behaviour was fine, and the unlock call did nothing bad there.

I added a note to the plan file under the browser update checks: after an update, load the page cold and listen to the first word without touching anything else.

One leftover is that the empty utterance sometimes makes a faint click on the tablet speaker. I could not decide if it is the unlock or the speaker, so I left it, and I will ask the kids if they notice.

The unit tests for the speech module use a fake synth, so I added a test that unlockSpeech is called once and not again.

summary: Asked the kids about the faint click from the speech unlock; neither noticed it, so the code stays as it is.
body:
I had left the faint click question open after the autoplay fix. This morning I let both kids play a round on the tablet and asked them if they heard anything odd at the start.

Neither of them noticed a click. The older kid said the game sounded the same as before. I also listened with the volume at the highest step and the click was only there when the room was completely quiet.

I tried a variant with a single space as the utterance text instead of an empty string, but it made no difference to the click, so I dropped it. The empty utterance stays.

I closed that item in the plan notes. Nothing was committed in this session.

summary: Added the next two school lists, ran the check and listening pass, and found the voice reads 'colonel' with the wrong sound so it got a say override.
body:
The user sent two new weeks of words, one about words from other languages and one mixed review. I added both files, updated the index and ran the check script.

The check passed with warnings for four repeats from the review week, which is the point of a review, so I left them. The warnings listed the file names correctly.

The listening pass at the normal speed found one real problem. 'Colonel' was read as 'co-lo-nel' by the tablet voice, which is the opposite of what the kid should hear. The laptop voice read it right, but the kid uses the tablet. I tried 'kernel', which gives the correct sound on both voices.

There was also 'ballet', which the tablet voice read with a hard final t. I wrote 'bally' as the override, and that sounded right at all three rates. 'Bouquet' was fine.

I listened to the overrides at the slow rate as well, since the slow rate sometimes breaks respellings. 'Kernel' was fine, 'bally' sounded a little short but clear.

The tests and the build passed. I committed both lists and the two overrides, and I added a line to the notes file listing the override words, so that the user can see which ones exist.

Nothing else is open for these lists.

summary: Looked at a report that the summary screen showed last week's results for the second kid after a profile switch, and fixed a stale profile id in the summary state.
body:
In the evening the user said the second kid saw the first kid's tick marks on the summary screen after the kids swapped on the same tablet. The totals were right in storage, so this was a display problem.

I reproduced it: finish a list as profile one, go back to the start screen, switch to profile two and open the summary from the week list. The rows were those of profile one. The summary module kept its results in a module-level variable that was filled when a round ended and never cleared when the profile changed.

The fix was to stop caching in a variable. The summary now reads the results from storage using the active profile id each time it opens, with the live round results only used right at the end of a round. I removed the module variable in src/summary.ts and made the profile switch handler reset the screen state as well.

I wrote a test with two profiles and a switch between them. It failed before the change, showing the other profile's rows, and passes now.

I also checked the print sheet, which reads from storage by profile and was correct, and the missed-words replay, which builds its list from the finished round of the active profile. That one has the same kind of state, so I tested a switch there. It cleared properly because the replay list is built at the button press.

On the tablet I switched profiles several times and the summary showed the correct rows each time. No data was changed, so there is no migration. I told the user the cause in a sentence and that the totals were never wrong.

summary: Checked the game after the latest browser update using the three-point list from the plan and found everything working, with only a small shift in the gear panel position.
body:
A new browser version arrived on the laptop and the tablet, so I went through the three checks from the plan: the first word read after a cold load, the on-screen keyboard with the letter boxes, and the stored voice still available.

The cold load test passed on both devices. The first word was read without any tap besides the start button, which shows the unlock fix is still working. The keyboard test also passed: the letter boxes stayed above the keyboard, also for a twelve-letter word, and the box sizes were the ones from the last change.

The voice check on the parent page showed no warning, so the preferred voice is still there. I opened the picker as well and the list had the same voices as before, with the same order.

While looking around I saw that the gear panel opens about 6 pixels lower than before on the tablet. It is not cut off, and I think it comes from a changed default for the safe-area inset. I decided not to spend time on it, since it looks fine and the kids will not notice.

I also ran the offline mode once and checked that the cache cleanup left only the current build cache. The storage panel showed one cache.

Nothing was changed in code during this session. I added a line to the plan notes with the browser version and the result of each check, so that the next update has something to compare with.

summary: Browser update broke the speech voice list: getVoices() returned an empty array on first call, so the game spoke in the default voice or stayed silent.
body:
The user reported that the game went quiet on the tablet after the browser updated overnight. I reproduced it in the desktop browser: speechSynthesis.getVoices() returned [] when called at page load, and the preferred voice from voice.json was never found. The old code read the list once in main.ts and fell back to the default, which here was no voice at all.

The cause is that the list now loads asynchronously. I added a listener for the voiceschanged event in src/speech.ts and a small promise, waitForVoices(), that resolves on the first non-empty list or after 2 seconds. The picker now runs after that promise, not at startup.

I also found that the saved voice name was stored by display name, and the update renamed two voices by adding a suffix. I changed the match to try the exact name first, then a prefix match, then any voice with the same language tag. That keeps the kids' chosen voice in most cases.

Tested on desktop and on the tablet with a cold start, a reload and a back navigation. All three spoke with the right voice. One case is still odd: after a reload with the tab in the background the event fires twice, so I made the handler idempotent. The next step is a visible message if no voice is found at all, so a silent game is not a mystery. I left that for the next session.

summary: Added a visible 'no voice found' notice and a manual voice picker on the parent page, so a missing voice no longer leaves the game silently mute.
body:
Following yesterday's fix for the empty voice list, I handled the case where no voice shows up even after the 2 second wait. The game now shows a yellow strip under the title: 'No voice available, tap here to choose one'. Before this, the kids just saw a word box and heard nothing.

The strip opens a small dialog listing the voices that match the page language. Each row has a Test button that speaks the word 'bumblebee' at the current speed. The choice is saved to local storage under the same key as before, so older saves still work.

I put the same list on the parent page as a select box. The user wanted it there because the kids tend to tap everything they see, and a parent should be the one to change the voice. The strip on the game page therefore only shows when the list is empty, not when a voice is merely unselected.

I wrote two small tests for the matching function with fake voice arrays: exact name, prefix, and language fallback. They pass. The build size grew by about 1 KB. I did not touch the speed settings. Open question for the user: whether the Test button should repeat the current week's first word instead of a fixed one.

summary: Answered the user's question about why scores looked reset on the tablet: the browser clears local storage for the site after long idle periods in private mode.
body:
The user asked why one kid's score board was empty on the tablet this morning. I looked at how scores are stored: one key per profile, a JSON array, written after every word. The code has no reset path except the parent page button, which asks for confirmation.

The tablet browser turned out to be in private mode, which the kids had switched on by accident. In that mode storage is dropped when the tabs close. That explains the empty board.

I added a check in src/storage.ts that writes and reads a test key at startup. If it fails or the mode looks private, the game shows a small notice that scores will not be kept. I did not add any export yet.

The user will switch the tablet back to normal mode. Old scores in the other mode are gone and cannot be recovered. I suggested a manual export button on the parent page as a later task.

summary: Built a score export and import on the parent page as a JSON file, so the kids' history survives a cleared browser or a new tablet.
body:
After the private mode scare earlier this week, I built the export and import for scores. The parent page now has two buttons: Export downloads spellbee-scores.json, and Import reads a file and merges it.

The file format has a version field, a list of profiles, and for each profile its attempts with word, typed text, correct flag and a timestamp. I kept the timestamps as numbers, the same as in storage, so no conversion is needed.

Merging was the interesting part. If the same attempt exists in both places, it should not count twice. I identified an attempt by profile, word and timestamp and skipped duplicates. Streak values are not imported but recomputed from the attempts, since streaks are derived anyway; this reuses the function from src/streaks.ts.

I added validation: a file with a wrong version, missing fields or more than 50,000 attempts is rejected with a readable message. I tested with a hand-edited broken file, an empty file and a normal one. The normal round trip kept 412 attempts and the streaks matched exactly.

On the tablet the download goes into the browser's download folder, which the user found fine. The import uses a file input and worked there too. Still missing: a reminder to export once a month. I will ask whether that is wanted or just annoying.

summary: Added a first-letter hint on the word box after the user said the younger kid gave up on long words; each hint costs a point and is counted per word.
body:
The user said the younger kid often gave up on words of eight letters or more, so the hint button the plan had for a while got built today. Pressing it shows the first letter of the word in the input box as a greyed placeholder, and the kid types the rest.

Each hint costs one point of the word's score, and a word never scores below zero, so the hint helps but does not make the game free. The first version removed the full point and made a hinted word look like a failure. The user did not like that, so the word now counts as correct with a smaller score.

The change is in src/game.ts and src/ui/hint.ts. The state per word has a new field, hintUsed, which is saved with the score record in local storage. Old records have no such field, so the loader treats a missing value as false and no stored history needed a migration.

The button is disabled after one press for the same word. A second hint with the second letter was tried and dropped, because it made the first-letter idea too easy and the user wanted something small.

I added four tests: hint shows the right letter, the score drops by one, the score floors at zero, and old records load without the field. All pass with the existing ones. On the tablet the button is big enough to hit with a thumb, but it sits close to the speaker button, and I saw one wrong tap in a quick check.

Next step is to move the two buttons apart a little and to show the hint count per kid on the score board. The parent page could also list which words needed a hint, but that waits until the user has seen a few days of real use.

summary: Small redesign step one: replaced the fixed-pixel layout with a flexible one so the word box and keyboard fit both the tablet and a phone.
body:
This was the first part of the small redesign. The old CSS used fixed pixel widths from the first weeks, which cut off the Check button on the phone in portrait mode.

I moved the main layout to a single column with a max width of 36rem and used clamp() for the font sizes. The word box now grows with the viewport but stays readable. The speaker button went from 48 to 64 pixels, as the kids kept missing it.

The score board was a table that overflowed on narrow screens. I turned it into a list of cards, one row per attempt, with the correct flag shown as an icon and text for screen readers.

I checked at 360, 768 and 1024 pixel widths in the dev tools and on the real tablet. Nothing overflowed. The colors and fonts are untouched; that is step two, where the user wants to pick a palette. I did not change any logic, and the existing tests still pass.

summary: Picked a new color palette with the user and applied it through CSS variables, keeping contrast above the readable minimum.
body:
The user chose a calmer palette: a dark blue background, cream cards and an orange accent for buttons. I moved all colors into CSS variables in src/theme.css, so that changing them later is a one-file job.

I checked contrast for the main pairs. Cream on dark blue is high. The orange button with white text was only 3.2 to 1, so I darkened the orange until it passed 4.5 to 1.

Right and wrong feedback used pure green and red. I changed them to a teal and a coral and added an icon next to each, so the feedback does not rely on color alone.

The kids looked at it on the tablet and liked the orange. The dark mode media query is not done; the page is dark anyway.

summary: Service worker cache served an old word list after the parent updated it, because the JSON files were cached cache-first with no version.
body:
The user typed in the new week on the parent page and then noticed the kids' tablet still showed last week's words. The words come from JSON files in the static host, and the service worker from the offline mode cached them cache-first forever.

I looked at public/sw.js. The cache name was a constant, 'spellbee-v1', and it was never changed after the first release, so the activate handler never deleted anything. Even a page reload gave the old files.

I made two changes. First, the word list files now use network-first with a cache fallback, so online devices always get fresh data and offline ones still work. Second, the cache name is built at build time from a hash of the asset list, injected by a small Vite plugin, so a deploy cleans old caches in activate.

I tested by loading the page, changing a word in the file, and reloading. The new word appeared at once online. Then I switched the dev tools to offline and reloaded; the last fetched list was used.

One edge case remains: the first load after the deploy still uses the old worker until all tabs close. I added skipWaiting and clients.claim, and a reload prompt is not needed because the data is fetched fresh. The tablet picked up the fix after one reload.

I should add a note in the README about how the cache version works.

summary: Wrote the README note on how the service worker cache version is built, and how to force a refresh on a stuck device.
body:
Following the cache bug this morning, I documented it in the README under a new section called Offline mode. It explains that the cache name comes from a hash computed in the Vite plugin at build time.

It also lists the steps to force a refresh on a stuck tablet: open the page, go to the parent page, and tap Clear offline data, a button I added now. It unregisters the worker, deletes all caches and reloads.

I tested the button on desktop. After the tap, the application tab showed no registered worker and then one again after the reload. Nothing in local storage was touched, so scores stay.

No other code changed except that button and its handler in src/parent.ts.

summary: Added a gentle replay limit for the spoken word after the user noticed one kid tapping the speaker dozens of times instead of trying.
body:
The user said one of the kids taps the speaker button many times per word and never guesses. Looking at the stored attempts, I saw that I never logged replays, so I could not measure it. First I added a counter of replays per word to the attempt record, with a default of zero for old data.

Then I tried a mild rule: after 5 replays the speaker button slows its animation and a small text appears saying 'Have a try!'. It does not block the kid, because the user did not want a hard limit.

The hint button from earlier months still works the same. I made the replay counter reset on each new word, and checked it does not count the automatic first reading.

I wrote tests for the counter and the threshold. The check for the first automatic read was wrong at first: it counted as a replay, giving a message after only 4 taps. I fixed this by tracking whether the playback was user-started.

The export format now includes the replays field. The importer accepts files with or without it. I will look at the numbers in a week and see whether the threshold should change.

summary: Looked at a week of replay counts: the average was 2.1 per word, and the nudge message appeared on only about one word in twelve.
body:
I read the replay numbers from the exported scores of both kids. Over the past days there were 140 attempts. The average replay count was 2.1 per word, the median 1, and the maximum 14.

The nudge after 5 taps appeared on 12 words, about one in twelve. Most of those were long words, like 'neighbour' and 'knowledge', where hearing the word again does help, so the message may be unfair there.

I changed the threshold to depend on word length: 5 replays up to 7 letters, 8 replays for longer words. That is a one-line change in src/replay.ts plus a test.

The kid who tapped a lot is not a pure tapper; the high counts came in two sessions late in the evening, when the kid was tired. I told the user it looked more like tiredness than a habit.

I did not change the message text. The user may want a shorter session limit instead, but we decided to leave that and watch for another week.

summary: Browser update changed how audio autoplay works, so the first word was read silently until a tap; added a start screen that unlocks audio.
body:
The user reported that the first word of each session was silent on the tablet since the last browser update. Following words were fine. I reproduced it on desktop: speechSynthesis.speak() called before any user gesture was ignored without an error.

The old flow began reading the first word directly on page load. Earlier browsers allowed that, now it needs a gesture. The sound effects were affected too, since the AudioContext stayed suspended and logged 'The AudioContext was not allowed to start'.

I added a start screen with one big button, 'Start', and a greeting with the kid's name. The button handler calls audioContext.resume(), speaks an empty utterance to unlock speech, then loads the first word. Profile selection happens on the same screen, so no extra tap is needed for the kids.

I had to take care of the case where the page is restored from the back-forward cache. There the start screen was skipped and audio stayed locked. I listened to pageshow with the persisted flag and showed the start screen again.

I wrote a test for the state machine in src/session.ts: locked, ready, playing. The three transitions work. On the tablet I tried a cold start, a reload and a return from another app. In each case the word was spoken after the button.

The offline mode still works with this. The sound files are in the cache list, and I checked that with the network off.

The kids found the Start button funny and pressed it a lot at first. The user found it fine. I think the fix is complete, though the next browser update may change the rules again.

summary: Wrote a parent-page bulk paste for the weekly words, splitting on lines and commas, with a preview before saving.
body:
Typing ten words into ten boxes each week annoyed the user, so I added a single text area on the parent page. You paste the school's list and the page splits it on newlines, commas and semicolons.

The parser removes numbering such as '1.' or '2)', strips bullets, trims spaces and drops empty entries. The apostrophe normalization from the earlier bug runs here too. Duplicates are removed but kept in the preview as crossed-out items.

Below the area a preview lists the final words in order, with a count. If the count is not 10, the count is shown in orange, not as an error, since some weeks have 8 or 12 words.

I tested with four real lists from the school PDFs that the user had saved. Three parsed well. One came with the words in two columns, which the PDF paste turned into alternate lines with the definitions mixed in. I did not try to solve this; the preview makes it easy to see, and the user can edit the text.

Saving writes the same JSON structure as before, so the game page needs no change. I added 9 tests for the parser. All pass.

The user tried it with this week's list and it took under a minute. A possible follow-up is to read the list from a photo, but that is too big for this project.

summary: Fixed a streak bug where a kid who played just after midnight got the streak reset, by computing the day from local time with a cutoff at 4 a.m.
body:
One kid's streak dropped from 9 to 1 although they had played every day. The user said the kid had played at around quarter past midnight a few times, because of a late evening.

I looked at src/streaks.ts. It grouped attempts by the day of the timestamp in UTC, using toISOString().slice(0,10). On the tablet, which is a few hours off UTC, an evening session could land on the next day, and a session after midnight local time looked like the same day as the one before. Both cases gave odd streaks.

I first switched to local time, using the date parts of a Date object. That fixed the UTC problem, but the after-midnight case was still counted as a new day, which the user did not think was fair since the kid was still on the previous evening.

I therefore defined a game day as local time minus 4 hours, so that anything before 4 a.m. belongs to the previous day. The function dayKey(ts) holds this rule in one place, and the streak code and the score board both call it. Before, the board had its own copy of the grouping, which I removed.

I wrote tests for these cases: 23:50, 00:15, 03:59, 04:01, and a daylight-saving change, using fixed timestamps with a mocked time zone. Seven tests, all green. The daylight-saving one failed at first because I used 24-hour steps; I changed the key to be built from date parts.

I then recomputed the streaks from the exported data. The kid's streak came back as 9, as it should be, and the other kid's streak did not change. Streaks are derived, so no stored data needed repair.

The import from earlier now uses the same function, so a file moved between devices gives the same result. I told the user the 4 a.m. rule; they thought it was sensible.

summary: Replaced the hand-rolled sound effects with two tiny audio files after the generated tones started clicking on the new browser version.
body:
Since the last browser update the right and wrong sounds crackled at the start. They were made with oscillators in the AudioContext, with a gain that jumped to full volume at once, and the clicks came from that sudden change.

First I tried a short ramp on the gain, linearRampToValueAtTime over 15 milliseconds. It reduced the clicks, but the wrong sound still had a rattle on the tablet speaker, because the square wave has strong overtones.

So I decided against generating the tones. I made two short sounds in an audio editor: a soft two-note chime for right and a low single note for wrong, both under 0.6 seconds. Exported as .ogg and .mp3, 9 KB and 7 KB each. The page picks the supported format at load.

The sound code in src/sfx.ts is now simpler: decode the buffers once after the start screen unlock, and play them with a small gain. I removed the oscillator code, about 60 lines.

The files are in the service worker cache list, and I checked offline play. A missing file does not throw: the game goes on silently, with a console warning.

I tested on desktop and the tablet at three volume levels. No clicks any more. The user and a kid listened and liked the chime. The wrong sound is deliberately gentle, since one kid gets upset with harsh buzzers.

I did not change the volume setting on the parent page. The build grew by 16 KB.

summary: Checked the site after a week without work: the host and service worker are fine, and the word list for the coming week is still missing.
body:
Early check on the live site. It loads, the start screen appears, and the offline mode still serves the page with the network off. The cache name changed with the last deploy as intended.

The word list of this week is not there yet. The user has not sent the words. The game falls back to the last week's list, which is fine, but the kids will see old words.

I did not change any code. I only noted that a banner 'Same words as last week' would help the kids and the parent notice this. Next step is to ask the user when the words arrive.

summary: Added a 'same words as last week' banner and a per-word accuracy table on the parent page to show which words the kids keep missing.
body:
Two small features that came out of the last week. First the banner: the game compares the id of the word list with the one the kid finished last, and shows 'Same words as last week' above the word box if they match. It is dismissible and does not appear for a new profile.

Second, the accuracy table. The parent page now lists every word of the current and previous list with the number of attempts, the number correct and the share. The sorting puts the hardest words first. It is built from the same attempt records used by the score board, so no new storage is needed.

The first version counted the hint button usage as a correct attempt when the kid typed the word after seeing the first letter. The user wanted these separated. I added a column for hinted attempts and compute the share only from attempts without a hint.

A word with fewer than 3 attempts shows a dash instead of a percentage, because 1 of 1 gave 100 percent and looked misleading.

I tested with the exported data, 3 weeks and 2 profiles. 'necessary' came out at 38 percent for one kid, and 'separate' at 44 percent. The user said that matches what they see at the table.

The table has a profile switch at the top. The layout holds at phone width because I used the card style from the redesign. I added tests for the aggregation: hinted attempts, few attempts, and words that appear in both lists. All pass.

One remaining idea is to feed the hardest words back into the next list as practice words. I did not start on it; the user wants to think about whether it would feel like a punishment.

summary: Built a practice mode that repeats a profile's hardest words, kept separate from the weekly list so it never touches streaks or the main score.
body:
After the accuracy table, the user decided that a practice mode was fine, as long as it is optional and framed as a game. I added a Practice button on the start screen, next to Start.

The mode picks up to 8 words with the lowest unhinted accuracy over the profile's last 3 weeks, requiring at least 3 attempts each. If fewer than 4 qualify, it fills up with words from the current list at random. The order is shuffled by a seeded function, so a reload during a round keeps the same order.

Attempts in practice mode are stored with a mode field set to 'practice'. The score board, the streak code and the accuracy table all filter on mode, so practice does not change a streak or count as a weekly result. I had to touch four places for this, and added a test for each.

For the feel, I replaced the word counter with stars: a word gets one star when typed right on the first try. At the end a small screen shows the stars and the words still hard. No red anywhere in this mode.

The old exported files have no mode field, and the importer treats them as 'weekly'. The export now writes the field, and I bumped the file version from 1 to 2, with the importer reading both.

The first run on the tablet had a bug: after the last word the page went to the weekly end screen and recorded a finished week. The end handler in session.ts did not know about modes. I passed the mode into it and fixed it.

A kid tried it for 10 minutes and asked to do it again. The other has not tried it. I will check the practice share in the data next week.

summary: Looked into a report of a stuck word box: the input kept focus on the tablet but the on-screen keyboard hid the Check button.
body:
The user said a kid could not press Check because the on-screen keyboard covered it, in landscape. I reproduced it on the tablet. In landscape the keyboard takes more than half the screen height and the layout was taller than what remained.

I first tried scrollIntoView on the button when the input got focus. It worked on some tries but jumped the page oddly.

The simpler fix was to make Enter on the keyboard submit the answer, which the kids' keyboards already offer as a Go key, and to set enterkeyhint to 'go' on the input. The code already listened for Enter in some paths, but not when the hint was open, which swallowed the key. I fixed that handler.

I also used the visualViewport API to place the Check button above the keyboard in landscape: a small bit of CSS with a variable set from the resize event. It is only used when the viewport height is below 500 pixels.

Tested in both orientations. Check is visible, and Go submits too. The portrait layout is unchanged.

summary: Cleaned up the word list files: merged old weekly JSON into one folder with a manifest, so the game no longer guesses the file name from the date.
body:
The word lists lived in weeks/ with names built from a week counter, and the loader computed the current name from the clock. That broke twice already when the user forgot a week, and the earlier banner logic had to work around it.

I introduced weeks/manifest.json, a list of entries with id, file name and a label. The parent page appends an entry when it saves a list, and the game loads the last entry. A missing week simply means the last list stays current, which is the behavior the user wanted anyway.

I wrote a one-time script, scripts/build-manifest.ts, which scanned the old files, sorted them by their stored creation field, and produced the manifest of 41 entries. Two files had no creation field; I put them by hand using the names.

The loader in src/words.ts now reads the manifest first and then the file. The manifest is fetched network-first like the lists, so the service worker needs no change. I checked offline: the last fetched manifest works.

The banner for the same words now compares the manifest ids, which removed a hack of about 20 lines.

The accuracy table finds the previous list through the manifest as well, so the 'last 3 weeks' for the practice mode are now the last 3 lists, not three calendar weeks. That is better when a week is skipped. I adjusted the test.

I ran the lint script for non-ASCII characters again over all 41 files: clean. I tried the whole flow on the tablet, with an old save and a new one, and everything loaded.

I have not removed the old date-based code path in case of a rollback; that can go next week.

summary: Removed the old date-based word loader and its tests after a week of the manifest working without problems.
body:
The manifest-based loading has run for a week on the tablet and on the phone, and the user added one new list through the parent page without trouble. So I removed the old code.

The deleted parts: computeWeekName() in src/words.ts, the fallback that tried the last four possible file names in a row, and six tests for them. In all, 94 lines went away.

I searched for other callers with grep. One more existed in the parent page, where it was used to suggest a file name; it now takes the next number from the manifest length.

The type check and the 52 remaining tests pass. The production build is 3 KB smaller. I deployed and tested the live site with the network on and off.

The removed code is in the history if it is needed. No behavior changed. One thing I noticed: the README still describes the file naming by date. I updated that paragraph and added how the manifest works, including the one-time build script and a warning not to run it again, since it would overwrite the manifest.

I renamed the script to build-manifest.once.ts to make that clearer. Nothing else is planned for this topic.

summary: Small redesign finished: new title art, rounded cards and a simple confetti burst for a perfect week, drawn on a canvas without a library.
body:
This closes the redesign that began with the flexible layout and the palette. The user wanted something nice for a perfect week, so I added a confetti burst on the end screen when all words were right on the first try.

The effect is a canvas overlay with about 120 particles, simple gravity and rotation, running for 2.5 seconds with requestAnimationFrame. No library, around 70 lines in src/confetti.ts. It uses the palette colors from the CSS variables.

I respected the reduced-motion setting: if prefers-reduced-motion is set, the burst is replaced by a static star badge. The canvas has pointer-events none, so the kids can tap through it to the next button.

The title now has a small bee drawn as inline SVG, 1.2 KB, in place of the plain text header. The cards got rounder corners and a softer shadow. The buttons got a pressed state so that the tablet taps feel responded to.

I checked the performance on the tablet: the burst ran at a steady frame rate, no stutter, and the canvas is removed from the DOM afterward. Memory looked flat over ten bursts.

One issue appeared: on the phone the canvas was sized in CSS pixels, so it looked blurry. I scaled it with devicePixelRatio, capped at 2.

The user showed it to the kids. One asked how to get a perfect week again. The other asked for a different color. I will not add choices, but I may put a few confetti color sets in later if the user asks.

summary: Checked usage after the redesign: both kids played on most days of the week, but the practice mode was used only twice.
body:
I exported the scores and looked at the past week. Kid one played on 6 days, kid two on 5, which is as before. The weekly list was completed on every one of those days.

Practice mode was started twice, both times by the same kid, with 8 words each. In both rounds they got at least 5 stars. The other kid has not touched it.

The average session is about 6 minutes. The perfect-week confetti was seen once.

I think practice mode is not discovered enough, since the button sits next to the big Start button and is smaller. I will not change the layout now. I noted it for the user, who may simply tell the kids about it.

No bugs were reported this week. The service worker and manifest loading behaved well.

summary: Tidied the dependency set and bumped Vite and TypeScript to current minor versions; the build and all 55 tests still pass.
body:
A maintenance pass, since little else was open. I ran npm outdated and found Vite and TypeScript a few minor versions behind, plus a test runner patch update.

I bumped the three in one commit and ran the build. It succeeded with one new deprecation warning about a config option for the manifest plugin I wrote. I renamed the option as the warning suggested, and it went away.

The type check found two new strictness errors in src/confetti.ts, where a canvas context could be null. I added a guard that returns early. No behavior changed.

All 55 tests pass. The bundle size is the same within 200 bytes. I deployed to the static host and tried the live site on the tablet: start screen, a few words, sound, offline mode. All fine.

I left the lock file changes in the same commit so that the build can be repeated. Nothing else is outdated. I do not plan more upgrades unless a browser change breaks something.

summary: Started the new school term's word lists: added ten words for the coming week and found two entries in the manifest pointing at files that no longer exist.
body:
The new term began, so the first job was the weekly list. I added the ten words to the words folder and registered them in manifest.json. While doing that, a quick script that checks every manifest path against the folder flagged two entries pointing at files that were merged away during the cleanup of the word list files.

The game never loaded those weeks, so nobody saw a problem, but the parent page's history view tried to list them and showed blank rows. I removed the two stale entries and added the check as an npm script called check:words. It runs in about 40 ms.

The check also verifies that each list has exactly 10 words and no duplicates. All lists pass now. Next I want to run it as part of the build so a bad manifest cannot ship.

summary: Wired the word manifest check into the Vite build so a missing file or a list without ten words now fails the build instead of shipping.
body:
Following the morning's stale manifest entries, I moved check:words into the build. The script runs before vite build through a prebuild npm hook. If any path is missing, any list has a count other than 10, or a word repeats within a list, it prints the offending file and exits with code 1.

I tested it by deleting one list on purpose, then by adding an eleventh word to another. Both runs failed with a readable message. Restoring the files made the build pass again.

One snag: the school sometimes sends a list with 12 words in a special week. I allowed an optional field in the manifest, expected, that overrides the count of 10. The default stays 10. The tests still pass, 55 of them, and I added 3 for the checker itself.

summary: Looked into a complaint that the spoken word sounds too fast for the younger kid on the tablet; the speed setting was clamped by a bad default rather than the voice.
body:
The user said the younger kid could not follow the words on the tablet. I first suspected the new voice, but the voice picker showed the same voice as before. The real cause was in settings.ts: the stored rate was read as a string, and a missing value fell back to 1.0 instead of the 0.8 chosen weeks ago.

Only profiles created after the second-kid change had no stored rate, so the younger kid's profile used the wrong default. I fixed the parsing with Number() and a fallback of 0.8, and gave each profile its own rate.

I left the slider on the parent page unchanged. The user will listen on the tablet tonight and tell me whether 0.8 is right or whether it should go lower.

summary: Added a per-profile speech speed slider after the user confirmed 0.8 was still too quick for the younger kid; the setting now lives with each profile.
body:
The user listened and said 0.8 was still a little fast for the younger kid but fine for the older one. So the slider I had left on the parent page now writes to the active profile rather than one shared value.

Changes: the profile object in storage gained a rate field, the parent page shows one slider per profile with a play-sample button, and the game reads the rate when a profile is selected. Old profiles without the field get 0.8 on load and the value is saved back.

I added a test for the migration of old profiles and one for clamping the rate between 0.5 and 1.2. Setting the younger kid to 0.65 was the user's choice after trying the sample. The sample button speaks the word 'rhythm' because it is long and shows the speed clearly.

The export file includes the rate now, so an import restores it too. Old exports still import fine, which I checked with a saved file.

summary: Checked why the confetti burst stutters on the old tablet: it redrew 300 particles every frame, so I capped it at 120 and it runs smoothly.
body:
The older tablet dropped frames when the perfect-week confetti played. Profiling in the browser showed each frame taking about 38 ms, almost all of it in the particle loop on the canvas. The burst created 300 particles with a shadow blur on each, and the blur was the expensive part.

I removed the shadow and cut the count to 120. Frames now take about 9 ms on my laptop with a 4x CPU slowdown, which is a fair stand-in for the tablet. The look is nearly the same since the particles are small.

I also stopped the animation loop when all particles have left the screen, because it was still running in the background. The user will check on the real tablet at the next perfect week.

summary: Found that the weekly word list loads twice on start because both the start screen and the game module fetch the manifest; one shared promise fixed it.
body:
While looking at the network panel for another reason, I saw manifest.json and the current list fetched twice on every page load. The start screen added for audio unlocking calls loadWeek() to show the word count, and the game module calls it again when the first word is requested.

With the service worker the second fetch came from cache, so nothing looked wrong, but on the first visit to a new device it doubled the traffic and sometimes raced: once the two responses arrived in the other order and the count shown did not match the game.

I made loadWeek() memoize its promise per week key in words.ts. A failed fetch clears the memo so a retry works. I wrote two tests: one counting calls to a mocked fetch, one checking that a failure can be retried.

After the change the panel shows one request per file. The build and all tests pass, 60 now. I did not touch the service worker.

summary: Fixed the typed answer compare so capital letters no longer mark a right word wrong; the check now ignores case and surrounding spaces, with new tests.
body:
The younger kid typed 'Because' with a capital B from the tablet keyboard's auto-capitalize and got a red mark. The user noticed it during an evening session and asked why. The compare in src/check.ts used strict equality after a trim, so any capital letter failed the word.

I changed it to lowercase both sides with toLowerCase() and to trim the typed text before comparing. I kept the stored word as the school wrote it, so the spoken form and the parent page stay unchanged. Words with an apostrophe, like 'don't', still need the apostrophe to match, because that is part of the spelling exercise.

I added six tests: a capitalized answer, all caps, a trailing space, a leading space, a wrong letter that must still fail, and an apostrophe word. The suite went from 55 to 61 tests and all pass. I also turned off auto-capitalize on the input with the autocapitalize="off" attribute, so the tablet keyboard no longer starts with a capital.

Open question: old stored answers were judged with the strict rule. I did not touch them yet and will check next how many would change before deciding anything about the history.

summary: Checked old stored scores against the new case-insensitive compare: 4 of 380 past answers would flip from wrong to right, so I left history untouched.
body:
After the normalizer change I wanted to know if past scores would look different. I wrote a small script that reads an exported JSON file from the tablet and re-scores each stored answer with the new compare.

Out of 380 answers, 4 changed from wrong to right, all of them capital letter or trailing space cases. The accuracy table would shift by a fraction of a percent for two words.

I decided not to rewrite history. Stored scores are a record of what happened, and the change is too small to matter. The new rule applies from now on.

The script stays in the tools folder as rescore.mjs in case a later change needs the same check. I noted this in the README next to the export format description.

summary: Designed and built a simple weekly progress strip on the home screen so each kid sees ten dots, filled as they spell words right during the week.
body:
The user wanted the kids to see their own progress without opening the score board. I sketched ten dots under the profile name, one per word of the week: grey for not tried, green for right on the first attempt, orange for right after a hint or a second try.

The data already exists. Each answer is stored with the word, the profile, the attempt count and whether a hint was used. I wrote a function weekProgress(profile, weekKey) that returns an array of ten states, built from the latest answer per word.

Rendering is plain DOM, a flex row of spans styled with the CSS variables of the new palette. I checked contrast of the orange against the card background and it came out at 4.8, above the readable minimum I used before.

A detail I got wrong first: practice mode answers were counted, because they share the answer store. Practice answers carry a mode field, so I filter on mode equal to weekly. That keeps the strip separate, as the practice mode was meant to be.

For weeks with the optional expected count of 12, the strip draws 12 dots. The row wraps on a phone width, which I checked at 360 px.

I added 6 tests: empty week, all right, mixed hint states, a practice answer ignored, a changed list in mid-week, and the 12-word week. Everything passes. The user will watch whether the kids notice it. If they like it, the same data could drive a small sticker at the end of the week.

summary: Fixed the progress strip showing stale dots after the parent edits the week's words, by keying progress on the word text instead of its position.
body:
The user edited a word in the middle of the week and the strip then showed a green dot for a word the kid had never tried. The cause was in weekProgress: I matched stored answers to dots by index, so replacing the third word kept the old third answer.

I changed it to match by the normalized word text. A replaced word starts grey, and the answers for the removed word are kept in storage but no longer shown. Reordering the list no longer moves any dots wrongly either.

I reproduced the bug first with a test that swaps one word, saw it fail, then fixed it. I added another test for a reorder.

One open question is what to do with a word that was typed wrongly by the parent and fixed on the same day. At the moment its old answers vanish from the strip, which seems right. Nothing else changed today. The build is green with 68 tests.

summary: Added a sticker at the end of a finished week, picked from twelve small drawings, as a reward that is kept on the kid's profile page.
body:
The user liked the dots and asked for something to collect. I drew twelve simple stickers as inline SVG, each under 1 KB: a snail, a kite, a moon and so on. Together they add about 9 KB to the bundle.

When a kid answers the last word of the week, the game picks the next sticker they do not have yet, shows it large for a moment and saves it in the profile as an id with the week key. After twelve stickers the choice starts again from the beginning, which I accepted as a simple rule.

A week counts as finished when all words have at least one weekly answer, correct or not. I considered requiring a perfect week, but the user said the younger kid would then rarely get one and lose interest.

The profile page shows a grid of earned stickers. Each profile has its own collection, and the export and import carry them. An old export without stickers imports with an empty set.

Tests: 4 new ones for choosing the sticker, finishing a week twice without a double reward, and the import. A refresh during the reward screen does not give a second sticker because the week key is stored first.

summary: Handled a sticker problem on the tablet: the reward showed twice when the last word was answered and the page reloaded from the service worker update prompt.
body:
The user reported that the older kid got the sticker animation twice in a row. I reproduced it by finishing a week and then triggering a service worker update while the reward screen was open.

The cause was ordering. The sticker was saved when the reward screen closed, not when it opened, so a reload in between left the week unrewarded and the game awarded it again on the next start. In some cases it awarded the next sticker as well, so a kid lost nothing but saw it twice.

I moved the save to the moment the last answer is stored, and the reward screen only displays the sticker id that was saved. On start, if a saved reward has not been shown, the screen shows it once, using a shown flag in the profile.
