I also delayed the update prompt while a reward or an answer is being checked. The prompt used to appear at any time, which is a bad moment for a child.

Four tests cover the reload case. I tried it by hand with the dev tools offline switch and a forced update. The tablet will get the new version by the next refresh. I need to ask the user to watch for a repeat of the report.

summary: Planned and started a larger change: a spoken sentence mode in which the game reads a sentence with the target word blanked out, to help with homophones.
body:
The school lists have started to include pairs like 'their' and 'there', and the kids guess because the word alone gives no clue. The user asked whether the game could read the word inside a sentence. This entry is the plan and the first step.

The design: each word in a list may have an optional sentence field. The game says the word, then, on request, a second button reads the sentence with the word replaced by a short beep or the word 'blank'. The kid still types the single word. Words without a sentence keep working as before, so nothing breaks for old lists.

Step one was the data format. The list files are plain arrays of strings today. Changing them all to objects would touch the loader, the checker script, the parent page and the export. Instead I allowed each array item to be either a string or an object with text and sentence, and wrote one function, toEntry(), that turns both into the object shape. Everything downstream calls toEntry first.

I updated check:words to accept both shapes and to check that a sentence contains the word, case-insensitively, since a sentence without the word could not be blanked. I also wrote the blanking function. It replaces whole-word matches only, so 'the' inside 'other' is left alone. It handles an apostrophe, for example the word 'don't'.

One case needed a decision: when a word appears twice in its own sentence, both are blanked. I think that is right, since otherwise the sentence gives the answer away.

Tests added: 9, covering toEntry on both shapes, blanking with punctuation, a capital letter at the start of the sentence, a word inside another word, and a missing word in the sentence. All 77 pass.

Next steps: the button and the speech part, then the parent page field for sentences. I will keep it hidden behind a flag until the parent page can enter sentences, so nothing half done reaches the kids.

summary: Added the 'read the sentence' button to the game, hidden unless the word has a sentence, and spoke the sentence with the word replaced by a pause.
body:
With the data shape in place, I built the button. It sits next to the speaker icon and appears only if the current entry has a sentence. A tap speaks the sentence with the target word cut out.

For the gap I first tried saying 'blank', which sounded clumsy and made the younger kid laugh each time. I switched to splitting the sentence at the word and speaking two utterances with a 400 ms silence between them. The speech API has no pause control, so I chained the utterances through the end event and a timer.

The chaining had a problem: on the tablet the end event sometimes did not fire when the page was in the background, and the second half never spoke. I added a timeout fallback of the estimated length plus one second.

The replay limit applies to the sentence button too, sharing the count with the word, since the nudge was built to stop endless tapping. The flag stays off by default. Tested on the laptop with two voices and on the tablet once, and it sounded natural.

summary: Built the parent page sentence field with a live preview of the blanked sentence and a warning when the word is missing from it.
body:
The parent page needed a way to enter a sentence for each word, otherwise the feature stays a developer toy. I extended the weekly editor so each word row has a second, wider input labelled 'sentence (optional)'.

The preview shows the sentence with the word replaced by a line of underscores, using the same blanking function the game uses, so what the parent sees is what the kid hears. If the sentence does not contain the word, the row turns yellow with the text 'word not found in sentence' and the sentence is saved but ignored by the game.

The bulk paste needed thought. It splits on lines and commas, and a comma now conflicts with sentences. I added a second accepted form: one word per line with a sentence after a vertical bar, like 'there | Put it over there.' If a line has a bar, commas are not split. The preview shows both columns before saving.

Saving writes the mixed format: a plain string when there is no sentence, an object when there is. This keeps old files minimal and small in git diffs.

Edge cases I tried by hand: a bar inside a sentence, which I handle by splitting only on the first one; an empty word before the bar, which is dropped with a notice; and leading and trailing spaces, which the normalizer trims.

Tests: 8 new ones for the bulk parser, including the mixed lines and the first-bar rule. The total is 85 and they pass.

I turned the feature flag on for the parent page only, so entries can be typed, while the game still ignores sentences. The next step is switching the game flag on and testing with a real list from school.

summary: Turned on sentence mode for a real school list; the first trial showed that two sentences gave the answer away through a longer form of the word.
body:
I typed this week's ten words with sentences and enabled the flag in the game. The test with the user went through all ten words.

Two problems came up. For 'sign', the sentence was 'Please sign the card, he said, and then signed it.' The whole-word blanking left 'signed' in the sentence, which gave the spelling away. For 'run' the sentence had 'running' in it.

I first considered blanking any word that starts with the target. That is too broad: 'the' would blank 'there' and 'then'. Instead I decided it is a data problem, and the parent page should warn. It now checks whether another word in the sentence starts with the target word and shows an orange note: 'signed looks like a form of the word'. The parent can edit the sentence.

The second issue was voice quality. On the tablet the pause sounded too long after a short first half such as 'Put it'. I made the pause 250 ms when the first half has fewer than three words and kept 400 ms otherwise.

The kids tried it in the evening. The older one liked it, the younger one used it on about half of the words. I added a counter of sentence taps per word to the stored data for later review.

Tests: 3 more for the prefix warning. All pass, 88 in total.

I also fixed a small thing in the checker script: it now prints a warning instead of failing for a sentence without the word, because the parent page allows saving that.

summary: Reviewed a week of sentence-mode use and cleaned up: sentence taps averaged 0.9 per word, and accuracy on homophones went up from 55 to 80 percent.
body:
After a week with sentences on, I pulled the numbers from the exported scores of both kids and from the new tap counter.

Sentence taps averaged 0.9 per word over 10 words and two profiles. The older kid used it on 4 of 10 words, the younger on 7 of 10. The replay limit nudge shows up on the combined count, and it appeared twice, both on the younger kid's long words.

For accuracy I picked the three homophone-like words in the list. Before sentence mode, the previous lists with such words had about 55 percent right on the first try. This week the three words had 80 percent. The sample is small, six answers per word at most, so I would not call it proof, but the direction is the one the user hoped for.

The cleanup part: the code had grown a few rough edges while I built it step by step. I merged two duplicate helper functions that split a sentence at the word, one in the game module and one in the parent page, into a single file, sentence.ts. I also renamed the flag from sentenceMode to sentences, removed the temporary console logging I added during the pause tests, and deleted the 'blank' word fallback that is never reached now.

I also considered whether to keep the flag at all. With the feature stable, it only adds a branch. I removed it, so sentences work whenever a word has one. Words without sentences behave as before.

The README got a section on the list format: plain strings, objects with a sentence, and the bar syntax in the bulk paste.

Still open: the pause timing on a very slow voice, and a possible limit for sentences longer than 15 words. No kid has hit either. The build is green at 88 tests.

summary: Dropped the idea of reading sentences for every word: the sentence files are only worth keeping for homophones, so the parent page now marks sentences as optional.
body:
After the week of sentence-mode use, I looked at which words really gained from a sentence. For plain words like 'garden' or 'jump' the sentence tap added nothing; accuracy there was already high and the kids rarely tapped the button. The gain came almost entirely from homophones such as 'their', 'there', 'whole' and 'hole'.

Because of that I stopped planning a sentence for each word. The parent page now labels the sentence field as optional, with the hint text 'Most useful for words that sound like another word'. The warning about a missing target word in the sentence only appears once something is typed, so an empty field is no longer flagged.

I also trimmed the sample sentence files for the last three lists, removing 14 sentences for easy words. This cut the sentence JSON by about a third, which helps the offline cache a little. The build and all tests still pass. Next I want to ask the user whether the school sends homophone words often enough to keep a short built-in list of common pairs as a suggestion.

summary: Wrote a precache step into the build so the next week's list and all sentence files are cached up front, closing the offline gap on new lists.
body:
Following the question about playing in the car, I fixed the real gap: lists are cached only after the first fetch. The service worker now precaches every file in the manifest at install time.

The build already makes a cache version string from a hash of the output files. I extended the build script to write precache.json containing the manifest and each list path. The service worker reads that file at install and adds the paths with cache.addAll(). If one path fails, the install fails and the old worker stays active, which is the safe behavior.

The size matters on a phone. The lists are small: 40 weeks at about 600 bytes each is roughly 24 KB. Even with sentences it stays under 60 KB, so caching everything is fine.

A second question was how an update finds the new list. The cache version changes whenever a list changes, since the hash includes the JSON files. This fixes the earlier case where the parent edited a list and an old copy was served, and the README note on forcing a refresh remains valid.

I hit one problem. The parent page saves lists to local storage for the current week rather than to files, and the game merges them over the files. Those local edits are not part of the build at all, so precache cannot help. They live on the device where the parent typed them, which is also where they are used, so that is fine for a single tablet.

But for a second device the parent would need to export and import, as with scores. I added the list overrides to the export file under a new key, and the import accepts files without it.

Tests: the build script now has a test that runs it on a fixture folder and checks that precache.json lists every file. I added 4 tests for the export key. Total 95, all green.

I tried the result on the phone: cleared site data, visited online once, switched to airplane mode, and the newest list loaded. Then I put a list in the folder, rebuilt, went online once more, and the phone picked it up on the second load as expected.

summary: Fixed the update prompt after the precache change: it appeared on every visit because the cache version included a timestamp in the hashed output.
body:
After the precache work, the user said the 'new version available' prompt came up on every visit. The service worker compares its version string with the old one, and it saw a change each time.

I built twice in a row without touching any source and diffed the output folders. The file precache.json contained a generatedAt field, which I had added for debugging, and the hash covered that file, so every build had a new version.

I removed the field and made the hash skip precache.json itself, since it is derived from the other files. Two builds in a row now give identical hashes, which I checked by comparing the version strings printed by the script.

I added a test that builds a fixture twice and asserts the same version. This should have been part of the earlier tests.

On the tablet the prompt will show once more for this update, then stay quiet until a real change. I told the user about that single extra prompt.

summary: Looked at the bundle after all the recent features: 71 KB total, with stickers and the confetti taking about a seventh, so no changes were needed.
body:
Several features landed in the last weeks, so I checked the weight of the site. A production build gives 71 KB of JavaScript, CSS and the HTML, before compression, and about 24 KB gzipped.

Breakdown by module, from the Vite build report: the game logic 22 KB, the parent page 19 KB, speech and settings 8 KB, stickers 9 KB, confetti 2 KB, the rest is CSS and small helpers. The sound files add 14 KB more, which are not in that figure.

I considered splitting the parent page into a lazy chunk, since the kids never open it. It would save about 19 KB on the main load, but the page is cached by the service worker anyway after the first visit, and the game loads instantly on the tablet. The added complexity is not worth it.

The sticker SVGs could be shared more, since they repeat a few path attributes, but a quick test of merging them saved under 1 KB.

I also ran a Lighthouse check on the phone profile. Performance 99, accessibility 94. The accessibility notes were two buttons that have only an icon and no label, the speaker and the sentence button. I added aria-label text to both: 'Say the word again' and 'Read the sentence'.

Touch targets are above the minimum size. The color contrast warning that appeared earlier on the orange dots is gone after the palette work.

Nothing else to do here. The numbers go in the README under 'size', so a later regression is easy to spot. The tests still pass at 95.

summary: Investigated a wrong answer that was marked right: the typed word 'recieve' was accepted because the compare ignored a swap, caused by a fuzzy match I had added for typos.
body:
The user noticed that the younger kid typed 'recieve' and got a green mark. That should never pass in a spelling game.

I searched the compare code and found the cause quickly. In the checker there was a small function, closeEnough(), used only for the message 'almost, try again' after a wrong answer. A refactor during the normalizer work had made the main compare call it as a fallback when strict equality failed, so any word within edit distance one was accepted.

I checked the history with git log on the checker file and found the commit. It came from merging the two compare paths into one function for the case-insensitive change. The test suite did not catch it because every compare test used clearly wrong words.

The fix was to restore the strict compare in the main path and keep closeEnough() only for the hint message. I wrote tests with transposed letters, a missing letter, a doubled letter and one extra letter, and each must fail the strict compare and pass closeEnough.

Then the harder part: how many past answers were wrongly accepted? I used the rescore.mjs script from earlier on the exported scores. Of 520 stored answers since the merge, 11 were accepted with edit distance one. They were spread over both kids, 7 for the younger and 4 for the older.

This time I think the history should be corrected, unlike the case-insensitive change, because these are real misspellings recorded as right. But the stored answers hold the typed text and a correct flag, so I can recompute the flag. I added a one-time migration on load that re-scores answers from the affected period and marks it done with a version number in storage.

The migration changes streak and score values, which depend on correct answers. Streaks are computed from answer days, so one fixed answer could shorten a streak. I looked at the two affected days and the streak lengths stay the same since other answers happened the same days.

I told the user what happened and that 11 marks were corrected. The build is green with 104 tests. The next check is to watch the first evening of play on the new version.

summary: Checked the evening's play after the compare fix: both kids played, no wrong marks, and the migration ran once without changing any stored streak.
body:
I looked at the exported scores after the evening. Both kids played about 10 words each. The older kid got 9 right, the younger 6, and I reviewed each stored answer against the typed text by hand. All marks were correct.

The migration ran once on the tablet. The storage version value is set, and a reload did not run it again. The 11 corrected answers show as wrong now in the accuracy table, and two words moved up in the 'hardest words' list as a result.

Streaks are unchanged, as predicted: 6 days for the older kid and 3 for the younger.

The 'almost' message still appears for close tries, which the younger kid seems to like because it encourages another try. I think this closes the issue. I added a line to the README testing notes: compare tests should always use near misses.

summary: Wrote a short list of how the game could end its life gracefully, after the user said the kids will probably get a school app soon.
body:
The user mentioned that the school plans its own spelling app for next term and that the kids may stop using this one. They asked what I would do to leave things in good shape without more big features.

I went through the project and wrote down a few points. First, the data: the kids' history exists only in local storage on the tablet, so the export file is the way to keep it. I would ask the user to export both profiles once a month and keep the files with the family photos or documents.

Second, the site: it is static and needs nothing from us. If the host stays up, it keeps working, since the service worker caches everything. A caveat is that browsers may change speech or autoplay behavior again, as happened twice already, so the game could break without anyone noticing.

Third, the code: it builds cleanly, 104 tests pass, the dependencies were bumped recently, and the README covers the list format, the cache version and the export. A new person could pick it up.

Fourth, the open ideas I would not do: a sentence length limit, a lazy parent page chunk, more stickers. None solves a real problem now.

What I would do if the kids stop playing is to freeze the repository, which is the user's call, and leave a note in the README that the project is finished.

I wrote the list into a file called ENDING.md. It is short, about 25 lines. The user said it was helpful and that they would decide after the next term starts. No code changed today.

summary: Added a monthly reminder on the parent page to export scores, shown only if no export happened in the last 30 days, as a safety net for the kids' history.
body:
Following the ending list, the cheapest useful change was a reminder to export. The parent page now shows a small banner at the top: 'Last export was 40 days ago. Save a copy of the scores.' It appears only if the last export is more than 30 days old, or if there never was one.

To know the time, the export button now stores a timestamp in local storage under lastExport. The banner reads it on load. A cleared storage also clears the timestamp, which then shows the 'never' text, and that is acceptable since a cleared storage is exactly when the reminder matters.

I kept it quiet on purpose. No pop-up, no sound, nothing in the kids' part of the game, since they never see the parent page. The banner has a button that exports right away and then hides itself.

The import does not change the timestamp, because importing does not mean the data is saved somewhere else.

For the day math I used whole days from local time, the same helper the streaks use with the 4 a.m. cutoff, so the two stay consistent.

Tests: 5 new ones for no export, a recent export, an old export, exactly 30 days and the button resetting the timestamp. The total is 109 and all pass.

I tried it with a faked timestamp in the dev tools and the banner showed and hid correctly. I told the user. Since this was the last item of the ending list, I do not plan more work unless something breaks.

summary: Exported the kids' scores for the first time after the new reminder fired, and checked that the file imports back cleanly into a fresh browser profile.
body:
The monthly reminder from yesterday showed up on the parent page this morning, so I used it as a real test. I tapped the export button and got a JSON file of 412 answers across both profiles. The size was about 38 KB.

To check that the file is actually a safety net, I opened the site in a private window with empty local storage and ran the import. Both profiles came back with their names, streaks and stickers. The speech speed slider values were also restored, which I had not been sure about.

One gap showed up. The import does not restore the 'last export' timestamp, so the reminder would fire again right after a restore. That is harmless but a bit silly.

I did not change the import yet. I noted the gap in the todo list at the top of the README. The export format itself is fine and I left it alone.

Next I want to look at what happens when the file is edited by hand and contains a word that is not in any list.

summary: Made the score import reject malformed files with a clear message instead of half-loading them; 6 new tests cover truncated, empty and wrong-shape input.
body:
Following the export check from earlier this morning, I tried feeding the import some bad files. A truncated JSON file threw an uncaught SyntaxError in the console and the page just did nothing. A file with the right shape but a profile missing its name loaded half the data and then crashed on the profile page.

I rewrote the import in src/scores/importer.ts as two steps. First it parses and validates the whole file, and only then does it write anything to local storage. Validation checks the version field, that profiles is an array, that each profile has a name and a list of answers, and that each answer has a word, a typed value and a boolean.

If validation fails, nothing is written. The parent page now shows a short red message such as 'This file is not a spellbee export' or 'Profile 2 has no name'. Before, the failure was silent.

I also decided that an unknown newer version number should be refused rather than guessed at. That seems the safer behavior for a file the user might keep for a long time.

Tests added:
- an empty file
- truncated JSON
- wrong version
- a profile without a name
- an answer with a number as the word
- a valid file, to confirm nothing regressed

All 61 tests pass. The build check for the word manifest still passes too. While in there I also made the import restore the last-export timestamp, which closes the small gap I noted this morning.

summary: Planned and began a practice mode that replays only the words a kid got wrong, after the usage check showed the old practice mode was hardly touched.
body:
Practice mode was used only twice in the week I checked, and I think the reason is that it offers all ten words again, which feels like repeating the test. The idea now is to make it a short round of only the words the kid got wrong in the past two weeks.

First I looked at what the stored scores allow. Each answer has the word, the typed text, a correct flag and a timestamp, so it is easy to compute the words with a wrong answer and no later right answer. For the older kid that gives 7 words, and for the younger kid 14.

I wrote a function in src/practice/pick.ts that returns up to 5 words, preferring those with the most recent wrong answer, and never the same word twice in a row. Five seemed right for a short round that a child can finish before getting bored.

I then reused the game screen for the round instead of building a new one. The game takes a list of words as input already, so the change was small. The round ends with a short message, 'Nice, 4 of 5 fixed', and does not touch the weekly progress dots, because practice should not count toward the sticker.

That last point took some care. The progress strip keys on word text, so a practice answer for a word from the current week could have filled a dot. I added a flag on the answer record, mode: 'practice', and the strip now ignores those.

Tests cover the pick function, the no-repeat rule and the flag. I have not yet put a button on the home screen. That is for the next session, along with a quick trial with the younger kid.

summary: Added a 'Practice mistakes' button to the home screen, shown only when a kid has at least one word to retry.
body:
The pick function from this afternoon now has a way in. The home screen shows a 'Practice mistakes' card under the progress strip, only if the current profile has at least one word to retry. If there is nothing to practice, the card is hidden rather than disabled, so there is no empty button to puzzle over.

The card also shows how many words are waiting, for example '3 words'. I capped the displayed number at 5 to match the round size.

I tried it on my own profile with some fake wrong answers and the round ran correctly. After the round the card count dropped by the number of words fixed. A wrong answer in practice keeps the word in the list, which is what I wanted.

One rough edge: the card uses the same blue as the start button, so the two compete. I changed it to the softer secondary colour from the redesign. The younger kid can try it tomorrow.

summary: Watched both kids use practice mode: the younger one finished two rounds, but a word they could never get right showed that repeats need a limit.
body:
The younger kid tried 'Practice mistakes' yesterday evening and again this morning before school, finishing two rounds. The older kid ignored it, which is fine since they had only two words waiting.

The interesting case was the word 'necessary'. It was wrong in every round, because the kid typed 'neccessary' each time. The pick function kept offering it first, since it had the most recent wrong answer. The result was a round that started with a word that was known to be hard, and the kid said it was 'that one again'.

I looked at the stored answers to see how common this is. Across the younger kid's history, 3 words have been wrong three or more times. Everything else is fixed within two tries.

I made two changes in pick.ts:
- A word that was wrong in the last three practice rounds is not placed first, but goes to the end of the round.
- After the round, if the word is still wrong, the end message shows the right spelling, in large letters, for a few seconds.

The second change is the more useful one, I think. Before, the game showed the correct word only inside the small feedback line, which is easy to miss. Now there is a clear look at the word before moving on.

I wrote tests for the ordering and for the end screen content, and the suite is at 66 passing. The end screen text reuses the speech call, so the word is also read aloud once more, slowly, using the profile's own speed setting.

I will keep watching a few days to see if the repeats shrink.

summary: Fixed the practice end screen speaking the corrected word at the default speed instead of the kid's profile speed.
body:
The younger kid noticed that the word read out at the end of a practice round was fast again, like it was before the speed slider existed. That matched what I expected from the code once I looked.

The end screen called speak(word) directly, while the game screen goes through a helper that reads the speed from the active profile. I had copied the direct call when I wrote the end screen last week and missed that it skipped the profile.

The fix was to route the end screen through the same helper. I also searched the source for other direct speak calls and found one more in the parent page preview, where the default speed is fine because a parent is listening.

I added a test that mocks the speech API and checks that the rate equals the profile's setting, 0.6 in the test. Tests pass at 67. The younger kid confirmed the next morning that the word now sounds slow enough.

summary: Answered the user's question about how many words each kid has gotten wrong more than twice: 3 for the younger kid and 1 for the older.
body:
The user asked whether it is worth adding more help for the hardest words, and wanted to know how many there really are. I counted from the stored scores of both profiles, using the exported file so I would not disturb the live data.

Results: the younger kid has 3 words with three or more wrong answers and no right answer afterward. They are 'necessary', 'separate' and 'definitely'. The older kid has just one, 'occasion'. All four are the usual double-letter or vowel traps.

That is a small number, so I recommended not building a new feature. Practice mode already puts these words in front of the kids, and the end screen now shows the correct spelling.

I mentioned one cheap option for later: let the parent page pin a word so that it always appears in practice. The user said they would rather just type those words into next week's list. That works with no code, so I left it there.

summary: Looked at why the service worker still served the old word list after a parent edit on the tablet; the cached manifest was winning over the network.
body:
The user edited this week's words on the parent page from the tablet, and the kid still got last week's list. A reload did not help, and a second reload only helped after a few minutes.

I reproduced it in the desktop browser with the offline tools. The service worker serves the manifest from the cache first and updates it in the background. That is fine for hashed asset files, but a parent edit is stored in local storage and merged with the manifest on start. The merge ran before the background refresh finished, so it merged into the stale copy.

Two possible fixes: switch the manifest to network first with a cache fallback, or make the merge wait. I picked the first, because the manifest is tiny at about 2 KB and a short network wait is cheap. It still works offline through the fallback.

I changed the route in the worker and bumped the cache name. Tests for the worker are limited, so I checked by hand: edit, reload and the new list appears immediately; offline, the last list still appears.

summary: Confirmed the network-first manifest fix on the real tablet: edit, reload and the new list shows at once, and airplane mode still loads the last list.
body:
I walked through the tablet check this afternoon since the earlier fix was only tried in the desktop browser. The tablet picked up the new worker after one visit and the update prompt.

The edit test: I changed two words on the parent page, went back to the home screen and the progress strip showed the new words right away. No second reload was needed.

The offline test: I turned on airplane mode and reloaded. The game opened with the latest list and the speech worked, since the voices are local on this tablet. The sentence files were also found, which confirms the precache from earlier still works with the changed route.

One small thing remains. With a very slow network the manifest request can take several seconds before the fallback kicks in. I set a 3 second timeout on the fetch inside the worker, which is a fair limit for a page this small. Nothing else to do on this topic.

summary: Built a first version of a weekly summary page for the parent: words right, words missed and a short note per kid, rendered from stored scores only.
body:
The user said the export file is not something they want to read, and asked for a simple view of how each kid did in the week. I added a parent page section called 'This week'.

For each profile it shows a line with the number of words right on the first try, the number that needed more than one try and the number never answered. Below that is a list of the missed words with what was typed, so a parent can see 'neccessary' next to 'necessary' at a glance.

The data comes from the same answer records as the progress strip. I wrote a small module, src/parent/weekSummary.ts, that groups answers by profile and by word and ignores practice-mode answers, using the flag added this week. That kept the numbers in line with the dots on the home screen.

A few decisions worth recording:
- A week means the current list in the manifest, not seven calendar days, so it stays right if the school list starts mid-week.
- Words are matched by text, as with the progress strip.
- If a kid has no answers yet, the section says 'Not started' rather than showing zeros.

I checked it with the test data of last month. The older kid showed 9 right and 1 retried, and the younger kid 6 right, 3 retried and 1 not started. Those matched what I counted by hand from the raw data.

I wrote 5 tests for the grouping and the empty cases, and the suite is at 72 passing. The layout is plain: two cards side by side on the desktop and stacked on the tablet.

What is left: a check that the typed text escapes properly, since it comes from a kid's keyboard and goes into the page. I will do that next.

summary: Made the weekly summary show typed answers as plain text, closing a spot where kid input was put into the page as HTML.
body: Reviewing the summary page from last night, I noticed that the missed-words list was built with innerHTML and a template string. The typed text comes from a kid's keyboard, so a typed angle bracket would be treated as markup. I tested it by entering 'x' as a wrong answer on a test profile. The summary showed a bold x instead of the literal text. Not dangerous in a private game, but it would break the layout, and it is a bad habit. I replaced the string building with createElement and textContent in the summary module. I also searched for the same pattern elsewhere. The profile page showed the profile name through innerHTML as well, so I changed that too. Everything else already used textContent. I added two tests: one for the summary and one for the profile name, each with angle brackets and an ampersand in the input. They now expect the literal characters. The suite is at 74 passing and the build is green.

summary: Handled a new school list with 'their' and 'there' style words by checking that sentence mode covers them, and wrote the missing sentences for four.
body:
This week's list from school has several homophones: 'their', 'weather', 'whether', 'knew', 'new' and others. This is exactly the case sentence mode was made for, so I checked which of them had sentences.

Only two did. The sentence field is optional and the user had not filled the others in. I drafted sentences for the four missing homophones and put them in the list file for the user to review, since the parent page is where they would normally be typed.

While writing, I used the live preview to check each sentence. The warning for a missing word fired on one of mine, where I had written 'whether' as 'wether' by mistake, so the preview did its job.

I also kept to the earlier lesson that a sentence should not give the answer away with a longer form of the word. 'Knew' next to 'know' would have done that, so I avoided any form of the same verb.

The four sentences:
- their: 'The kids left ___ shoes by the door.'
- weather: 'The ___ was cold and grey.'
- whether: 'She asked ___ it would rain.'
- knew: 'He ___ the answer at once.'

I ran the manifest check in the build and it passed, with ten words and all sentence files present. The user can edit any of them on the parent page. I did not touch the other words.

summary: Investigated why the younger kid's streak reset after a day of play, and found the day boundary was computed in UTC so late evening play counted for the wrong day.
body:
The user reported that the younger kid's streak went back to zero even though they played every day. The kid plays late, around 20:30 to 21:00, and the streak broke on a day with a late session.

I looked at the streak code in src/streaks.ts. It turns each answer's timestamp into a day key with toISOString().slice(0, 10). That gives the UTC day, not the local one. In this timezone late evening is still the same local day as UTC, but the clocks changed recently, and the offset moved enough that a 22:30 session lands on the next UTC day in some cases.

To confirm, I took the kid's stored answers and printed both day keys. Three answers had a UTC day one ahead of the local day, and two of those sat on days where the kid also played earlier. That produced a day with two sessions and a gap the next day.

I wrote a failing test first: answers at local 21:30 and the next local day at 08:00 should be a streak of two. It failed as expected, showing a streak of one.

The fix computes the day key from local date parts, using getFullYear, getMonth and getDate, in one helper, dayKey(date). I also replaced two other places that built day keys the old way: the monthly export reminder and the weekly summary.

The harder part is history. Stored streak values were computed with the old keys, so I did not want to rewrite them blindly. I added a one-time recompute that rebuilds each profile's streak from the raw answers using the new key. It only runs if the result is longer than the stored value, never shorter, so a kid cannot lose a streak to the change.

On the test data the younger kid's streak went from 0 to 6, which matches what the kid says. The older kid's streak did not change. A flag in local storage makes the recompute run once.

Tests are at 78 passing, including a case across a clock change. I will ask the user to look at the streak on the home screen tomorrow.

summary: The user confirmed the younger kid's streak shows 6 again, and the recompute flag is set so it will not run twice.
body:
I asked the user to open the home screen on the tablet after the streak fix. The younger kid shows a streak of 6, which matches the real play, and the older kid is unchanged.

I also looked at local storage on the tablet through the remote inspector. The migration flag is present, so the recompute ran once and will not repeat. The stored streak value is the new one.

One more check: I played a short late-evening round on a test profile and compared the day key with the local clock. They agree. Nothing else was needed, and I closed the topic.

summary: Upgraded to the newest browser release's speech behavior check and found that the voice list loads late, so the voice picker showed empty on first open.
body:
After the browser auto-updated on the user's laptop, the voice picker in settings opened empty on the first visit and filled only after leaving the page and returning. Speaking worked, since it falls back to the default voice, but the user could not choose a voice at first.

The cause is in how the speech API reports voices. speechSynthesis.getVoices() returns an empty array until the browser has loaded them, and then a voiceschanged event fires. My picker called getVoices() once at render time. Before, the voices were ready by then, but the new release loads them a little later.

I wrote a small helper, loadVoices(), that returns a promise. It resolves right away if getVoices() is not empty. Otherwise it waits for voiceschanged, with a 2 second timeout so the page never hangs on a browser that has no voices at all.

The picker now renders with a 'Loading voices' line and replaces it when the promise resolves. If the timeout wins and the list is empty, it shows 'Using the default voice'.

I also checked the game screen. It picks the saved voice by name when speaking, and if the voices are not yet loaded the name lookup fails and falls back to the default. That means the first word of a session could be read in a different voice than the kid chose. I made the speak helper wait for the same promise, which adds no noticeable delay when the voices are ready.

I tested by throttling in the developer tools and by reloading about 20 times. The picker was filled each time, and the saved voice was used for the first word. On the tablet, where voices load fast, nothing changed.

I wrote 4 tests with a mocked speech object: voices ready, voices arriving by event, timeout with none, and the saved name missing from the list. All pass, 82 in total. The change is in src/speech/voices.ts and the two callers.

summary: Checked whether the saved voice survives a browser update by name; it does, but a voice that vanishes silently falls back, so I added a visible note in settings.
body:
Earlier this year a voice disappeared after an update, and I wanted to see how the game behaves now. I removed the saved voice name from the list in a test, by setting the profile to a name that does not exist.

The game spoke with the default voice, which is the right fallback, but nothing told the user. The settings page still showed the missing name as if it were chosen, or an empty dropdown.

I added a short note under the picker: 'The saved voice is not available here, using the default.' It only shows when the saved name is not in the list. I left the saved name as it is, so it comes back if the voice returns. One test covers it.

summary: Wrote and ran a plan to shrink the sound effects, which were the biggest files in the build after the bundle check, cutting them from 210 KB to 64 KB.
body:
The bundle check from a few weeks ago covered the code but not the audio. Looking at the dist folder, the five sound effects for right, wrong, streak, sticker and confetti add up to 210 KB, three times the size of all the code. That slows the first load on a weak connection and they also go into the offline cache.

The files were stereo WAV exports at 44.1 kHz. For short beeps and chimes that is a waste. I converted them with ffmpeg to mono, 22.05 kHz, and then to Ogg Vorbis with MP3 as a fallback for older browsers. The command was ffmpeg -i in.wav -ac 1 -ar 22050 -q:a 3 out.ogg.

Results:
- right: 48 KB to 12 KB
- wrong: 40 KB to 11 KB
- streak: 52 KB to 16 KB
- sticker: 38 KB to 13 KB
- confetti: 32 KB to 12 KB

The total is 64 KB. I listened to each on the laptop and on the tablet speakers. The wrong sound had slight hissing, so I raised its quality to 4 and it is still small at 13 KB.

The loader now picks the Ogg file when canPlayType says it is supported and otherwise the MP3. I updated the precache step so it caches only the chosen format list, not both, which keeps the offline cache small too.

One thing to watch: the sound effects play through a pool of audio elements, and the older tablet had a short delay on the first play. After conversion the delay was no worse than before.

The build and 82 tests pass. The cache version changed, so the update prompt will appear once on each device.

summary: Fixed the update prompt that showed on the tablet but did nothing when tapped, because the waiting worker was not told to skip waiting.
body:
After the sound change, the user tapped the update prompt on the tablet and nothing happened. The prompt stayed, and the old version kept running.

I looked at the service worker registration code. The prompt button called registration.update(), which only checks for a new worker and does not activate one that is already waiting. The new worker sat in the waiting state.

The fix has two parts. The button now posts a SKIP_WAITING message to the waiting worker, and the worker listens for it and calls skipWaiting(). The page then reloads on the controllerchange event, once only, so it does not loop.

I had to be careful about the sticker double-show problem from the past, where a reload at the end of the last word caused the reward to appear twice. The reload on controllerchange only runs when the user taps the prompt, never automatically, so that cannot return.

I tested by deploying a build to the local server, changing a file, and watching the cycle: prompt, tap, reload, new version. It worked twice in a row. The tablet picked it up the same way.

summary: Looked into a report that the game accepts a word typed with a trailing full stop, found no bug, and instead tightened the compare for accented and stray characters.
body:
The user said the older kid typed 'island.' with a full stop and was marked right, and wondered whether the compare had become too loose after the fuzzy match story. I checked before changing anything.

First I read the compare in src/answer.ts. It lower-cases both sides, trims the spaces and compares for equality. The fuzzy match for typos was removed after the 'recieve' problem, so it does not apply. A full stop at the end should make the answer wrong.

I then looked at the stored answers of that evening. The kid had typed 'island' and then, on a later word, 'island.' as a wrong answer, so the game had behaved correctly. The user had remembered the first of the two.

So there was no bug in this case. Still, while reading the code I found two small gaps worth closing:
- A typed non-breaking space, which the tablet keyboard can produce, is not removed by trim in some cases, and 'cat ' with it would be marked wrong for no visible reason.
- Decomposed accents, such as an e followed by a combining mark, differ from the single-character form, which matters for a word like 'café' from a school list.

I normalised both sides with NFC and replaced non-breaking spaces before trimming. I did not remove punctuation, because a full stop is a real mistake that the kid should notice.

Tests added for the non-breaking space, the two accent forms and the explicit full stop case, which must stay wrong. The suite is at 86 passing.

I told the user the full stop result in plain words and that the kid had done that once as a wrong answer. The history check from earlier shows no past answers changing with the NFC step.

summary: Added a gentle 'try again' for a first wrong answer before the word counts as missed, after the younger kid kept losing dots to slips of one key.
body:
The younger kid often hits a wrong key and sees the word counted as missed. A single typo then removes a dot for the week. The user asked if a second chance is possible without making the game too easy.

I added a retry rule: a first wrong answer shows 'Almost, try once more' and the word is read again. The second try is final. A right answer on the second try fills the dot but is recorded with tries: 2, so the weekly summary can still show it as retried.

The rule is a profile setting, on by default for the younger kid and off for the older one, who wanted the strict game. It is stored with the other profile settings.

The answer record gets a tries field. Old records have none, and the code treats a missing value as 1. The weekly summary uses it for the 'needed more than one try' count, which before had to be guessed from repeated answers.

I wrote tests for both outcomes and the settings default. Tests pass at 91.

summary: Measured how the retry rule changed the younger kid's results over a few days: first-try accuracy stayed at 71 percent, but dots filled went up and no word was skipped.
body:
A few days of play are now in the data after the retry rule, so I compared the younger kid's results with the days before it. I used the exported file and a small script that I did not commit.

Before the rule, over the last two weeks: 96 answers, 68 right at once, which is 71 percent, and 28 wrong. After: 41 answers, 29 right on the first try, which is again 71 percent, and 12 first wrong answers. Of those 12, 7 were right on the second try and 5 stayed wrong.

So the kid did not start typing sloppily because of the second chance. First-try accuracy is the same, which was my main worry. The rule rescued 7 of 12, mostly one-key slips like 'frend' for 'friend' that were fixed at once after hearing the word again.

The five that stayed wrong were real spelling errors, and they went into practice mode as before. Two of them were the hard words from earlier, 'necessary' and 'separate'.

I also looked at timing. The average time per word went from 14 seconds to 16, which is expected given the extra step. No session was cut short.

One side effect I had not planned for: the weekly progress strip fills a dot on a second-try right answer, but the sticker at the end of the week does not care about tries. That seems fair to me, and the user agreed when I described it.

I thought about whether the older kid should get the rule. They said no, they like the strict mode and their accuracy is 90 percent anyway.

No code change was needed from this check. I wrote down the numbers in the README under the notes on the game rules. If the kids' use keeps falling as the school app takes over, these will be among the last useful figures.

summary: Fixed the retry prompt not clearing when the kid started typing the second try, so the old message stayed on screen over the new answer.
body:
The younger kid pointed out that 'Almost, try once more' stayed visible while typing the second attempt, and it stayed even after the right answer until the next word. It looked like the game was still unhappy.

In the game module, the message element was set when the first answer was wrong, and only cleared in the function that loads the next word. For the second try, the input handler did not clear it. After a right second answer the success feedback was written into a different element, so both messages were visible.

I introduced one feedback area, a single element whose text is replaced each time. The retry message goes there, and the first keypress after it clears it. The success and failure messages go to the same place, so only one can show.

There was also a screen reader label tied to the old element, which I moved to the new one with aria-live set to polite. That way the message is announced once.

I wrote a test with a simulated first wrong answer, a keypress and then a right answer, and it expects an empty area after the keypress and the success text at the end. A second test checks that two messages never appear together.

The sound effects also played once per answer, which was right. The retry has no sound of its own, only the wrong sound on the first miss. I considered a softer tone for the retry but left it, since the kids did not mind.

Tests at 94 passing. I tried it on the tablet with the younger kid beside me. The message cleared at the first key press and the right answer showed a clean success line.

summary: Reviewed the open items in the README and the todo list, closed four that were done, and wrote down that two ideas will not be built.
body:
The usage of the game has been dropping slowly, and the user mentioned again that the school app may come soon, so I took an hour to tidy the notes instead of adding features. The README has a todo list that had grown out of date.

Done and removed from the list:
- the import restoring the last-export timestamp
- the streak recompute, with the day key fix
- the empty voice picker on first open
- the manifest being stale after a parent edit

Still open, and kept:
- a pinned word list for practice, which the user decided to handle by hand
- a check that the export file is not too large for the kids' history after a year, which I estimate at about 150 KB and so not a problem

Two ideas I wrote down as not planned. One is a leaderboard between the two kids, which the user thinks would cause arguments. The other is syncing scores between devices, since export and import is enough for a project that is likely to end soon.

I also read through the notes on how the game could end gracefully from a while ago. They still hold. The main points are: keep the site up as it is, make the export easy to find, and make the repository read-only at the end.

One more addition to the README: a short section on the game rules, with the retry setting, the practice flag and the way tries are counted, so that anyone coming back later can understand the data in the export file.

No code changed in this session besides the notes. The build and the tests were run once to be sure the README edits did not break anything, and both are fine.

summary: Checked the build output after the audio and worker changes: the deployed site is 142 KB in total, and every file is in the offline cache list.
body:
After several changes to the sounds, the worker and the manifest handling, I looked at the final build once more. The dist folder is 142 KB: 71 KB of code and data as before, plus the 64 KB of audio and about 7 KB of images and title art.

I compared the files in dist with the precache list written by the build step. Every file is listed, and no file is listed that does not exist. The cache version changed only when content changed, over three builds in a row, so the update prompt will not appear without a reason.

I also turned the network off in the browser and played through a full list in sentence mode with the tablet's size set. All sounds played and all sentences were read. Nothing needs changing.

summary: Prepared this term's new word list with the user's ten words, including three with sentences, and the manifest check passed on the first build.
body:
The user sent the ten words for the coming week. I typed them into a new JSON file in the word list folder and added the entry to the manifest, in the order the school gave them.

Three of the words are homophones, 'break', 'brake' and 'heard', with 'herd' close by. For those I wrote sentences with the blank, and checked each in the parent page preview. I made sure that no sentence contained a longer form of the target word, which was the problem in the first trial of sentence mode.

The sentences:
- break: 'Please do not ___ the glass.'
- brake: 'He pressed the ___ to stop the bike.'
- heard: 'We ___ a noise upstairs.'

The build runs the manifest check, which verifies that each list has ten words and that every listed file exists. It passed at the first attempt this time, unlike the day it found two stale entries. The precache step also picked up the new file and the three sentence files.

I ran the full tests, 94 passing, and then played the first three words myself on the laptop to hear the voice at the slower speed. The words were read clearly, and the sentence button appeared only for the three that have one.

I left the practice and retry settings alone. Deployment of the new list goes out with the next push. The user will check on the tablet tomorrow morning before school, and the younger kid will use the default retry rule as before.

Nothing else is pending on word lists until the next batch from school arrives.

summary: Reviewed the new term's word list in play: the kids hit two words with silent letters that the voice pronounced oddly, so I added spoken hints for both.
body:
After the list went live this morning, the older kid played an evening round and the younger one a short one. The voice read 'knight' and 'island' in a way that made the kids type guesses that were phonetically fair but wrong.

I checked how the other voices on the tablet read the same two words. Two of them did better, but the saved voice is the one the kids like, so I did not change it.

Instead I added an optional 'say' field to the word entries in the JSON. When present, the speech call uses that text instead of the word itself. For 'knight' it is 'night, as in a knight in armor' and for 'island' it is 'island, a piece of land in the sea'. I kept the displayed answer and the compare on the real word, so only the spoken text changes.

The loader needed a small change in src/words.ts to carry the new field through, and the manifest check script now accepts it as a string. I added two tests: one that the field is used for speech and one that it is never used for compare.

I ran the build and it passed. Bundle size moved by a few hundred bytes. I played the two words myself on the tablet and the reading sounded clear.

Next I want to see whether the older kid gets them right tomorrow without the hint note. If the field works, I will add it to the other awkward words from earlier terms when they come back in review. Nothing else is open from this session.

summary: Checked that the new 'say' field does not leak into the score export, and found it did not, but the import test needed a fixture update.
body:
Since I touched the word shape this afternoon, I wanted to be sure exports and imports stay stable. Scores store only word text and results, not the word objects, so the 'say' field cannot get in. I confirmed it by exporting from the tablet profile and reading the file.

The import test fixture, however, still used an older word shape in one sample and failed with a type error after the loader change. I updated the fixture to match the type and the 6 import tests passed again.

I also ran the full test suite: 58 tests, all green, in about two seconds. Then I tried a round in the browser with the offline mode on, because the word list is cached by the worker. The list with the new field loaded from the cache and the spoken hints worked.

One small thing I noticed is that the cached manifest version string is not shown anywhere on the parent page. That made it harder to tell which list the tablet had. I added the list name and the number of words under the parent page header, in a small grey line.

I did not change any kid-facing screen. The deploy is done and the live site matches the local build. That closes this thread unless the kids report a strange reading tomorrow.

summary: Planned a small fix list from a week of kid feedback: a larger input box on the tablet, a clearer dot display, and a faster replay button, with only the first done today.
body:
The user passed on three comments from the kids. The younger one finds the input box small when the on-screen keyboard is open, the older one says the dots for progress are hard to count, and both want the replay button to be quicker to reach.

I wrote the three items down in the todo list in order of effort. The input box is a CSS change, the dots need a layout tweak, and the replay button needs a position change that could affect the hint button next to it.

I did the input box first. With the keyboard open on the tablet, the viewport shrinks and the input was squeezed to about 36 pixels high. I set a minimum height of 56 pixels and a larger font size, and moved the input above the button row so it stays visible. I checked in landscape and portrait.

The layout held in both orientations. In portrait the word counter above it was pushed off the top on the smallest screen, so I reduced its margin. After that everything fit.

I did not start the dots or the replay button. The dots will need a short look at how they wrap for 10 words, and I want to check with the user whether the kids prefer numbers instead.

The build passes and the change is deployed. The two remaining items stay open in the todo list.

summary: Redid the progress dots so ten words wrap as two rows of five, which the older kid can count at a glance, and added a number as a fallback for screen zoom.
body:
The dots had been one long row. On the tablet in portrait they shrank and the ones for correct and wrong answers became hard to tell apart. This was one of the comments from last week.

I changed the container to a grid with five columns, so ten words show as two neat rows. The dot size grows with the viewport up to a cap, and the filled state has a clear ring now in addition to color, which helps with the color confusion I had suspected.

I also added a small text 'word 4 of 10' next to the dots. It is hidden visually on wide screens but stays for screen readers and appears when the page is zoomed past 150 percent, because the grid breaks down there.

I tested with the real word list and with a list of 8 and 12 words. Eight words give a row of five and a row of three, twelve give three rows. That looked fine, though the parent page can only enter ten, so it is a safety check only.

The retry rule from before still works: a first wrong answer does not mark the dot. I confirmed that the dot stays empty during the retry and fills after the second attempt.

I looked at the tablet and my laptop. The older kid tried it in the evening and said it was easier. The younger one did not comment.

One CSS rule for the confetti overlay had a z-index conflict with the new ring, so the ring showed over the confetti. I fixed it by lowering the ring's stacking order. Build size changed by about 0.2 KB. The replay button position is still open.

summary: Moved the replay button next to the input so it is under the thumb on the tablet, and kept the hint button where it was to avoid mis-taps.
body:
The kids said the replay button was too far away. It sat at the top, while their hands were at the keyboard. I moved it into the row right under the input, on the left, with the hint button on the right.

The risk I had noted was that the two buttons next to each other could be pressed by mistake. I gave them different shapes: replay is a round speaker icon and hint stays a rounded rectangle with a letter. I also put a gap of 24 pixels between them.

I tried it with the younger kid for a few minutes. They hit replay correctly each time and did not touch hint by accident. The older kid wanted a keyboard shortcut and I added Ctrl plus R replay? No, that clashes with page reload, so I used the Tab-friendly focus order instead and left shortcuts out.

I checked the layout on three widths. At the narrowest the row wraps to two lines, so I made the buttons shrink slightly before wrapping.

The todo item for the three feedback points is now complete. The build passes and the change is live.

summary: Started on a bigger word-list tool: a parent page preview that plays each typed word aloud before saving, to catch typos like 'seperate' that the kids would then learn wrong.
body:
The user mentioned that a typo in a list last term, 'definately', was only caught after a kid had already practiced it. The parent page saves whatever is typed, so the game would teach the wrong spelling.

I planned two checks. First, a play button next to each field, so the parent hears the word and can notice a mismatch. Second, a check against a small list of commonly misspelled words that flags a likely typo. I decided to do only the first today and think about the second.

In the parent page code, each of the ten rows now has a speaker button. It uses the same speech function as the game, with the voice and speed of the first profile. If the word field is empty the button is disabled.

I found a problem in the first test: the speech call sometimes fired while a previous word was still speaking, so the words overlapped. I added a cancel before each new utterance. That fixed the overlap.

The second check needs a word source. There is no dictionary in the project, and adding a large one would hurt the bundle that I have worked to keep small, 142 KB in total. A list of 200 common misspellings would be about 3 KB and catch the usual mistakes, but would miss the rest.

I wrote this tradeoff in the todo list and left the second check undecided. The preview button works on the tablet and desktop. I added two tests for the disabled state and for the cancel call.

Nothing was deployed yet, because I want to check the page with the user's real list first.

summary: Tried the new preview button on the user's real list of ten words and it surfaced one real typo, 'neccessary', before saving.
body:
The user typed the ten words of the next list and used the speaker buttons. One word was entered as 'neccessary', and when it was read aloud the user noticed the spelling on screen did not look right next to the sound.

They fixed it to 'necessary' and saved. That was the exact kind of slip the feature is for, so I counted it as a good sign.

The preview worked on every row with no overlap. I deployed the page change after that.

The common-misspelling list idea stays open.

summary: Decided against a misspelling list for the parent page: the speaker preview already caught a typo, and a 3 KB list would miss most cases anyway.
body:
I weighed the second check again after the preview worked on the real list. A list of about 200 commonly misspelled words costs around 3 KB, which is roughly two percent of the site, and would only warn about words on it.

The school lists include odd words that are not on any common list, so the check would give a false sense of safety. The speaker preview helps with all words, because the parent sees the text and hears it.

I wrote the decision into the README under the ideas that will not be built, next to the two already there. I removed the item from the todo list.

No code changed in this session. The user agreed over a short message.

summary: Found that the speaker preview on the parent page stays silent on the tablet until the first tap anywhere, and added a one-time unlock tap.
body:
On the tablet, the first press of a speaker button on the parent page did nothing, while later presses worked. On the laptop it worked at once.

The cause is the audio rule of the tablet browser: speech needs a user gesture before it plays, and in my code the first click handler ran an async voice lookup first, so the gesture was no longer counted when speak was called. The voice list loads late, as I found before.

I changed the handler to call speak straight away with the default voice if the list is not loaded yet, and to switch to the saved voice for later calls. That keeps the call inside the gesture.

I tested on the tablet: the first press now speaks, with the default voice, and the second with the saved voice. The difference is slight but audible. To avoid it I added a tiny silent utterance on the first touch of the page, which warms up the voice list. After that, the first press used the saved voice too.

The silent utterance has a volume of zero and no text length beyond one space. I confirmed there was no click or sound.

I added one test for the fallback path. The change is deployed and the tablet check is done.

summary: Checked the evening's play after the preview and focus fixes: both kids finished their rounds, with no errors in the console and no overlapping speech.
body:
I looked at the tablet after the kids played this evening. The older one did a full list and one practice round, and the younger one did the list twice.

The console showed no errors. I had added the silent warm-up utterance earlier today, so I listened for any stray sound at the start of the page and heard none.

The progress dots in two rows were used by both kids with no problems. The replay button position seemed fine; the younger kid used it often.

No code changes were made. I wrote a short note in the todo list that the feedback round is done and nothing is open for the next few days.

summary: Looked at why the younger kid's saved name showed as blank on the tablet after clearing site data, and found profiles were not restored from the last export automatically.
body:
The user cleared site data on the tablet to free space, and the game then asked to create a profile again. The scores were gone, which is expected. The surprise was that the export from the month before was sitting in the downloads folder, but there was no clear way to bring it back.

The import exists on the parent page, but it is hidden behind a settings link and the user did not remember it. I added a line on the first-run screen: 'Have a saved file? Import it here', which opens the same import dialog.

I tested it by clearing storage in a fresh browser profile, opening the page and importing the file. Both profiles came back with their streaks. The checks from last term for malformed files still apply.

I did not change the import logic itself. The new link is only a shortcut. Deployed after the tests passed.

summary: Wrote a short test for the first-run import link and found the dialog lost keyboard focus when closed, which I fixed so focus returns to the page.
body:
After adding the first-run import link this morning, I wrote a browser-level test that clears storage, opens the page, clicks the link and imports a fixture file. It passed on the first run.

While checking by hand, I noticed that after the import dialog closed, keyboard focus was lost and Tab started from the top of the page. For a parent using a keyboard that is awkward.

I stored the element that opened the dialog and called focus on it when the dialog closes, both after a successful import and after a cancel. For the first-run screen the element disappears after import, so I focus the main heading instead.

I tested with a keyboard only: open, cancel, focus returns to the link. Open, import, focus lands on the heading of the home screen.

I added two tests for these focus cases. The suite now has 61 tests and runs in about two seconds.

I also read through the parent page dialogs for the same problem. The export dialog has the same bug, so I applied the same fix there. The word editor has no dialog.

Build passed, deployed, and the notes in the todo list are updated. Nothing else is open.

summary: Answered the user's question about how many words the older kid has gotten right on the first try this term: 41 of 60, about 68 percent.
body:
The user asked how the older kid is doing compared with last term. I read the stored scores from the exported file rather than the live profile, to avoid touching anything on the tablet.

This term has six lists so far, so 60 words. The older kid got 41 right on the first try, 68 percent, and 57 right overall after the retry, 95 percent. Last term the first-try number was 64 percent.

The words missed most often are the ones with double letters, such as 'occurred' and 'beginning'. I listed the five most missed words for the user.

I did not change code. The numbers came from a short script I ran once in the console and did not save.

summary: Kept the stats script after all: the user asked for the same numbers for the younger kid, so I put it in a small parent page section showing first-try and overall accuracy.
body:
The user wanted the same figures for the younger kid, and likely again next term, so a throwaway script was not enough. I added a small section to the weekly summary page: first-try accuracy and overall accuracy per kid, for this term and the previous one.

The term boundary is taken from the list names stored with the scores. That works because each list has a name with a number. I did not add a calendar-based boundary.

For the younger kid the numbers were 59 percent first-try and 90 percent overall. The page shows both kids side by side with the same layout, in plain text.

I wrote 3 tests with sample score data, including a kid who has no scores for the previous term, which shows a dash instead of zero.

summary: Fixed the stats section dividing by zero for a new profile: it showed NaN percent instead of a dash, caught while testing with an empty profile.
body:
I tried the new accuracy section with a freshly created profile that has no scores. It displayed 'NaN%' for both numbers on the summary page.

The cause was a division of correct answers by total answers with a total of zero. The test for the missing previous term covered the missing-data case, but only when the term had no scores, not when the profile itself was empty and the current term was empty too.

I changed the percent function to return null when the total is zero, and the render code to show a dash for null. I also checked the other place that uses the same function, the streak note, and it already guarded against zero.

I added a test with an empty profile and one with a profile that has only retry answers.

The full suite passed, 64 tests. I deployed the fix after a visual check on the tablet.

The summary page now works for a third kid as well, in case the user adds one, though the profile creation limits it to two for now. That limit is not planned to change.

summary: Checked the site after the browser's latest update on the tablet: speech, offline mode and the install prompt all work, with no changes needed.
body:
The tablet's browser updated overnight, and since a past update changed how voices load, I ran the usual checks.

Speech worked with the saved voice and the voice picker was filled on first open. Offline mode loaded the last list in airplane mode. The service worker updated normally after a deploy of a trivial change, and the update prompt worked when tapped.

The only thing I noticed was a console warning about a deprecated meta tag in index.html, which does not affect function. I left it for now.

summary: Replaced the deprecated meta tag and used the chance to audit index.html, finding a missing theme color and a viewport setting that blocked pinch zoom.
body:
The console warning from the browser update pointed at an old mobile web app meta tag. The newer standard tag does the same, so I swapped it.

While I was in index.html I read the rest of the head. Two things stood out. The viewport tag had a maximum-scale of 1, which stops users from zooming. For a game for kids that may seem harmless, but a parent with poor eyesight on the parent page has no way to zoom, so I removed it.

The second is that there was no theme color, so the browser bar on the tablet was white against the dark game. I added a theme color matching the header and set the same color in the web manifest.

I tested the install flow on the tablet. The installed app now shows the right color in the task switcher. Before this it showed white at the splash screen for about half a second.

I also checked the title and the language attribute. The language was set to 'en', which is correct for the word lists, and speech uses the voice's own language.

I looked at whether the page works with the zoom now allowed. At 200 percent zoom the buttons wrap and the dots grid stays at five columns, so it is fine. The game input stays visible with the keyboard open.

The manifest change means the worker's cache list has to include it. It was already in the list. The build output went from 142.0 to 142.1 KB.

I ran the tests, deployed, and confirmed that the update prompt appears once on the tablet and the new color shows after the update. Nothing else is open in this area.

summary: Began a plan for a sticker reward after every fifth full list, after the older kid asked for something to collect, and built the data side first.
body:
The older kid asked if there could be something to collect. The game already has confetti and streaks, and the bundle check showed stickers taking a share of the size, so I expected the design to be cheap: stickers are small SVGs, not images.

I planned three steps. First, the data: a sticker is earned after every fifth list finished with all words right after retries. Second, a sticker page showing the earned and the locked ones. Third, the award moment at the end of a list.

I did the first step today. I added an 'earned' array to the profile with the sticker id and the list name where it was earned. I did not store a time, since the rest of the app avoids dates in the scores. The array is optional so old profiles load unchanged.

The award rule runs once when a list finishes. To avoid awarding twice for the same list when it is replayed, it checks the list name against the earned entries.

I wrote 7 tests: first award, no award for a list with a missed word, no double award, award on the fifth and tenth, and loading an old profile without the array.

The import and export need to carry the new array. The export already writes the whole profile, so it did. I checked that the import validation does not reject the new field, since it rejects wrong shapes. It does reject an array of wrong items, which is right.

There are twelve sticker designs planned. I drew none yet, and I am going to reuse the existing shapes from the confetti code in different colors.

Nothing is visible to the kids yet and nothing was deployed. The sticker page is next.

summary: Built the sticker page with four shapes in three colors and a locked silhouette for those not yet earned, then checked it on the tablet.
body:
I continued with the sticker feature from yesterday. The page lists twelve slots, as a grid of three columns, with earned ones in color and the rest as grey silhouettes.

There are four basic shapes, a star, a heart, a bee and a book, each in three colors, so twelve in all. They are inline SVG strings generated from a small function, which keeps each one to around 150 bytes and avoids extra files in the offline cache list.

The page is reached from a new button on the home screen, shown only if the kid has earned at least one. This matches how the 'Practice mistakes' button is shown.

I tested on the tablet with a profile with 3 earned stickers. The grid fit without scrolling in landscape and needed a short scroll in portrait. I left it as is.

One issue: the silhouettes were announced by screen readers as unnamed images. I gave each a label 'locked sticker' and each earned one a label with the shape and color.

I added 3 tests for the grid: count of earned, count of locked, and the labels.

The award moment at the end of a list is still to do.

summary: Added the award moment: when a list earns a sticker, the end screen shows it with a short pop animation and a soft sound reusing an existing effect.
body:
The end screen now checks whether the finished list earned a sticker. If so, it shows the new sticker at the center with a pop animation of about 400 milliseconds, and the text 'New sticker!'.

For sound I reused the existing right-answer effect at a lower pitch rather than adding a file, because the sound effects were shrunk from 210 KB to 64 KB not long ago and I did not want to grow them again.

The animation respects the reduced-motion setting: it shows the sticker with no movement. I tested that by turning the setting on in the system.

I played a whole list on the tablet with a profile set to be one list away from the fifth. The sticker appeared at the end after the confetti, and the sticker page showed it afterwards.

One rough edge is that the confetti and the sticker pop overlap for a moment. I delayed the sticker by 600 milliseconds, which looked better.

Tests: 2 added for the end screen with and without an award. All pass.

summary: Checked the offline cache list after the sticker work and found the build output still totals 143 KB, with every file listed in the worker.
body:
I looked at the build output after the sticker and animation changes. The deployed site is 143 KB in total, up about 1 KB from before, which comes from the sticker code and styles.

I compared the files in dist with the worker's cache list. All of them are listed and none is missing. The sticker SVGs are in the main bundle, so nothing new needs caching.

I then ran the site in airplane mode on the tablet and opened the sticker page. It loaded and displayed the earned stickers from local storage.

Nothing needed changing.
