summary: Wrote the README section for stickers, covering the award rule, where earned stickers are stored and how they appear in exports.
body:
The README had a section for each major feature except the newer ones. I added a section on stickers.

It says a sticker is earned after every fifth list that was finished with all words right after retries. Earned stickers are stored in the 'earned' array of the profile, with the sticker id and the list name. The array is optional so older exports still import.

I also noted that a replayed list never awards twice, and that sticker shapes are generated from a function, so adding a new one means editing that function and the count in the grid.

I added a line to the section on exports to say the stickers go along with the profile.

No code changed.

summary: Watched the older kid earn the first sticker in real play, and the pop and sound worked, though the kid wanted the sticker page to open straight from the award.
body:
This evening the older kid finished a list perfectly and got the first sticker. The pop appeared after the confetti, and the kid said 'oh nice' and tapped it, expecting it to open the page.

It did nothing, since the sticker on the end screen is just an image. I added a tap handler that opens the sticker page, and a back button there that returns to the home screen.

I tested it on the tablet. Tapping the sticker opens the page and the new one is highlighted with a thin ring. The back button returns correctly.

Tests: 1 added. Deployed.

summary: Investigated a report that the younger kid's sticker did not show after a perfect list, and found the list had a word that was only right on the retry, which the rule counts as a miss for stickers.
body:
The user said the younger kid finished a list with every dot filled but got no sticker. I first suspected a bug in the award code, so I read the profile from the tablet's stored data.

The list had 10 words. Nine were right on the first try and one was right on the second try, after the gentle 'try again'. The dot was filled, as the retry rule says, but the sticker rule I wrote requires every word right on the first try.

That is not what I wrote in the README. It says 'all words right after retries'. So the code and the documentation disagree. Looking at the code, the check used the first-try flag by mistake, and the tests I wrote used lists with no retried words, so they did not catch it.

The intended rule is the README one, since the retry was added exactly so that a slip of one key would not count against the younger kid. I changed the check to use the final result of each word.

I added three tests: a list with one retried word that is right earns a sticker, a list with one word wrong after retry does not, and a list with all retried words right earns one.

The harder question is whether to give the sticker to the younger kid for the list that was missed. The award runs when a list finishes, and the list name is stored with the score, so I wrote a small one-time check on load that looks at the last stored lists and awards any that qualify under the corrected rule but were not awarded. It sets a flag so it never runs twice, as with the streak recompute earlier.

I ran it on a copy of the exported data first. It awarded one sticker to the younger kid and none to the older, as expected. Then I deployed.

The user will open the game on the tablet tonight and I will check the profile after.

summary: Confirmed on the tablet that the one-time sticker check gave the younger kid the missed sticker exactly once and the flag stopped a second run.
body:
After the deploy this morning the tablet got the update and the user opened the game. I looked at the stored profiles through the export.

The younger kid now has one sticker, with the list name of the list that was missed, and the older kid still has the one earned in play. The recompute flag is set on both profiles.

I reloaded the page three times and the number of stickers stayed the same, so the check does not run twice. I also imported the earlier export into a fresh profile, which has no flag, and the check ran once there and awarded the same one sticker, which is the expected behavior for an old file.

The younger kid saw the sticker page with the new item and was pleased. There was no award animation, because the check runs silently on load. I considered adding it and decided against it, since a pop at an unrelated moment could confuse a young kid.

I also played a list on the tablet with a deliberate retry on one word and got the sticker at the end, which confirms the corrected rule in the live path.

The test suite has 73 tests and all pass. The README rule and the code now agree, and I added a line there that a retried word that ends right counts as right.

The bundle size is unchanged at 143 KB. Nothing is open for stickers now. The next items will come from the kids' feedback.

summary: Added a sticker page shortcut from the award screen, so the older kid can open the collection with one tap right after earning a sticker.
body:
The older kid asked for this after the first sticker was earned: the award screen showed the sticker, but getting to the sticker page took three taps. I added a 'See my stickers' button under the pop animation on the end screen. It links to the sticker page with a hash, #new, which scrolls to the newest sticker and gives it a short outline pulse.

The first version broke the back button. After the sticker page opened, back went to the start screen and not to the end screen, and the finished list was lost. I changed the link to open the sticker view as an overlay inside the same page, so back closes it and returns to the end screen. That meant moving the sticker rendering from sticker.ts into a function that both the page and the overlay call.

I checked three cases on the tablet. A first sticker, a later sticker and a list with no sticker all behaved correctly. In the last case the button does not appear at all, which I preferred to a disabled button the kid might poke at.

One leftover: the overlay does not trap keyboard focus yet. I noted it in the todo list. The build is still under 144 KB. Next I want to watch the older kid use the button in real play before changing anything else.

summary: Watched the kids use the new sticker shortcut at lunch: the older kid found it at once, the younger one tapped it by accident and could not get back.
body:
The older kid opened the sticker overlay straight from the award screen and was pleased. The younger kid tapped the button by accident while celebrating, then pressed the corner of the overlay and nothing happened. The close target was only a small x in the corner.

I made the close button bigger, 56 pixels square, with the word 'Back' next to it. Tapping the dark area outside the overlay now closes it too. I also added the focus trap that I had left on the todo list, so Tab stays inside the overlay while it is open.

I tested with a keyboard and with the tablet. Both closed cleanly and focus returned to the end screen button. No change to the cache list was needed.

summary: Planned and built a weekly 'review' round that replays words the kid missed in earlier weeks, after the user asked whether old mistakes ever come back.
body:
The user asked whether words a kid got wrong two weeks ago ever show up again. They do not: each week's list is played once and then only scores remain. I proposed a review round of up to five missed words, offered after the normal list, and the user agreed on the condition that it is optional and does not touch the sticker rule.

The data was already there. Each score record stores the word, the number of tries and the result, so a missed word is any record with a miss or a retry-only success. I wrote a small function, pickReview(profile, limit), in review.ts. It takes the most recent misses first, skips words already reviewed correctly, and returns at most five.

I hit an issue with duplicates. A word missed in three different weeks appeared three times in the candidate list, so I deduplicated by lowercase word before the limit is applied. A unit test covers that case, along with an empty profile and a profile with fewer than five misses.

The round itself reuses the normal game screen. The only differences are a title that says 'Review' and that the dots use a different color. I did not want a second game screen to maintain.

Scores from the review round are stored under a separate key, so the first-try accuracy numbers on the parent page do not change. This took some care, because the stats code reads every record it finds. I added a 'kind' field and made the stats script filter on it.

On the tablet the end screen now asks 'Try some old words?' with two buttons, Yes and Not now. Both worked. The speech played normally for the review words.

Remaining: the older kid's profile has only two misses so far, so the round is short for them. I need real data to judge it. I will look at it after a few days of play.

summary: Checked the review round after two evenings of play: the younger kid took it every time and fixed four old words, the older kid skipped it twice.
body:
I looked at the stored scores for the last two evenings. The younger kid accepted the review round both times and got four of the six old words right on the first try. The older kid pressed 'Not now' twice, which is fine because there were only two misses to review.

No review records leaked into the first-try stats; the numbers on the parent page matched my hand count. The console had no errors.

One small thing: a word fixed in review stays in the miss history, so it can be offered again later. I will change the picker to skip words that were later answered correctly in a review. That is for tomorrow.

summary: Made the review picker skip words already answered correctly in a later review, which stopped the younger kid from seeing the same four words each evening.
body:
The picker looked only at the original misses. A word fixed in review was still a miss in the history, so it came back the next evening. The younger kid noticed and said that the game was repeating itself.

I changed pickReview to build a set of words with a correct review record and drop them from the candidates. Reviews are stored under their own key, so the function now reads both keys. I added a field for the review's result and a test with a miss, a fixed review and a second miss of the same word. The expected result is that the word returns, because the newer miss counts.

That test failed at first. I had compared record order by array position, but imports merge the records in a different order. I switched to the stored timestamp. After that all eleven tests passed.

I also tried a run with the user's exported data from last month. The picker gave sensible words for both profiles, and the older kid's list was now empty, so the round is not offered at all. The end screen goes straight to the usual buttons in that case.

Build size is 144 KB. Nothing else changed.

summary: Wrote the README section for the review round, covering how words are chosen, where results are stored, and why they do not affect stats or stickers.
body:
I added a section to the README after the stickers one. It explains that a review round offers up to five words the kid missed before, newest first, once per word until it is missed again.

It also describes the storage. Review results sit under their own local storage key with a 'kind' field of 'review', and the export includes them. The import accepts older exports that lack the key and treats them as empty.

I added two sentences on what review does not do: it does not change first-try accuracy and does not count toward a sticker. The user cares about that rule, and it is the first thing I would want to know when I come back to the code.

While checking the export format I found the example JSON in the README was missing the 'say' field from this term's list. I fixed the example and ran the import test to confirm that it is still valid.

No code changed in this session.

summary: Found that the offline cache served an old word list after the weekly update on the tablet, and fixed it by versioning the cache name with the build hash.
body:
The user said the tablet still showed last week's ten words after the new list was deployed. The laptop showed the new words. That pointed at the service worker.

The worker used a cache-first rule for everything, including the JSON word lists, and its cache name was a fixed string. So once the lists were cached, the worker never fetched them again. This worked until now only because the lists were bundled with each new build, and I had been bumping the version by hand.

I made two changes. First, the cache name now includes the build hash that Vite already generates, so each deploy creates a new cache and the activate step deletes the old ones. Second, the word list requests use network-first with the cache as a fallback, so a connected tablet always gets the newest list and an offline one still works.

Testing took the longest. I deployed twice with different lists and loaded the page on the tablet between the two. The first run still showed the old words, because the old worker has to be replaced before the new rules apply. A reload after that picked up the new list. I told the user that the tablet needs to be opened once while online after this fix.

I also tested airplane mode. The game loaded, played the voice and showed the cached list. The scores were saved normally.

The total is now 144 KB, and every file is still in the cache list. I wrote a note in the README under offline mode about the cache name and the network-first rule for lists.

summary: Confirmed on the tablet that the new service worker replaced the old one overnight and the fresh word list loads, with offline play still working.
body:
First thing in the morning I opened the game on the tablet while connected. The page showed the new ten words straight away, so the worker had been replaced after the earlier visit.

I checked the cache storage in the browser tools through the laptop's remote inspector. Only one cache was listed, named with the new build hash. The old fixed-name cache was gone, which means that the activate cleanup works.

Then I switched the tablet to airplane mode and reloaded. The game started, the list was there and the voice read the first word. I played three words and the dots moved normally. The scores were still there after I turned the network back on.

One thing I wanted to rule out was a stale list during a slow connection. I throttled the network to a very slow setting. Network-first waited too long before it fell back to the cache, about ten seconds, and the kid would see a blank start screen. I added a three-second timeout on the list request with the cache as the fallback. That meant a small helper function with a Promise.race between the fetch and a timer.

With the timeout the slow case showed the cached list after three seconds and updated the cache in the background. The fast case was unchanged.

I ran the full test file and it passed. The build is 144 KB. This closes the stale list problem from yesterday.

summary: Started adding a simple weekly progress chart to the parent page, showing first-try accuracy per week as bars, and built the data grouping first.
body:
The user said that the numbers on the parent page are correct but hard to read as a trend. I suggested bars for each week, one row for each kid, and the user agreed to try it without a chart library.

Today I did the grouping. The scores have timestamps, but the weeks of school do not match calendar weeks, since lists start whenever the user types them in. So I group by list id instead, which already marks the week's list. For each id I count the first-try correct answers and total words for each profile.

The first result was wrong for the younger kid. Some lists had 11 records for 10 words because a replay of a word wrote a second record. I checked the game code and found that the replay button does not write a record, but a page reload in the middle of a word does. A reload restarts the word and the first attempt was already stored. I decided to count only the last record per word and list, which matches what the kid actually finished.

I wrote chartData(profile) in stats.ts. It returns an array of objects with list id, first-try count and total. Tests cover an empty profile, a profile with a single list and the duplicate record case. I also made sure that review records are filtered out, as for the other stats.

The rendering is not started. My plan is to draw each bar as a div with a percentage width, since that scales on the tablet and needs no canvas. Labels will use the list's first word, because the ids are not meaningful to a parent.

One open question is the order of lists when two ids were played on the same day. I will sort by the timestamp of the first record. The data function is finished and tested; the page is next.

summary: Rendered the weekly accuracy bars on the parent page with plain divs, with a percentage label and the first word of each list as the row name.
body:
I built the chart on top of chartData from yesterday. Each row is a label, a bar and a number. The bar is a div whose width is set to the percentage, with a minimum visible width so a zero shows as a thin line and not as nothing.

The labels use the list's first word, for example 'because' for that week. A long word wrapped badly on the narrow tablet, so I limited the label column to 8 characters with an ellipsis and set the full word in the title attribute.

The older kid's bars were mostly high, with a dip in one week. The younger kid's bars were steadier at around 70 percent. The user will be interested in the dip, which matches a week that had several silent-letter words.

I used two colors, one for each kid, which are the same as in their profile. I checked the contrast against the background and the lighter one failed, so I darkened it a little.

The page also needed a no-data state. A new profile shows a short line of text, 'No lists played yet', where the chart would be. I tested that with an empty profile because of the earlier NaN problem.

I added the chart to the parent page below the stats numbers. The page still loads fast, and the build is 145 KB. The new code is about 1 KB.

What is left: a screen reader check and the README note. I did not add anything for lists older than twelve weeks, so the page now shows only the most recent twelve.

summary: Checked the weekly chart with a screen reader and added text alternatives, since the bars were silent and conveyed nothing without sight.
body:
I turned on the screen reader on the laptop and went through the parent page. The numbers were read, but the chart rows were announced as empty groups, because the bars were only divs with a width.

I gave each row role='img' and an aria-label such as 'because: 7 of 10 first try, 70 percent'. The visible label and number are hidden from the reader inside that row, so nothing is said twice.

I checked again and the rows were read one by one in order. Then I wrote the README note for the chart: grouping by list id, last record per word, twelve most recent lists.

No other code changed. Build size is unchanged at 145 KB.

summary: Investigated the voice speaking too quickly on the younger kid's tablet after an update, and found the saved rate was ignored by the new voice.
body:
The user said the younger kid's tablet reads the words faster than before. The kid cannot catch them on the first play. The laptop sounded normal, so I looked at what differs on the tablet.

The game sets utterance.rate from the voice settings, currently 0.8 for the younger kid. I logged the utterance on the tablet. The rate was still 0.8 in my code, but the voice in use had changed name after the last system update. The saved voice name no longer matched any voice, so the code fell back to the default voice.

The default voice is a different engine, and it appears to treat 0.8 as relative to its own faster base speed. I timed the word 'necessary' at the same setting with both voices. The old one took 1.4 seconds and the default took 0.9 seconds.

There were two things to fix. The fallback should be chosen by language and quality, not by whichever voice comes first. And the rate needs a quick way for the user to adjust when the voice changes.

For the first I wrote pickVoice(saved, voices). If the saved name is missing it takes the voices with the language en and prefers one marked as local, then one whose name contains the old voice's first word. For the second I added a rate slider to the parent page, 0.5 to 1.0 in steps of 0.05, which saves in the profile.

I tested pickVoice with the saved name present, missing and with an empty voice list. The empty list returns null, and the game then uses the browser default without a voice setting. All three tests passed.

On the tablet the fallback now chose a local English voice. It was still a little fast at 0.8, so the user set 0.65 with the slider and the kid was happy. I have not yet added a warning on the parent page when the saved voice is missing. That would have caught this earlier.

summary: Added a parent page warning when the saved voice is missing, with a play-sample button, so a changed voice after an update is noticed straight away.
body:
This follows the speed problem from earlier tonight. The root cause was silent: the saved voice went missing and the game quietly picked another one. The user only noticed because the kid complained.

I added a check that runs when the parent page opens. It compares the saved voice name for each profile with speechSynthesis.getVoices(). If the name is absent, a yellow box appears with the text 'The saved voice is not available. Using: <name>.' It has a button to play a sample word and a link to the voice picker.

There was a timing bug. On the tablet getVoices() returns an empty list on the first call, and the list arrives later with the voiceschanged event. My first version showed the warning every time, because it ran before the list was loaded. I fixed it by waiting for voiceschanged, with a one second fallback timer, before comparing.

I also found that the game page had the same race. The start screen could pick the default voice before the list arrived. I moved the voice choice to the moment the first word is spoken, so it uses the list at that time. That is a small change in speak.ts, and it makes the choice lazy.

Testing: I renamed the saved voice in local storage to something fake, and the box appeared with the right fallback name. With the correct name, no box. With the name restored, the sample button played the word at the chosen rate.

The voice picker now shows the saved name at the top of its list, even if missing, marked 'unavailable', so nothing disappears quietly. I decided against deleting the missing name automatically, because the voice often comes back after the next update.

I ran all tests, and they passed. I added a test for the pickVoice fallback with an empty list that arrives later. The build is 145 KB.

The README has a short paragraph in the voice section about what to do after a system update. Next I want to check if the older kid's profile has the same problem; the same name was saved there.

summary: Checked the older kid's profile for the same missing voice, then made both profiles share one voice choice with an optional override, to cut the settings in half.
body:
I opened the older kid's profile on the tablet. Its saved voice was the same missing one, so the game used the fallback there too. The older kid had not complained because the rate of 1.0 was fine with the new voice.

That showed me that two profiles with two separate voice settings did not give much. In practice the user set the same voice for both and only changed the speed. I proposed one default voice for the household with an optional override for each profile, and the user agreed.

The settings structure had voice and rate in each profile. I added a top-level voice default. A profile now has voice as either a name or null, and null means the default. Rate stays per profile, since it differs between the kids.

Migration was the careful part. For existing data, if both profiles share the same voice name, I move it to the default and set both profile values to null. If they differ, I keep them as overrides and set the default to the older kid's. I wrote the migration as a function with a version number in the settings, so it runs once.

The tests used four fixtures: both the same, both different, one empty and no settings at all. The last one initially threw because I read a property of undefined. I fixed it with a default settings object. All four passed.

The parent page now has a single voice picker at the top, a rate slider for each kid, and a small 'use a different voice for this kid' checkbox that shows a second picker. The warning box from earlier works for the default and for any override.

I tried it on the tablet. Both profiles used the default voice, and the younger kid's rate of 0.65 was kept. Switching the override on for the older kid changed only their voice.

I exported and imported the scores and settings. The export has the new version number, and an older export without it is migrated on import. I tried an export from a month ago and it imported fine.

The README is updated. The build is 146 KB, and every file is in the cache list. The remaining item is to clean up the old per-profile voice keys after a few weeks, once the user is sure there is no need to roll back.

summary: Prepared the new word list from the user's ten words, tested the preview, and fixed a sentence field that the voice read with an odd pause.
body:
The user sent this week's ten words. I typed them into the parent page with the preview, which plays each word before saving. It did not find a typo this time.

Two of the words had sentences for context. The voice read the first sentence with a long pause after the comma, which sounded like two phrases. The sentence was 'The cat, however, did not move.' I tried a few options. Removing the commas worked but changed the user's text, which I did not want to do for the display.

So I added the 'say' field idea from last term to sentences too. The display text stays as typed, while a say value can be given for speech only. For this sentence I set say to 'The cat however did not move.' The pause was gone.

I checked that the field does not appear in the score export and that the manifest check still passed. The build was clean on the first try.

I tried the list on the tablet. All ten words were read in order and the sentence played after the word on request. The younger kid's rate setting of 0.65 was applied to the sentences too.

One question I raised with the user is whether the sentences should be read automatically on the second try. They said no, only on request, so I left it. I did not change the game code today, only the list and its JSON. The list is live.

summary: Looked at the evening's play on the new list: both kids finished, and the younger kid used the sentence button twice, with no console errors.
body:
I checked the stored scores after dinner. The older kid got nine of ten on the first try. The younger kid got seven, and used the sentence button on two words.

The missed words were 'neighbour' and 'weight', both with silent letters. The voice read them clearly, so I did not add spoken hints.

The console was clean and the voice rate was right. No stickers were due. The review round was offered to the younger kid with three words and accepted.

summary: Fixed the review round offering words from the current week that the kid had already missed on the same list, which made it feel like a repeat.
body:
The younger kid said the review round asked about words that they had just played. This was true. The picker took the most recent misses, and those included misses from the list that had just ended.

That is not review in the sense the user meant, which was words from earlier weeks. I added a filter that excludes records with the current list id. The function now takes the current list id as an argument, and the end screen passes it.

I wrote a test with a profile whose only misses are from the current list. The expected result is an empty array, and so the round is not offered. Another test has misses from the current and an earlier list, and only the earlier ones are returned. Both passed, along with the earlier tests.

The change affects the README text as well, since it said 'newest first'. I changed it to 'newest first, from earlier lists'.

On the tablet I played a short list with two deliberate misses. The end screen did not offer review, as expected. With an earlier miss in the history it offered exactly that word.

The build is 146 KB. This was a small fix, but it changed what the round does, so I told the user in the summary of the session. They were fine with it.

summary: Began a small redesign of the start screen, replacing the plain button stack with a large play button and the list name, and built it behind a quick tablet check.
body:
The user said the start screen looks like a form, and the younger kid sometimes taps Settings instead of Play. I proposed a layout where Play is large and central, the list name is shown above it, and the other buttons are small and placed at the bottom.

I started with the markup in index.html. The Play button is now 160 pixels high and spans most of the width. Above it there is the line 'This week: <first word>…' so the kid knows which list is active. The links to stickers, review and the parent page are in a row at the bottom, in a smaller size.

The small buttons were a problem for the tablet. At 32 pixels they were too small for the younger kid's thumb. I raised them to 48 pixels, which still looks small next to Play. The parent link is intentionally the smallest, because the kids do not need it.

I used the same colors as the sticker page for consistency. The older kid's profile color is the accent on the Play button. That means the button changes color when profiles switch, which is a small thing, and the kids like it.

There was a layout bug in landscape. The Play button pushed the bottom row off the screen, and it needed a scroll. I switched the container to a flex column with min-height 100vh and let the middle part grow. That fixed landscape, and portrait was unchanged.

I checked zoom at 200 percent as before, because the older kid sometimes zooms. The bottom row wrapped to two lines but stayed visible.

I did not touch the game screen. The profile picker is the next item, since it sits above the Play button and still looks like the old design.

The build is 146 KB, with about 400 bytes more CSS. The cache list needed no change. I took two screenshots for the user to see before it goes live, and I have not deployed this yet.

summary: Showed the user the new start screen screenshots, who liked the big Play button but asked for the profile names to be larger, so I raised them and deployed.
body:
The user looked at the two screenshots this evening. They liked the Play button and the list name line. They said the profile names above it looked too small for the younger kid to read.

I raised the profile name from 16 to 24 pixels and made each profile chip a larger tap target. The selected one has a thicker outline in its color.

I checked it on the tablet in both orientations. Nothing overflowed, and the Play button was still reachable without a scroll. I deployed after the build and test run passed.

The build is 146 KB. I will ask the kids tomorrow if anything confuses them.

summary: Heard from the kids that the new start screen is easier, but the younger kid could not find the review round, which now sits in the small bottom row.
body:
The user passed on feedback from this afternoon. Both kids tap Play without trouble now, and the younger kid has not hit Settings by mistake once. That was the goal of the redesign.

The cost is that the review link is in the small row and the younger kid did not notice it. Review also appears on the end screen, but only when there are words to offer, so a kid who skips it once does not see it again until the next list.

I considered three options. One was a bigger review button on the start screen, which would bring back the clutter. A second was to remove the link and leave only the end screen offer. The third was to show a small badge with the number of words ready on the link.

I chose the badge. The number comes from pickReview with the current list id, the same function the end screen uses, so the two always agree. A link with a badge of 0 is hidden, which also saves space. The badge is a small circle in the profile's color, with the number in white.

The first version computed the badge when the page loaded, before the profile was chosen, so it showed the previous profile's number. I moved the calculation to the profile switch handler too. That fixed it, and I tested switching back and forth four times.

I also wrote an aria-label for the link, 'Review, 3 words ready', so the number is spoken with it.

The tests cover the badge count function for a profile with several misses, none and only current-list misses. They passed.

On the tablet the younger kid's link showed a 3 and the older kid's link was hidden, since their history is clean. The younger kid tapped the 3 without being told, which was a good sign.

The build is 147 KB. I have not changed the cache list, since no new files were added. I will watch whether the younger kid uses it on their own over the next days.

summary: Checked a few days of play after the start screen and badge changes: the younger kid started the review round twice from the badge, and there were no errors.
body:
I looked at the stored scores and the review records. The younger kid opened the review round twice by themselves in the last two days, each time from the start screen badge, and fixed five of six words in total.

The older kid's link stayed hidden because their misses were all from the current list. That is correct. The first-try numbers on the parent page were the same as my own count, so the review records are still kept apart.

The console had no errors on either profile. The tablet's cache held only the latest build.

One thing I noticed is that the badge number stays the same until the page reloads when a word is fixed in the same session. It is minor, because the kid returns to the start screen through a reload. I wrote it in the todo list instead of changing the code.

summary: Fixed the stale review badge by recomputing it whenever the start screen is shown, and used the session to tidy the todo list and remove the old voice keys.
body:
The badge number was computed once at load and when the profile changed. After a review round the kid went back to the start screen without a reload, so it still showed the old count. The younger kid noticed a 3 on the link after fixing all three words.

I moved the badge calculation into a function showStart() that runs every time the start screen is displayed. Both the profile switch and the return from a round call it. This is less code than before, since the separate handler is gone.

I tested it by finishing a review round and tapping Home. The badge went from 3 to 0 and the link disappeared. Then I missed a word on purpose on a new list, and the badge rose by one on the next visit. The unit tests for the count function did not need changes.

Then I did the cleanup I had planned for the voice settings. It has been three weeks since the shared voice migration and the user has not asked to roll back. I removed the old per-profile voice keys from the migration and from the export, and kept the code that reads old exports, so an old file still imports. The settings version is now 3.

I checked the import with an export from before the migration and one from after. Both loaded, and the voice came out the same in each case. I ran all tests, and they passed with two fewer fixtures than before.

I went through the todo list. I closed the focus trap item and the stale badge item. I also removed the idea of showing sentences automatically on the second try, because the user said no. Three items remain: the larger input box on the tablet, a faster replay and a note about how to add a third profile.

The build is 146 KB after the cleanup. Every file is still in the offline cache list. I deployed after the checks.

summary: Started a plan for a spelling-bee style streak freeze after the younger kid lost a long streak to one sick day, and built the date logic first.
body:
The younger kid lost a nine-day streak because of one sick day, and was upset enough that the user asked whether the game could forgive a single missed day. I wrote down the idea before touching code: one freeze per kid, earned after a week of daily play, spent automatically when exactly one day is skipped.

The streak code in src/streaks.ts compared the last play day with today by subtracting timestamps, which was already fragile around clock changes. I rewrote it to compare local calendar days as plain year-month-day numbers, with a small helper called dayNumber. That helper has tests for the clock change night and for midnight play, and all of them pass.

Then I added a freezes field to the stored profile with a default of zero, so old saved profiles load without a migration step. The streak function now returns the new streak and whether a freeze was spent, instead of a single number. The callers on the start screen and the end screen were updated to use the new shape.

I did not build the earning rule yet. For now the freeze count can only be set by hand in the console, which was enough to test the spending path. With one freeze and a one-day gap the streak held. With two missed days it reset and the freeze stayed unspent, which is what I intended.

Next steps are the earning rule, a small snowflake icon on the start screen, and a line in the parent page so the user can see the count. I also want to ask the user whether the older kid should get the same rule, since that kid never loses streaks anyway.

summary: Added the rule that earns a streak freeze after seven days of play in a row, capped at one held at a time, with tests for the edge cases.
body:
This continued the freeze work from earlier today. The earning rule is simple: when a kid's streak reaches a multiple of seven and they hold no freeze, they receive one. A kid can hold at most one, so a long streak does not pile up a stock that makes the streak meaningless.

I put the rule in the same function that updates the streak, so there is a single place to read. The function now returns three things: the new streak, whether a freeze was spent, and whether one was earned. I wrote tests for day seven with no freeze, day seven with one already held, day fourteen after a spend, and a gap of two days.

One case surprised me. If a freeze is spent on day six and the kid plays on day seven, the streak reaches seven and a new freeze is earned at once. I decided this was fine and even kind, and I added a test so the behavior is deliberate.

The parent page now shows the freeze count next to the streak for each profile. I have not added anything to the kid screens yet. That is the next piece, together with the question of how to tell a kid that a freeze was used without making it feel like a punishment.

summary: Showed the freeze as a small snowflake on the start screen and a gentle note after it was used; the younger kid understood it straight away.
body:
I added a snowflake icon beside the streak count on the start screen. It is drawn in plain SVG inline in the page, so the worker cache list does not change and the build output stays about the same size. When a kid holds a freeze the snowflake is blue, and when none is held it is a faint outline.

When a freeze has just been spent, the start screen shows one line: the streak is saved by the snowflake. I kept the wording friendly on purpose and avoided any phrase about missing a day. The note shows once and is cleared by a flag stored in the profile, the same pattern as the one-time sticker check.

I tried it on the tablet by setting the last play day to two days ago in the console. The streak held, the snowflake turned to an outline, and the note showed once and did not return after a reload.

The younger kid was nearby and asked what the snowflake was. After a short explanation, the kid said it was a day off ticket, and wanted to know how to get another one. That seemed the right level of understanding.

The older kid has not seen it yet. Open question: whether the parent page should let the user hand out a freeze by hand. I left that out for now, because it seems easy to abuse and not needed.

summary: Investigated a tablet update that made the speech voice list load empty on first page open, and fixed it by waiting for the voiceschanged event with a timeout.
body:
The user reported that after the tablet updated its browser, the first word of a new session was read in a flat default voice, and only later words used the chosen one. Replaying the same word fixed it. That pointed at timing rather than the saved setting.

I reproduced it by clearing the page and reopening it on the tablet with remote debugging attached. The call to speechSynthesis.getVoices() returned an empty array at the moment the first word was spoken, and the list filled in a fraction of a second later. Our voice lookup found nothing and fell back to the default silently.

The old code handled this only in the parent page, where the warning about a missing voice lives. The play screen read the voices directly. I made a single function in src/voice.ts called whenVoicesReady that returns a promise. It resolves at once when the list is not empty, otherwise it waits for the voiceschanged event, and it gives up after 1500 ms and resolves with whatever there is.

The timeout matters. On some devices the event never fires, and without a limit the game would hang before the first word. With the limit, the worst case is a one and a half second delay and a default voice, and the parent page warning still explains why.

Both the play screen and the parent page now use this function. I also removed a duplicate lookup that had crept into the sample button.

Tested four times on the tablet from a cold start: the chosen voice spoke the first word every time, and the delay was not noticeable. I also tried the desktop browser, where the list is ready immediately, and nothing changed.

I wrote a short note in the README troubleshooting part about the empty list on first load. No tests were added for the event path, because the browser speech API is hard to fake well, and a manual check on the tablet seemed more honest.

summary: Watched a morning of play after the voice timing fix and saw the chosen voice on the first word every time, with no console errors.
body:
The younger kid played the weekly list before school and the older kid did a review round. I watched with the console open on the tablet.

The first word of each session was spoken in the chosen voice, which was the thing that had been broken. I measured the delay between pressing Play and the first sound at about 300 ms, which is not noticeable for a kid.

The review round ran without trouble, and the badge on the start screen updated afterward. No errors appeared in the console during either session.

One small thing: the younger kid pressed the sample button on the parent page by accident while looking for the sticker page, and the voice spoke the sample sentence. Nothing is wrong, but the two pages look alike on a small screen.

I consider the voice timing issue closed. I will keep the 1500 ms limit as it is.

summary: Replaced the rough sound-effect volume with one shared gain setting, after the younger kid said the wrong-answer buzz was too loud at night.
body:
The younger kid plays in the evening, and the wrong-answer sound was loud next to the quiet voice. The effects were played through separate audio elements at their file volume, so I had no single place to change them.

I added a small module, src/sound.ts, that creates one gain node and routes every effect through it. The default gain is 0.5, and the wrong-answer sound has a further factor of 0.7 so that a miss is noticeable but not harsh.

The parent page got a volume slider for the effects, stored with the shared voice choice. It plays the right-answer chime when released, so the user hears the level they set.

I tested it on the tablet at low system volume and the balance was better. The sticker pop uses the same module now, and it sounded fine.

The older kid did not mind the louder level, so the slider is per device and not per profile. That keeps the settings simple.

summary: Fixed the text field losing focus after a wrong answer on the tablet, which made the kid tap again before retyping the word.
body:
The younger kid noticed that after a wrong answer the keyboard slid away and had to be brought back by tapping the field. On the tablet this took a second and broke the rhythm of the game.

The cause was in the code that shows the wrong-answer feedback. It replaced the input element with a fresh one to reset the shake animation, and a new element has no focus. I changed it to keep the element and restart the animation by toggling a class with a forced reflow in between.

I also moved the focus call into one function, focusInput, so the right-answer path and the wrong-answer path do the same thing. Checked on the tablet: the keyboard stayed up through five wrong answers in a row, and the shake still showed each time.

The fix is deployed. The kid did not mention it again, which I take as a good sign.

summary: Looked at why the weekly chart on the parent page showed an empty bar for a week the kids skipped, and decided it should show a gap label instead.
body:
The user asked about a bar at zero percent for the week of the school trip. It looked as if the kids had failed everything, when in fact they had not played at all.

The grouping code produces one row per list, and a list with no attempts had an accuracy of zero because the division of correct answers by tries returned zero for no tries. I changed the function to return null in that case.

The renderer now shows a grey row with the text no play this week and no bar. The text alternative for screen readers says the same.

I checked it with the stored data of both profiles. Only the one skipped week changed, and the other bars were the same as before.

summary: Built an export of scores to a CSV file from the parent page, so the user can keep a copy outside the tablet's local storage.
body:
The user worried that clearing the browser data on the tablet would erase all scores and stickers, and asked for a way to keep a copy. I decided on a CSV download, since it opens in any spreadsheet and needs no server.

The export has one row per word attempt: profile, list name, word, number of tries, first-try result, and a local timestamp in plain text. Review round attempts are included with a column that marks them, because the README says they do not affect stats and the user may want to filter them out.

The code is in src/export.ts. It reads the same storage keys as the chart, builds the text with proper quoting for commas and quotes in the sentence field, and starts a download through a temporary link and a Blob. I added a byte order mark at the start so the spreadsheet on the user's computer reads accents correctly.

A first test with the real data gave a file of 41 KB with 1,180 rows. It opened cleanly, but the timestamps were in a format the spreadsheet did not treat as dates. I changed them to year-month-day with a space and the time, and then they sorted correctly.

On the tablet the download went into the downloads folder without a prompt, which is fine. I also put a button on the parent page labelled Export scores, with a line below it that says what is included.

The sticker data is not in the CSV, because stickers are not attempts. I made a second small export for stickers as plain JSON, which the README already mentions as the format in exports, and I checked that the field names matched what the README says.

There is no import yet. If the data is ever lost, the user would have to reconstruct by hand, so an import is the logical next step, but I want to talk to the user first about whether it is worth the risk of a bad file overwriting good data.

summary: Added a score import for the JSON backup with a preview step and a merge rule, so a bad file cannot overwrite good scores.
body:
After the export work, the user agreed that a backup is only half useful without a way to load it. We talked about the risk of a wrong file, and settled on a preview before anything is written.

The import reads the JSON file chosen on the parent page and checks its shape: a version number, a profile list, and attempts with the expected fields. A file that fails the check is refused with a message that names the first problem found.

If the file passes, the page shows a preview: how many attempts are new, how many already exist, and which profiles are affected. Only after the user presses Confirm does anything change. The merge rule is to add attempts that are not present, matched by profile, list, word and timestamp, and never to delete or change existing ones.

I wrote tests for four files: a good one, a file with a missing field, an empty one, and one from a newer version number. The newer version is refused with a note to update the game.

To make this possible the export now includes a version number, set to 1. Backups made earlier today have none, so the import treats a missing number as 1.

I tried a full round trip on the tablet: export, clear the storage, import. The chart looked the same as before, and the streaks and stickers were intact, since they are part of the JSON backup.

One gap remains. The streak freeze count is stored in the profile, and I forgot to put it in the export at first. I added it and bumped nothing, since an absent count is read as zero.

summary: Wrote the README section on backup and restore, including the file format, the merge rule and what the CSV leaves out.
body:
The export and import work had no documentation yet, and the user will be the one who needs it after a long gap, so I wrote the section while the details were fresh.

The section starts with when to make a backup, which is before clearing browser data and before changing tablets. It gives the steps on the parent page in order, with the exact button names.

Then it describes the JSON format: the version number, the profiles with their freeze counts and stickers, and the list of attempts. A short example with two attempts is included, so the shape is clear without opening a file.

The merge rule gets its own paragraph. Attempts are matched by profile, list, word and timestamp, nothing existing is changed, and a file with a newer version is refused.

I also noted what the CSV is for: reading in a spreadsheet only. It has no stickers or freezes and cannot be imported.

I checked every name in the text against the code, and corrected one place where I had written Backup instead of Export scores.

summary: Tracked down a crash on opening the parent page for a profile with no attempts, caused by the new gap row in the chart, and added a test fixture for it.
body:
The user created a profile for a cousin who visits, and opening the parent page then showed a blank area where the chart should be. The console had an error: cannot read properties of null, reading toFixed.

The cause was my own change from a few days ago. Accuracy is now null for a list with no attempts, and the renderer handled that case. But the label under the chart, a line giving the average over all weeks, called toFixed on an average that was null when there were no weeks at all.

I reproduced it first by creating an empty profile in a fresh storage, then wrote the failing test before the fix. The test builds a profile with no lists and expects the summary line to read no data yet.

The fix is small: the average function returns null for an empty list, and the label code checks for null. While I was in the file I looked for other places that assumed at least one list, and found two more.

The first was the best week line, which took the maximum of an empty array and showed negative infinity. The second was the streak summary, which was fine. I fixed the first and added to the test.

I made a small fixture file, test/fixtures/empty-profile.json, and a helper that loads it, so later tests of the parent page can start from an empty profile. Before this each test built its data inline, which hid the case.

After the fix I opened the parent page with three profiles: two with data and one empty. All of them rendered, and the empty one showed no data yet in place of the chart.

The cousin's profile also revealed that new profiles start with the shared voice, which is right, and with a freeze count of zero, which is also right. I deleted the profile afterward from the parent page, and checked that deleting does not touch the other profiles' data.

The lesson is about the null I introduced: every consumer of accuracy should handle it. I searched for the function name across the source and found it used in four places, all now checked.

summary: Checked the build size and the worker cache list after the backup features and found 149 KB total, with the new files all listed.
body:
After the export and import code I wanted to confirm that the offline cache still covers everything, since a missing file would only show up when the tablet is offline.

The build output is now 149 KB, up from 143 KB at the time of the sticker work. The growth comes from the export, import and sound modules.

I compared the file list in the generated worker with the files in the dist folder, and every file was there, including the new script chunk. The cache name still carries the build hash, so the update replaces the old cache.

I then put the tablet in flight mode and opened the game. The start screen loaded, a list played with voice, and the parent page opened. The export button worked offline, which makes sense since it needs no network.

Nothing needed fixing. I noted the size in the todo list as a baseline.

summary: Looked into whether a hyphenated word such as ice-cream is graded correctly, and fixed the comparison to accept a missing hyphen only when the list says so.
body:
The user's new word list includes ice-cream, and asked what happens when a kid types icecream or ice cream. I tested it and found that both were marked wrong, and the kid saw no hint about why.

I decided that spelling lists from school are strict, so I did not want to accept the missing hyphen in general. Instead each word in the JSON can have an optional field, alsoAccept, with an array of other spellings. The list for this week uses it for none of the words, so the behavior stays strict.

What I did change is the feedback. When the typed word equals the right word with hyphens or spaces removed, the wrong-answer message says the word has a hyphen, so the kid knows the letters are fine. The grade is still a miss.

I wrote tests for the hyphen case, an apostrophe case, and a normal miss. The comparison already lowercases and trims, and I left that alone.

The parent page word entry preview shows the same hint, so the user can see it while typing the list. I tried it on the tablet and the message read well.

The field alsoAccept is described in the README now, in a single line.

summary: Made the end screen show which words were missed on the first try, in the order they came, so the kid can look at them before moving on.
body:
The older kid said that after finishing a list there was no way to see which words had been wrong, and asked to see them. The end screen only showed the score and sometimes a sticker.

I added a list of missed words under the score. Each shows the correct spelling and what the kid typed first, side by side. Words answered right on the first try are not shown, so a perfect list keeps the clean screen it had.

The data was already there, since the attempt records hold the first typed text. I only had to read it back at the end of the round and render it.

There is one subtle thing. A word right only on the retry counts as a miss for stickers, and it should be shown in this list too, so the kid understands why a sticker did not come. I tested this with the case from the earlier sticker report.

On the tablet, a list of six misses fits without scrolling, but ten would not. I let the area scroll and kept the buttons fixed at the bottom.

The review round button stays visible below the list. I did not change its position, remembering the trouble with its place on the start screen.

summary: Watched both kids use the new missed-words list: the older kid studied it for a minute, the younger one skipped it and went straight to the sticker page.
body:
I sat in on the evening session on the tablet. The older kid finished the list with three misses, read the missed words aloud and said one of them was obviously a typo. It was a real error, since the kid had swapped two letters.

The younger kid finished with all words right, so the list did not show, and went to the sticker page. That is the intended path for a perfect list.

Later the younger kid had one miss in a second round and tapped past the list at once, so the list does not help every kid. The older kid is the one who uses it.

No errors in the console, and the screen scrolled properly with seven misses I made on purpose. I do not plan changes. I will look again after a few weeks of play to see whether the older kid's review round start rate went up.

summary: Replaced the flat word list files with a loader that validates each weekly JSON and reports the exact bad entry on the parent page, after a typo broke a list.
body:
Last night the user typed a new list into the JSON by hand and left out a comma. The page loaded with no words and no message, and the kid saw a blank screen until I looked at the console. I wanted a failure that explains itself.

The old loader fetched the file and passed the parsed result on. If the parse failed, an exception went to the console and nothing else happened. I wrote a new function in src/lists.ts, loadList, that does three things: it fetches, it parses with a try block, and it validates the shape.

The validation checks that there is a name, that words is an array of one to thirty entries, and that each word has a text field with only letters, hyphens and apostrophes. A sentence is optional, and so is alsoAccept. Each failure produces a message with the list name and the index of the entry, for example: list week-31, word 7: missing text.

On a failure the play screen now shows a short note telling the kid to ask a parent. The parent page shows the full message in a red box at the top. The previous week's list stays available, so the kids can still play something while it is fixed.

I had to decide how to find the previous list. The loader reads an index file that already orders lists by week, so I take the next entry back. If that also fails, it keeps going back to the first valid list, and gives up only when none is valid.

I wrote tests with six broken files: invalid JSON, no name, an empty words array, a number in place of text, a word with a space inside, and a list with thirty-one words. All six give the expected message, and a valid file passes.

A small surprise was that the older words files had a few entries with a trailing space. They passed before because of trimming at grading. The validator now rejects them, which found two real ones in old lists, and I fixed those by hand.

I tried the whole thing on the tablet by breaking this week's file on purpose. The play screen showed the note, last week's list was offered, and the parent page showed the red message pointing at the right entry. After restoring the file everything was normal again.

The build grew by under 1 KB and the worker list is unchanged, since the code is in an existing chunk. The README now has a paragraph on the list format and the messages the user can expect.

The next step is a check button on the parent page word entry, so that the user can validate a list before saving it. For now the preview does a looser check, and I want it to call the same function.

summary: Made the parent page word entry call the same list validator, so a bad list is caught while the user types and not after the kids start playing.
body:
This finished what the loader work began. The word entry page on the parent side had its own looser check, which only tested that ten lines were present. It let through a word with a number or a stray space.

I moved the shape check from loadList into a separate pure function, validateList, and made both the loader and the entry page call it. The loader uses it after parsing the file, and the entry page uses it on the data built from the text area.

The entry page now shows messages next to the line concerned. Typing a word with a digit marks that line and says letters only. An empty line in the middle is ignored, and a line of more than forty characters is flagged as too long, because the voice would read it oddly.

The Save button is disabled while there is any error. I also made a count at the top show how many words are entered of the ten the school gives, though it only warns when the number is not ten, since a list can be shorter.

Tests were added for the pure function, taking the six broken files of last week as fixtures, and I reused them for the entry page by building text from them. One of the fixtures, the thirty-one word list, cannot come from the text area in the normal way, but the check still works.

On the tablet I typed a list with two mistakes, and the page marked both lines. After fixing them, the Save button woke up, and the saved file loaded in the game.

The parent page file got shorter by about sixty lines, since the old check is gone. The build size stayed at 149 KB.

summary: Reviewed the whole settings storage after the validation work and found six different local storage keys with no version, so I wrote a plan to group them.
body:
While adding the export, import and validation I kept bumping into the storage layout. I listed what lives in local storage now: profiles, scores, stickers, review results, the shared voice choice, and the effects volume. Six keys, each with its own shape, and none has a version number.

The risk is not today but later. If the shape of one key must change, the code needs to detect the old shape, and with no version it can only guess. The sticker flag and the streak freeze field were both added with defaults because of exactly this.

My plan has three steps. First, add one key, spellbee.schema, holding a number, set to 1 for the current layout. Second, write a function that runs at start, reads the number, and runs steps in order to bring older data to the current layout. Third, make the export include the same number.

I decided against merging all six keys into one object. A single large value is rewritten on every answer, and a write that fails midway could damage everything. Separate keys limit the damage.

I also thought about the cost for the kids. None of this changes what they see, and the user would never notice it. That makes it a low priority against anything the kids ask for, but it is cheap and I would rather do it while the layout is small.

I wrote the plan into the todo list with the three steps and the decision about the keys. No code today.

One point to ask the user: whether to keep old backup files importable forever. I lean toward yes, since the import already accepts a missing version as 1, and that is enough.

summary: Added the schema number key and the start-up migration runner with no steps yet, and checked that existing data loads unchanged.
body:
Following the plan from earlier, I implemented the first two steps. A new module, src/schema.ts, reads spellbee.schema from storage and treats a missing value as zero.

There is a list of migration functions, one per version. The first function only writes the number 1, since the layout today is the first layout. The runner applies each function from the stored number upward and writes the number after each one, so a failure leaves the data at the last good version.

The runner is called before anything else reads storage, at the top of the main file. I wrote tests with the stored number at zero, at one, and at a number higher than the code knows. The last case does nothing and logs a warning, because a newer layout must not be touched by older code.

On the tablet I loaded the page with the real data. The number appeared in storage, and the profiles, streaks, stickers and review results were all the same as before. A second load did nothing, as it should.

The export now includes the number, replacing the separate version field I had added for the file format. The import still reads the old field when it finds it.

The third step is done by this. I am marking the plan as complete in the todo list.

summary: Looked into a report that the younger kid's streak showed as one after playing on both tablet and the user's laptop, and found that local storage is per device by design.
body:
The user played a round on the laptop to test a new list and the younger kid's profile there showed a streak of one, while the tablet showed eleven. The user asked whether the streak was broken.

It was not broken. Local storage belongs to the browser on one device, and the laptop had never held this kid's data apart from a short test a long time ago. The two devices simply do not share anything. I confirmed this by checking the schema number and the profile list on the laptop, which had one old test profile of its own.

This is how the game was designed from the start, since there is no server, and I told the user so. There are two ways to get a shared view. The first is to use the backup and import across devices, which already exists and works but is manual. The second would be a small server, which would change the nature of the project and bring up questions about the kids' data.

I recommended the first. For the laptop the user only needs to import a backup before testing, and that gives the real streaks for the check. I tried it: export on the tablet, send the file by message, import on the laptop. The preview showed the new attempts and the freeze count, and after confirming, the streak on the laptop read eleven.

The round on the laptop then added a day to a copy of the streak, which is not wanted for the real record. The user should not import back to the tablet after testing on the laptop. I wrote a short warning in the README backup section about this.

I also thought about making the laptop test less risky. A test profile named test is already possible from the parent page, and I suggested the user use that profile when trying lists, which keeps the kids' profile clean.

The user agreed with the plan and said the import preview was clear. I did not change any code today besides the README.

summary: Made the game tolerate the tablet rotating mid-round by laying out the input and keyboard area with dynamic viewport units, fixing a hidden Submit button.
body:
The older kid held the tablet in portrait during a round and the Submit button went under the on-screen keyboard. In landscape it was fine, and rotating halfway through left the layout in a broken state until a reload.

I reproduced it with the tablet in portrait with the keyboard open. The play screen was sized with 100vh, which on this browser counts the area behind the keyboard and the toolbar. The button sat at the bottom of that tall box, so it was hidden.

I replaced the height with 100dvh in the main container, which follows the visible area as the keyboard opens. The fallback for older browsers is the old rule placed before it, so a browser that does not know dvh uses the previous value.

That solved portrait, but the rotation case remained. After a turn, the container kept the earlier size for a moment. I added a resize listener that scrolls the input into view after a short delay of 150 ms. It only acts when the input has focus, so it does not move the page otherwise.

I also moved the Submit button above the input in the document order for portrait through a small media rule on orientation. A kid who types and then reaches up for the button finds it near the field in either case. The enter key still submits, which most kids use anyway.

I tested four rotations during a round, each with the keyboard open. In every case the button was visible and the input kept its text. One more test was on a smaller phone screen of the user, where the layout was tight but usable.

The review round and the end screen have the same container, so they got the fix at the same time. I checked the end screen with ten missed words, and the area scrolled properly with the buttons visible.

I added a note in the todo list that the sticker page uses its own container and I have not tested rotation there. I checked it quickly, and it is a plain scrolling page, so it has no problem.

The build size is unchanged at 149 KB. The fix is deployed and the older kid used it in the evening in portrait with no complaints.

summary: Checked two days of play after the rotation fix and the schema key: no errors, and the older kid used portrait mode for a whole list.
body:
I looked at the console log and the stored attempts for the two days since the layout fix. Both kids played each evening, and nothing unusual appeared in the log.

The older kid played a full list in portrait, and the Submit button stayed visible the whole time. The younger kid used landscape as usual.

The schema number is still 1 on both profiles' tablet storage, and no migration ran, which matches the plan since no layout has changed.

The weekly chart on the parent page shows the older kid at a steady accuracy of about 85 percent, and the younger kid's is slowly going up. I did not find anything that needs a change.

summary: Wrote a short maintenance note covering the pieces added since the stickers, so the user can pick the project up after a long break.
body:
The kids use the game a little less each week, and the user mentioned that the school may bring in its own tool. I took that as a reason to write down how the project works while it is all clear to me.

The note lives in a new file, docs/maintenance.md, and is linked from the README. It starts with the weekly routine: type the ten words on the parent page, check the validator messages, save, and watch that the tablet picks up the new list the next day.

The second part is for when something goes wrong. It covers the blank list screen and what the red box means, the voice that changes after an update and the warning with the sample button, and the empty voice list on first load with the 1500 ms limit.

The third part is about data. It explains that everything is stored on the device, how to make and import a backup, the merge rule, and the warning about importing back after testing on another device. The schema number and the migration runner are described with the steps for adding a new migration.

The fourth part lists the build and deploy commands: install, run the dev server, run the tests, build, and the way the output is copied to the static host. It also notes the cache name with the build hash, and why a changed file list needs a new build.

I ended with a short list of known limits. There is no sync between devices, no accounts, the review round is not part of stats, and sounds are routed through one gain setting.

I read the text once as if I were a stranger, and fixed three places where I had used a name from the code without explaining it. The file runs to about two pages.

summary: Listed what is left after the maintenance note: a possible word-of-the-week audio cache, a fix for the sticker page layout, and a decision to keep the dependency set frozen.
body: After writing the maintenance note I went through the todo list and sorted it into three piles. The first pile is things worth doing: the sticker page grid breaks on the narrow tablet in portrait, and the audio for slow replay is generated every time. The second is things to leave alone, such as moving off local storage. The third is deleting items that no longer apply, like the old voice keys, which were already removed. I also decided to keep dependencies frozen except for Vite security fixes, since the kids use the game less each month. The list now has four items and each has a one-line reason. Nothing was changed in the code in this session.

summary: Found the sticker page grid overflowing sideways in portrait on the tablet, caused by a fixed column width, and switched it to auto-fill columns.
body:
The younger kid said the stickers 'fall off the screen' when the tablet is held upright. I reproduced it in the browser's device mode at 768 by 1024 and saw a horizontal scrollbar on the sticker page. The grid in sticker.css used repeat(4, 160px), which needs 640 px plus gaps and padding, more than the portrait width allowed once the side margin was added.

I replaced it with repeat(auto-fill, minmax(120px, 1fr)) and reduced the gap from 24 to 16 px. In portrait it now shows three columns and in landscape five. I also checked that the sticker count label under each picture does not wrap with a two-digit number.

I first tried keeping four columns and scaling the images with a media query, but the ragged last row looked worse with only nine stickers earned. The auto-fill version fills rows evenly enough. I checked the page on the real tablet in both orientations, then rotated mid-view to make sure the layout from the earlier rotation fix still held. It did. I deployed after the build size stayed at 149 KB. Nothing else touched the sticker data, so earned stickers are unchanged. The next item on the list is the slow-replay audio.

summary: Measured the delay on the slow replay button and found the browser rebuilds the speech utterance each time, taking about 400 ms on the tablet before any sound.
body:
The older kid mentioned that the slow replay button feels laggy compared with the normal one. I added timing marks around the speak call and tried both buttons twenty times on the tablet.

Normal replay averaged 120 ms from tap to first sound. Slow replay averaged about 400 ms, with a few at 550. The code path is the same except that slow replay calls cancel() first, then creates a new SpeechSynthesisUtterance with rate 0.6 and looks up the chosen voice again by name.

The voice lookup is the cheap part: it takes under 2 ms. The delay comes from cancel() followed immediately by speak(), which on this tablet's engine seems to wait for the previous utterance to be torn down. Normal replay does not cancel when nothing is playing, so it avoids this.

I tried three changes in a scratch branch of my own working copy, not a repository branch. First, only calling cancel() when speechSynthesis.speaking is true. That brought slow replay to about 150 ms when idle. Second, caching the utterance object, which made no difference and sometimes repeated the old text, so I dropped it. Third, adding a 50 ms gap after cancel, which helped only when something was actually playing.

I kept the first change and wrote down the numbers in the commit message. It is not deployed yet, since I want to hear it with the kids first. The remaining case, tapping replay while a word is still playing, still pays the cancel cost and I think that is acceptable.

There is a small risk that speaking is briefly false while the engine is still queued. I will watch for double playback.

summary: Deployed the cancel-only-when-speaking change for slow replay and confirmed on the tablet that it starts in about 150 ms with no double playback.
body: I rebuilt and deployed the change from earlier this morning. On the tablet I tapped slow replay thirty times: idle taps started at roughly 150 ms, and taps during playback cut off the first utterance and began the new one within about 400 ms. I did not hear any doubled word. I also tried fast alternating taps between normal and slow replay, which is what an impatient kid does, and the last tap always won. The console showed no errors. I left the timing marks in a debug flag that is off by default.

summary: Tried a word-of-the-week audio cache idea on paper first and found the speech API cannot be recorded, so the plan changed before any code was written.
body:
Slot 3's replay measurement raised the question of whether the first spoken word could be made instant by caching audio for each week's list. Before building anything, I spent the session checking what the browser actually allows.

The speech synthesis API plays through the system voice and gives no audio stream to the page. There is no way to capture it with MediaRecorder or the Web Audio graph. I tested this on the laptop by routing the output through an analyser node, and it stayed flat while a word was spoken.

That leaves two options. One is to ship pre-generated clips for each word, which means a separate tool, a fixed voice and a new file for every weekly list. The other is to keep live speech and only warm up the utterance. The first changes the sound the kids know, and the voice would no longer match the one chosen in settings.

I also estimated the size. Ten words a week at roughly 20 KB each would add about 200 KB per list, which is more than the whole build, currently 149 KB. The worker cache list would grow every week as well.

I decided not to start with clips. The first step will be to measure how long the first word takes after the page opens and how long a replay takes, so the choice rests on numbers from the tablet. I wrote the findings and the size estimate into the todo list under the audio cache item, and left the code untouched. Next I will time the replay button on the tablet, since that is the delay the kids notice most.

summary: Built a first version of cached audio for each week's words, using a generated clip per word, then dropped it because the speech API voices cannot be recorded in the browser.
body:
The idea was to remove the voice dependence entirely: record each word once and store it in the service worker cache, so the game would sound the same after any tablet update. The earlier voice disappearance made this attractive.

I started by checking whether the speech API can be captured. It cannot: speechSynthesis speaks to the device output and gives no audio data. Capturing through the microphone would pick up room noise and needs a permission prompt, which is not acceptable for a kids' game.

The other route was generating the clips outside the browser. I tried the operating system's say command on the laptop to produce files for one week's ten words, converted them to small mono files, and measured the size. Each clip was about 14 KB, so one week is 140 KB. That alone almost doubles the 149 KB build, and a year of lists would be several megabytes in the offline cache.

I also listened to the clips against the tablet voice the kids know. They sound different, and the younger kid noticed at once in a quick test and said the new voice was 'a different person'. That broke the point of keeping the sound stable.
