So there were three problems: size, a changed voice, and a build step for every weekly list that the user would have to run. The user types the words on the parent page and has no build step, so this would have removed the simplest part of the workflow.

I decided to drop the idea. I deleted the scratch folder, kept no code, and wrote a short entry in the maintenance note under 'things tried': recorded clips are too big, sound different and need a build step. The existing fallback when the chosen voice is missing, picking the first voice of the same language, stays as the safety net.

Nothing was deployed from this work. I spent about two hours on it.

summary: Answered the user's question about whether the games scores survive clearing the browser history: they do not, so the backup button is the only protection.
body:
The user asked whether clearing history on the tablet would remove the kids' scores. I checked how the browser handles it. Local storage is deleted when the user clears site data, which most clearing dialogs include by default if 'cookies and site data' is ticked. Clearing only browsing history and cached images leaves it alone.

I tested it on the tablet: clearing only history kept the scores, and clearing site data removed them along with the profiles. After that the game started with the first-run profile screen.

I told the user that the CSV and JSON backup on the parent page is the real protection, and that the JSON import can restore everything. I suggested a backup once a month, perhaps at the same time as the tablet update. I did not add an automatic reminder yet.

summary: Added a small line on the parent page showing when the last JSON backup was made, so the user can see at a glance whether a backup is overdue.
body:
Following the answer about clearing site data, I added a key for the time of the last backup export, written when the JSON file is downloaded. The parent page now shows 'Last backup: 12 days ago' or 'No backup yet'. The text turns amber after thirty days.

The key went into the existing settings group and the schema number was not changed, since a missing key is treated as no backup. I wrote two tests: one for the label text with a missing value and one for the thirty-day threshold. I checked the page on the tablet and the line fits under the export buttons. The CSV export does not set the value, because it cannot be imported again.

summary: Replaced the old fixed sound-effect files with short synthesized tones after the service worker cache list kept missing one of them, and measured a smaller build.
body:
A check of offline mode on the tablet showed the right-answer chime silent when the network was off. The cause was that the service worker's cache list named chime.mp3 but the file had been renamed to chime-soft.mp3 when I worked on the volume. The list was written by hand, which is how it went wrong.

I considered generating the list from the build output, but the sounds are tiny and simple, so I looked at synthesizing them instead. The shared gain setting from before already routes through the audio context, so adding oscillators is easy.

The right answer is now two sine tones, 660 and 880 Hz, 90 ms each with a short fade. The wrong answer is one 180 Hz triangle tone for 200 ms, softer than the old buzz. The finish chime is a rising run of four notes. All use the same gain node, so the night volume setting still applies.

I removed the three audio files and their cache entries. The build went from 149 KB to 131 KB. I ran the offline check again with the network off: all three sounds play, and the word lists and pages load as before.

The kids heard the new tones in the afternoon. The older kid did not notice the change, and the younger kid said the wrong sound was 'nicer but still wrong'. That is the result I wanted.

One caveat is that the audio context must be started by a tap, so the first sound after page load is created on the first answer, which was already the case. I added a test that the tone function does not throw when the context is suspended.

I updated the maintenance note: sounds are generated in sounds.ts and there is no audio file to cache. The worker cache list still has to be edited by hand for new pages, and I wrote that down too.

summary: Generated the service worker cache list from the Vite build output so renamed files can no longer be missed, after the sound file mishap.
body:
Since a hand-written cache list failed once, I replaced it. A small Vite plugin in vite.config.ts now reads the emitted asset names at the end of the build and writes them into the worker file as an array, with a hash of the names as the cache version.

The word list JSON files are in the public folder and so are not emitted assets. The plugin also lists that folder explicitly. I checked that a new weekly file shows up in the list after a rebuild.

I tested by renaming a stylesheet on purpose. The old way would have left a hole, and the new list followed the rename. I also checked that the cache version changes when a file name changes, so old caches are deleted on activation.

The build size is the same, 131 KB. The worker file grew by about 300 bytes.

One thing I noticed is that the cache version does not change when only the content of a file changes and its name stays the same. Vite hashes names for scripts and styles, so that is covered, but the JSON lists have fixed names. For those I added a hash of their contents to the version. That means editing a list on the parent page does not matter, since lists typed there live in local storage and not in the cache.

I tried offline mode again in the browser and on the tablet, and everything loaded. I deployed after that.

summary: Wrote tests for the cache list plugin, covering a new file, a renamed file and a changed list file, since the earlier failure was silent.
body:
The cache list plugin from earlier has no visible failure mode, so a test matters more than usual. I factored the logic into a function that takes a list of file names and file contents and returns the array and version string, and tested that.

Three cases are covered. A new file name changes the array and the version. A renamed file changes both. A changed content of a JSON list file changes only the version. A fourth test checks that the order of the input does not change the result, because the build may emit files in a different order and that would bump the version for nothing.

Writing the fourth test found a real bug: the version was built from the joined names in emitted order. I sorted the names first and the test passed.

I also added a check to the build script that fails if the worker file lacks the placeholder, which would happen if somebody edited the file and removed it. It is a plain string search.

All twenty-three tests pass. I ran the build twice in a row and compared the worker files: they are identical, so deploys will not cause needless cache refreshes. I committed with a short note about the ordering.

summary: Watched the kids play on the tablet after the sound and cache changes and saw no silent sounds or console errors across two full word lists.
body:
This evening both kids played their lists while I watched with the debug flag on. The older kid played the full week of ten words twice and the younger kid played a list of ten and then the review round.

All the sounds played: the two-tone chime, the soft wrong tone and the finish run. I turned the night volume down in the middle and the sounds followed it. Offline mode was tested at the end by switching the tablet to flight mode and reloading, and the game started and played normally.

The console showed no errors. The timing marks, which I had left behind the debug flag, showed slow replay at 140 to 160 ms when idle, matching the earlier measurement.

The younger kid asked if the wrong sound could be a different animal noise. I said maybe later and noted it in the todo list as a low priority idea. It would need files again, so I am not keen.

Nothing needed fixing. I will check again after the next weekly list is added.

summary: Added the new weekly list through the parent page and found that a word with an apostrophe was rejected by the validator, then fixed the rule.
body:
The user typed in this week's ten words on the parent page and the validator rejected 'they're' with the message 'entry 4: unexpected character'. The user sent me a screenshot.

The validator in listcheck.ts allowed letters and hyphens only, which I wrote when hyphen handling came in. It had never seen an apostrophe. School lists do include contractions now and then, so this was a real gap.

I changed the character rule to letters, hyphens and the straight apostrophe. Tablets often type a curly apostrophe, which looks the same but is a different character, so I also normalize the curly one to the straight one on input. Without that, the kid would type a curly apostrophe and be marked wrong against a straight one in the list, or the other way round.

The grading code needed a look as well. The comparison strips spaces and lowercases, and it handles hyphens by the list flag. The apostrophe is kept as it is, so a kid who leaves it out is marked wrong. I asked the user, who said the school marks that wrong too.

I added tests: a valid contraction, a curly apostrophe being normalized, a missing apostrophe being wrong, and a lone apostrophe being rejected as an empty entry.

The speech voice reads 'they're' correctly. The hint shows the first letter as before. I loaded the list on the tablet, played the word with the on-screen keyboard, and the apostrophe key is on the second keyboard page, which the kid will have to find. I told the user about that. The list was saved, and the kids can play it.

summary: Looked at whether the apostrophe keyboard page on the tablet slows kids down and decided to add a small apostrophe button next to the input.
body:
Following the contraction word, I watched the younger kid try 'they're'. It took about nine seconds to find the apostrophe on the second keyboard page, and the kid switched back to letters and lost the rest of the word's focus.

I considered setting the input to a different keyboard type, but the browser decides the layout and none of the types puts the apostrophe on the first page reliably.

A small button next to the input that inserts an apostrophe at the cursor is simple and works on every device. I planned it to show only when the current word contains an apostrophe, so other words look the same as before.

I wrote the plan in the todo list with three points: show only for words with an apostrophe, keep the input focused after the tap, and insert at the cursor position and not at the end. The focus point matters because of the earlier fix for focus lost after a wrong answer. I have not started building yet.

summary: Built the apostrophe button, which appears only for words with an apostrophe, keeps focus in the input and inserts at the cursor, with tests and a tablet check.
body:
I built the button in the input row, next to the Submit button, with the label being the apostrophe itself in a large font.

Visibility is decided when a word is shown: if the word contains an apostrophe, the button is displayed, otherwise it is hidden with the hidden attribute so it does not take space or focus. I checked the list loader to confirm that the word is available at that point, and it is.

The first version inserted the character by appending to the value. That went wrong when the kid had tapped into the middle of the text, so I switched to setRangeText with the selection start and end, then moved the cursor after the new character. Tapping the button twice gives two apostrophes, which the grader marks wrong, as it should.

Focus was the tricky part. Tapping a button normally takes focus from the input and the keyboard closes on the tablet. I prevented this by handling pointerdown with preventDefault on the button, so the input never loses focus. On the tablet the keyboard stayed open and the cursor stayed where it was. I tried it in both orientations.

I also checked the layout. In portrait the button fits between the input and Submit when the input is shrunk by 56 px, and I used the dynamic viewport units from before so the row is still visible with the keyboard open.

For tests I wrote four: the button is hidden for a plain word, shown for an apostrophe word, inserts in the middle of text, and keeps the input focused. The test environment is jsdom, which handles setRangeText, so no mock was needed.

One gap is that a hardware keyboard user does not need the button, but it does no harm. Another is that a screen reader reads the button as 'apostrophe', which I set as its aria-label so it is not read as 'quote'.

The younger kid tried it with 'they're' and 'don't' and did both in about two seconds each. I deployed the change. The build is 132 KB.

summary: Reviewed the three newest features for accessibility and found the streak freeze snowflake, the apostrophe button and the missed-words list each lacked a text label for screen readers.
body:
The user asked for a quick review of how the game works without sight of the screen, mainly out of curiosity, since a relative uses a screen reader. I turned on the screen reader on the laptop and went through the start screen, a round and the end screen.

The start screen read the play button and the list name well. The snowflake for the streak freeze was read as nothing, since it is an image drawn with CSS. I gave it role img and an aria-label of 'Streak freeze held', shown only when one is held.

The apostrophe button already had its label from this morning's work. The Submit button and the replay buttons were labelled well.

The missed-words list on the end screen was a set of div elements, which the reader treated as loose text with no sense of order. I changed the container to an ordered list with list items, keeping the same styling by resetting the list style and using the same class names. The order the words came in is now announced as a numbered list.

The right and wrong feedback was only visual, a colour and a sound. A blind user would hear the sound but not know which word was wrong. I added a polite live region that says 'Correct' or 'Not quite, the word was' and the word, in a visually hidden element. I made sure it does not read the word before the kid has tried, since it is only updated after an answer.

The score board on the parent page is a table with headers, which read fine. The chart is an image-like canvas and has no text. I added a short summary line for it, such as 'Last six weeks: 8, 9, 10, gap, 7, 9'.

I ran the browser's accessibility audit on each page. It reported two contrast problems: the grey hint text and the amber backup line. I darkened both to meet 4.5 to 1 and checked that the amber still looks amber.

Tests were updated for the list markup, and I added one for the live region text after a wrong answer. All pass. I deployed the changes. There is still no keyboard-only way to reach the sticker page detail, which I put on the todo list.

summary: Made the sticker page reachable and usable with the keyboard alone, fixing a missing focus ring and a click handler that was attached to a non-focusable div.
body:
This continues the accessibility review of last night. The sticker page showed each sticker as a div with a click handler that opens a larger view. A div cannot take focus, so keyboard users could not open one.

I changed each sticker to a button element, kept the same classes, and reset the default button styling so the grid looks identical. The button has an aria-label with the sticker name and whether it is earned, such as 'Fox, earned' or 'Owl, not earned yet'.

The larger view is a dialog. I switched it to the dialog element with showModal(), which handles focus trapping and the Escape key without custom code. Before, it was a div with a backdrop, and Escape did nothing. After closing, focus returns to the sticker button that opened it, which I set by remembering the element.

The focus ring was removed globally in the original stylesheet with outline none, which I wrote early on for a cleaner look. I replaced it with a focus-visible rule that draws a 3 px outline in the accent colour with a 2 px offset. Mouse and touch taps show no ring, keyboard navigation does.

I went through every page using only Tab, Shift-Tab, Enter and Escape. On the start screen, the order was profile, play, review, then the bottom row, which matches the visual order. In a round, the input is focused at the start of each word and Enter submits. The replay buttons come after Submit, which is a little odd, so I moved them before the input in the document order and kept the visual position using CSS order.

One problem appeared in the parent page: the word entry list had delete buttons that were only shown on hover, so keyboard users never saw them. I made them visible when the row has focus within.

I added tests for the sticker button labels and the dialog opening and closing with focus return. jsdom does not fully support showModal, so I stubbed it with a small shim in the test setup file.

I tried it on the tablet with a paired keyboard as well, and Tab moved through the page as expected. The younger kid used the touch version and noticed nothing different, which is the goal.

The build is 133 KB. I deployed in the early afternoon. The accessibility todo item is now closed. I wrote one line in the maintenance note about using native buttons and dialogs for any new control.

summary: Checked the stale focus ring rule on the older browser version the tablet runs and confirmed focus-visible works there without a fallback.
body:
After changing the outline rules, I worried the tablet's browser might not know the focus-visible selector. The tablet runs a browser two major versions behind the laptop.

I looked at the browser's version in the about page and tested directly. Tapping any button showed no ring, and attaching a paired keyboard and pressing Tab showed the ring. So the selector is supported.

I still added a safe fallback order: the focus rule first with outline, then a focus-visible rule. Browsers that ignore focus-visible would show the ring on tap, which is acceptable, and I did not need to care about it here. I checked the CSS output after the build and Vite kept both rules. Nothing more was needed.

summary: Found that the live region announcement repeated after a rotation and traced it to the round re-rendering, then fixed it by updating the text only on an answer.
body:
While trying the screen reader on the tablet itself this afternoon, I rotated the device after answering a word and heard 'Correct' a second time. It was easy to repeat.

The live region from the accessibility changes is written by a render function that also runs on resize, since the layout code from the rotation fix calls render after the viewport changes. The render function set the region's text to the feedback message every time, and the screen reader treats any set of the text as a new announcement, even with the same content.

I first tried clearing the text after two seconds. That stopped the repeat after the timeout but not for a rotation in the first two seconds, and it made the region empty when a reader user moved to it manually. So I dropped that.

The better fix was to separate the two jobs. The announcement is now made by a function called from the answer handler only, and the render function no longer touches the live region. I stored the last announced answer id and the announce function does nothing if it is the same id as before, as a second guard.

I also noticed that the render on resize reset the input text. A kid half way through typing a word would lose letters when the tablet turned. The earlier rotation fix kept the input visible, but the value was kept only by luck, because the input element was reused. After my change to the structure of the round view it was re-created in one path. I checked the code and found a template string that rebuilt the whole row when the apostrophe button visibility was recalculated. I changed it to toggle the hidden attribute on the existing button and leave the input alone.

That was the real cause of the lost text. I tested by typing 'bea' on the tablet, rotating twice, and seeing the text still there with the cursor in place. Before the fix, the text was gone after a rotation, and I reproduced this first to be sure.

I wrote two tests. One checks that dispatching a resize event does not change the live region text. The other checks that the input value survives a resize and a word with an apostrophe. Both failed on the old code and pass now.

I ran the whole suite, 31 tests, all passing, and deployed. I will ask the kids whether anything feels different, though I expect it only matters to someone who rotates in the middle of a word.

summary: Heard from the kids that nothing feels different after the input and live region fixes, and saw no lost letters during a morning of play.
body:
The kids played before school, and I asked them afterwards if anything had changed. The older kid said no. The younger kid said the tablet 'still turns around' and was pleased that the word stayed when it did.

I looked at the debug log for the morning. There were no errors and no repeated announcements. The younger kid rotated the tablet once in the middle of a word and the letters stayed. I did not turn on the screen reader for this session, since the point was normal play.

The round view code is now simpler than before: the input is created once per round, and only labels and visibility change per word. I wrote a line in the maintenance note about this, so nobody rebuilds the row again.

summary: Audited the project's dependencies and found two outdated dev packages and one build warning, and upgraded Vite within its current major version.
body:
With the game stable I ran an audit of the dependencies, because a long quiet period makes small drift easy to miss. The project has only four dev dependencies: Vite, TypeScript, Vitest and jsdom. There are no runtime dependencies.

npm audit reported no known vulnerabilities, but npm outdated showed Vite one minor version behind, Vitest one minor behind and jsdom two minor behind. TypeScript was current.

I upgraded Vite and Vitest first, ran the build and the tests, and compared the output. The built size was the same, 133 KB, and the tests passed. The worker cache list plugin still worked, since I checked the generated array and the version hash against the last build and they differed only in the changed hashed names, as expected.

The build printed a deprecation warning about a configuration option I had used in vite.config.ts, the old way of setting the public directory path for the plugin. I changed it to the current option. The warning disappeared.

Then jsdom. The upgrade changed the behavior of focus handling slightly and two tests that check the input focus after a wrong answer failed. Reading the changelog, jsdom now only focuses elements that are attached to the document, and my test created the element without attaching it. I fixed the tests by appending the container to the body, which is closer to a real page. I did not change any game code.

I also looked at the TypeScript config and turned on noUncheckedIndexedAccess, to see what it would find. It reported eleven places where an array access might be undefined. Eight were in test code. Three were in the game code: the word at the current index, the sticker lookup and the profile by id. I added guards for all three, with a visible fallback message for the profile case. This is a bit of risk for no visible gain, but each guard is tiny and each has a test.

After the changes the full suite is 33 tests, all passing. I built, checked offline mode in the browser and on the tablet, and deployed. I will leave the dependencies alone again until something forces a change. I added the versions to the maintenance note.

summary: Checked an evening of play after the dependency upgrade and strict index checks, with no errors, correct sounds and the worker updated on the tablet.
body:
I wanted to be sure that the upgrade and the new guards did not break anything that tests cannot see, such as the worker update on a real tablet.

Before the kids played, I opened the game on the tablet once with a network connection. The old worker was still active, and after a reload the new one took over, which I confirmed by the new cache name in the developer tools on the laptop attached to the tablet. The old cache was deleted.

Both kids then played. The older kid did the week's list and the review round. The younger kid did a list and then looked at the stickers, using the keyboard-friendly dialog without noticing.

I looked for the three guard messages that I added for the missing word, sticker and profile cases and none appeared. The console was clean.

I turned on flight mode and reloaded once more at the end of the evening. The start screen, the lists and the sounds all worked offline.

I also checked the score board on the parent page, since it uses the profile lookup that I guarded. The numbers matched the numbers from before the upgrade, and the CSV export produced the same file as it did last week, byte for byte, apart from the new rows.

Nothing needed to be fixed. I am treating the upgrade as done.

summary: Answered the user's question about how many words each kid has practiced in total, by summing attempts from local storage, and found 412 for the older kid and 268 for the younger.
body:
The user asked how many different words each kid has practiced so far. There is no screen for it, so I wrote a small snippet for the browser console that reads the scores key and counts unique word strings for each profile.

The older kid has 412 unique words and the younger kid has 268. The total number of attempts is higher: 1,930 and 1,104. The older kid's most missed word is 'necessary', missed on first try eleven times, and the younger kid's is 'because', missed seven times.

I also counted how many of the words were passed on the first try at the latest attempt. For the older kid it was 81 percent and for the younger kid 74 percent.

I gave the user the figures in the reply. I did not add anything to the app, since the user only wanted to know, but I noted the snippet in the maintenance note under useful console commands. If it is asked again, a small stats section on the parent page would be simple, because the data is already there.

summary: Added a small words-practiced counter to the parent page after the user said they would like to see the numbers without opening the console.
body:
The user liked the totals from the other day and asked if they could be on the parent page. I took the console snippet and turned it into a function in stats.ts that returns unique words, attempts and the share passed on the first try for a profile.

On the parent page, each profile card now shows a line such as '412 words practiced, 81 percent right first time'. I checked that a profile with no attempts shows '0 words practiced' and no percentage, because dividing by zero was the obvious crash after the earlier chart problem.

I wrote three tests: a normal profile, an empty profile and a profile with repeated attempts on the same word. The unique count uses a set of lower-cased words, so a case difference in a list does not count twice.

The line fits on the tablet in both orientations. The build is 134 KB. I deployed it and told the user it is there.

summary: Reviewed the full set of changes since the maintenance note and updated the note with the sound synthesis, the generated cache list, the accessibility rules and the stats line.
body:
A lot changed after the maintenance note I wrote at the start of this stretch, so I went through the commit history from that point and brought the note up to date.

The new items are these. Sounds are synthesized in sounds.ts and no audio files exist, so nothing needs caching for them. The worker cache list is generated by a plugin in vite.config.ts from the build output and from the public lists folder, with a version made from sorted names and the contents of the lists. The round view creates its input once per round and must not rebuild it, because that lost letters on rotation. The live region is updated only by the answer handler.

I added a short accessibility section: use native buttons and dialogs, keep the focus-visible outline, label images and the chart summary, and keep the numbered missed-words list.

I also listed the apostrophe handling: the validator allows letters, hyphens and the straight apostrophe, curly ones are normalized, and the apostrophe button shows only for words that need it.

The stats line on the parent page and the module that computes it are in the note, with the useful console commands from before. I added the tool versions after the upgrade, Vite, Vitest, jsdom and TypeScript, and the strict index check setting.

Then I wrote a list of known gaps. The offline cache only updates when the user opens the game online. The data is per device and there is no sync, only manual backup. The wrong-answer sound is a plain tone and the younger kid would like an animal noise. There is no test on a real screen reader other than my own check.

I re-read the note from the point of view of the user coming back after a long break and cut two paragraphs that repeated each other. It is now about a page and a half. I ran the tests and the build one more time to be sure the note matched the code: 36 tests pass and the build is 134 KB.

summary: Planned the last stretch of work: a few small cleanups, one more check of the backup flow, and then leaving the project alone unless the kids ask for something.
body:
After updating the maintenance note, I sat down with the open list and sorted it into what is worth doing and what is not. The kids use the game less each week, so the bar for new work is high.

Three items stayed. First, the parent page word entry still allows a list of 11 words if the user pastes in a stray line, and the validator should say so. Second, the missed-words list is long for the older kid and should show only the latest 20. Third, the backup button should name its file with a counter so that two backups on one day do not look the same.

I dropped two ideas: a themed redesign and a second voice choice for the younger kid. Neither was asked for, and the voice list on the tablet changes after updates anyway.

For the order I picked the validator first, since it protects the data, then the missed-words list, then the backup file name. Each should be under an hour. I wrote the three items at the end of the maintenance note under a heading-free line saying what is planned.

Nothing was changed in code in this session. The checks I ran were the existing test suite, which passed with all tests green, and a production build, which came to the same size as before. The next session starts with the validator and its tests.

summary: The parent page now rejects a pasted list that does not have exactly 10 words and tells the user which line is the problem, instead of silently saving a bad week.
body:
The user once pasted a week's list that had a blank line and a trailing note from the school, and the page saved 11 entries. The kids then got a word that was really a sentence fragment. I added a stricter check in the word list validator.

The rules now are: trim each line, drop fully blank lines, and require exactly 10 words. Each word may contain letters and a single apostrophe, as fixed a few days ago. Anything else produces a message naming the line number, for example 'Line 7: contains a digit'.

The tricky part was the count message. If the user pastes 11 lines, the message says 'Found 11 words, expected 10' and keeps the text in the box so nothing is lost. Before, the box was cleared on save, so I changed that to clear only after a successful save.

I wrote tests for ten good words, nine words, eleven words, a blank line in the middle, a digit, and a word with an apostrophe. All pass. One test failed at first because a word with a trailing space and a tab was counted twice; trimming with a regex for any whitespace fixed it.

I also tried it on the tablet with the on-screen keyboard. The message shows below the box and does not get hidden by the keyboard, which matters after the earlier rotation fix.

The error text has a role of alert so a screen reader announces it, following the accessibility rules in the note. I deployed after the build. Next up is the missed-words list.

summary: Capped the missed-words list at the latest 20 entries, because the older kid's list had grown to over 60 words and was slow to scroll on the tablet.
body:
The missed-words list stores every word that was ever answered wrong, with a count. For the older kid it had reached 63 entries, and the page was a long scroll that nobody read.

I changed the display, not the stored data. The page sorts by the last time a word was missed and shows the first 20. A small line under it says 'Showing 20 of 63' so nothing seems lost. The full data stays in local storage, and the backup still contains all of it.

I considered deleting old entries, but a word missed once many weeks ago and never again is information the user may want when counting words practiced. So I left storage alone.

The sort needed a timestamp that older entries do not have, since the field was added only with the schema number work. For entries without it I treat the time as zero, so they sink to the bottom. I added a test for that case and one for a list with fewer than 20 entries, where the line is hidden.

On the tablet the page loads at once now and the screen reader label from the accessibility review still reads the count. I ran the full tests and they pass.

I did not add a 'show all' button. If the user asks, it is a ten-line change.

summary: Backup files now carry a running number in the name, so two backups made on one day no longer overwrite each other in the downloads folder.
body:
The backup button downloads a JSON file named after the day. When the user made two backups in one session, the browser added its own '(1)' suffix, which is confusing when restoring.

I added a small counter in local storage under its own key, incremented on every backup. The file name is now spellbee-backup-N.json. I chose a number rather than a time because the project avoids time formatting differences between the tablet and the laptop.

The restore path did not care about the name, but I checked that anyway by restoring from backup 3 on a copy of the data. Scores, streaks and the missed words all came back the same, and the schema number was preserved.

One thing I found while testing: the line on the parent page that shows when the last backup was made reads the same stored value as before, so it was unaffected. I added a test to make sure the counter does not break it.

A small edge: if local storage is cleared, the counter restarts at 1. That is fine, since the backup then comes from a fresh state anyway. I noted this in the maintenance note so nobody is surprised.

The tests all pass and the build size grew by under 100 bytes. I deployed it. That finishes the three planned items, and I put a line in the note to say so.

summary: Checked the evening's play after the three small changes and saw no errors, a correct list of 10 words, and the backup counter working on the tablet.
body:
I watched the console on the tablet while the younger kid did the week's list. No errors or warnings appeared.

The list had exactly 10 words, the sounds played, and the service worker had picked up the new build without a manual reload.

I also made one more backup on the laptop and the file was named with the next number. The missed-words page showed the cap line for the older kid.

Nothing else needed doing. The next step is to leave things alone for a few days.

summary: Looked at the kids' play logs from the last two days and found the older kid played only one list and the younger none, so no new work was started.
body:
I read the attempt counts in local storage on both profiles. The older kid did the week's list once, with 9 of 10 right. The younger kid did not open the game.

That fits the pattern of recent weeks, where use falls a little each time. The school's own app now sends its own word practice home, and the user mentioned the kids like its rewards.

I did not want to build anything to chase that. A streak reminder was one idea, but the game has no notifications and adding them would need permission prompts on a tablet the kids share.

I wrote a line in the note with the counts so a later reader sees the trend. No code was changed.

summary: Fixed a flaky test in the cache list plugin that failed when the temporary folder name contained a dash, by escaping the path in the matcher.
body:
The test suite failed once on the laptop with a mismatch in the cache list test for a renamed file. It passed on rerun, which made me suspect something about the environment.

The test creates a temporary build folder with a random name. When that name contained a dash followed by a digit, the pattern I used to strip the folder prefix treated part of it as a range, and the stripped path was wrong.

I replaced the hand-written pattern with a plain string prefix removal, which needs no escaping. I ran the plugin tests 50 times in a loop and they passed every time. Before the change, a loop of 50 gave 4 failures.

The plugin itself in the real build was never affected, since the real output folder is always dist. Only the test used random names.

Build and the other tests are unchanged. I left a short comment in the test explaining why a plain prefix is used.

summary: Answered the user's question about whether the game can run offline on a plane: yes, after one online visit the service worker serves everything, speech included if the voice is local.
body:
The user asked if the kids could play on a trip with no network. I checked the facts rather than answering from memory.

The service worker caches the page, scripts, styles and the word lists, using the generated cache list. I put the tablet in airplane mode, reloaded the game, and played a full list. Everything worked.

Speech was the one open question. The browser's speech API uses the voice chosen in the settings. If it is a local voice, it works offline. If it is a network voice, it fails silently. On the tablet the chosen voice is local, and it spoke all ten words.

The weak point is the first visit: the worker must have run once online. A new weekly list added through the parent page is stored locally, so it works offline too.

I told the user to open the game once online before the trip and to not change the voice setting. I added the answer to the maintenance note under a line about offline use. No code changed.

summary: Started checking the voice picker after the tablet's system update notice, and found the saved voice name still resolves but the fallback was never tested.
body:
The user said the tablet will update its system soon. Earlier a voice disappeared after an update, so I wanted to know what happens if it happens again.

The game stores the voice name in local storage. At start-up it looks for that name in the list the browser returns. If it is missing, the code falls back to the first voice of the same language. I read the function and it looked right.

The gap was tests: nothing exercised the fallback. I wrote a small test with a fake voice list that lacks the saved name, and one with an empty list.

The empty list case failed. The code assumed at least one voice and threw on reading the first item. That can happen briefly at page load, since some browsers fill the voice list late.

I have not fixed it yet in this entry. The plan is to guard the empty case and listen for the voiceschanged event to retry. I wrote down the failing test so the next session picks it up.

I checked that the tablet currently returns 14 voices and that the saved one is among them, so no kid is affected today.

summary: Fixed the empty voice list crash by guarding the first-voice fallback and retrying when the browser reports its voices have loaded.
body:
This continues the voice check from a few minutes ago. The failing test showed a throw when the voice list was empty.

I changed the picker to return nothing when the list is empty, and the speak function then uses the browser's default voice instead of a chosen one. That keeps the word audible even in the worst case.

I also added a listener for the voiceschanged event. When it fires, the picker runs again and, if the saved voice has now appeared, switches to it. The listener is registered once so it does not stack up on rotation or re-render, which was a lesson from the live region bug.

Tests now cover four cases: saved voice present, saved voice missing, empty list, and a list that fills in later. All pass.

On the tablet I cleared the cache and reloaded to simulate a slow voice list. The first word used the saved voice, so the timing was fine there. I also forced the empty case in the console, and the word was still spoken with the default voice.

I deployed the change. The build grew by about 200 bytes. The remaining risk is a voice that sounds odd after the system update, and only listening can check that.

summary: Listened to all ten words of the week on the tablet after its system update and the saved voice still spoke them at the right speed.
body:
The tablet updated its system overnight. I opened the game first thing to see if the voice had changed.

The voice list had 15 entries now instead of 14, and the saved voice was still among them. The ten words were spoken clearly. Slow replay started quickly, close to the 150 ms measured earlier.

The one change was a new voice added at the top of the list. Because the picker uses the saved name and only falls back by language, the new one was not chosen by mistake.

The sound effects and the service worker also worked. I saw no console errors.

Nothing else to do. I noted in the maintenance note that the fallback code was tested for this case and worked.

summary: Checked the voice picker after the tablet's system update notice and found the saved voice still resolves, but the empty-list fallback had never been exercised by any test.
body:
The tablet showed a system update notice this morning, and since a voice that vanished after an update was the worst past failure of this project, I checked the voice picker before the update was installed. The saved voice is stored by name in local storage under the voice key. I opened the game on the tablet and confirmed that the name still resolves against the list returned by speechSynthesis.getVoices(), and that the word was read at the usual speed.

The saved name resolving is the easy case. The harder question is what happens when it does not, so I read the fallback code in the voice module. When the saved name is missing, the code picks the first voice whose language starts with the game's language, and if none match, it takes the first voice in the list. I wrote down three cases to test: the saved voice is gone but others exist, the list holds only voices of another language, and the list is empty.

I could not make the tablet lose its voice, so I replaced getVoices with a stub in a small test file. The first case worked and picked the language match. The second case also worked and took the first voice, which is acceptable because it still speaks. The third case threw 'Cannot read properties of undefined (reading name)' on the first line of the fallback, because the code indexes element zero of an empty list without a check.

That third case is real. Browsers often return an empty list on the very first call and fill it later, and the browser then fires the voiceschanged event. The current code does not listen for that event after the first read. On a freshly updated tablet the first page load could therefore hit exactly this crash.

I did not fix it in this session. I added the three stub tests, with the empty-list one marked as expected to fail, so the problem is recorded in the test suite. The plan for the next session is to guard the first-voice fallback, retry when the voiceschanged event arrives, and show the word on screen if no voice is available at all. After that I will listen to all ten words of the week on the tablet once its update is installed.

summary: Added the duplicate-word check to the parent page, so a week's list that repeats a word is refused with a message naming the repeated word.
body:
This is the second half of the list cleanup. The script found a list that had the same word twice, and the page validator had let that kind of list through in the first place.

The new rule compares words after trimming and lowercasing, so 'Because' and 'because ' count as the same. When a repeat is found, the message reads 'The word because appears twice'. If several words repeat, only the first is named, to keep the message short; the user fixes it and sees the next.

I placed the check after the count check, since a list with the wrong number of words is the larger problem. The text box keeps its content as before.

Tests added: one repeat, a repeat that differs only by case, a repeat with trailing space, and no repeat. All pass, together with the earlier validator tests, 23 in total for that file.

I tried the page on the tablet with a deliberately repeated word. The alert text appeared and was read by the screen reader label. No layout problem with the keyboard open.

I deployed it. The word list script from earlier is separate and was not changed.

summary: Looked at the bundle after the recent small changes and found it is 38 KB compressed, so no further trimming is worthwhile.
body:
I ran the production build and looked at the sizes. The main script is 27 KB compressed, styles 4 KB, and the HTML under 2 KB, with the sound tones now synthesized instead of loaded as files. In total that is about 38 KB.

The word lists are loaded one at a time and each is under 1 KB. The service worker precaches them, which adds a little at first visit.

I thought about splitting the parent page into its own chunk, since the kids never open it. The saving would be about 5 KB, and the extra request would complicate the cache list. I decided against.

No changes were made. I wrote the numbers in the note so a later change can be compared.

summary: Handled the user's report that the younger kid's sticker count looked too low, and found the count is right: two stickers were earned but in the older kid's profile.
body:
The user said the younger kid had earned a sticker for a perfect list, but the sticker page showed fewer than expected. I looked at the stored data for both profiles.

The younger kid had 5 stickers, and the older had 9. The user remembered a perfect list on the tablet that evening. I checked the attempts and found that the perfect list was recorded under the older profile's key, because the older kid had been playing just before and the profile switch had not been used.

So the game worked as designed. The sticker went to whoever the active profile was.

The cause is a usability gap: the active profile is shown only as a small name in the corner. I made the name larger on the start screen and added the kid's name to the 'Start' button, such as 'Start as Mia'. I kept the layout safe for portrait mode, which was checked on the tablet.

I did not move the sticker between profiles. Editing scores by hand would break the real record, and the user agreed it was fine to leave it.

Tests for the start screen label pass. I deployed the change.

summary: Built a small profile confirm step: when the last play was by the other kid more than an hour ago, the start screen asks 'Is this still the older kid?' before beginning.
body:
After the sticker mix-up I wanted a gentler guard than a large name. A prompt on every start would annoy the kids, so it should only appear when it is useful.

The game already stores a last-played time for each profile. On start, if the active profile has not played for more than an hour and the other profile played more recently, it shows a one-line question with two buttons, 'Yes' and 'Switch'.

The rule had a catch. The tablet is shared, and the profile stays active after a session. So the common case is the other kid picking it up next, which is exactly when the question helps.

I wrote the logic as a pure function that takes both times and now, and returns whether to ask. That made testing easy: eight cases, including equal times, no history for one profile, and exactly one hour. All pass.

The buttons got text labels for screen readers, and the focus goes to 'Yes' when the prompt appears, so the keyboard works. I checked rotation, because the prompt sits above the input area, and it stayed visible in both modes.

On the tablet I tested by faking the stored times in the console. The prompt appeared, 'Switch' opened the profile list, and 'Yes' continued without a flash of the game.

One more thought: an hour is a guess. The kids often play after school and again after dinner, which is more than an hour apart. If the user finds the prompt too frequent, the threshold is one constant in the file.

I deployed it. I will ask after a few days how it feels.

summary: Heard from the user that the profile question appeared once and was useful, since the younger kid had picked up the tablet right after the older.
body:
The user played with the kids over two evenings and reported the prompt appeared once. It was the younger kid's turn after the older, and the prompt caught it.

I checked the stored data. The younger kid's attempts that evening were under the right profile, and the sticker count went up by one as expected.

No one complained about extra taps. The user said it was fast.

I kept the one-hour threshold. No code changes.

summary: Wrote tests for restoring a backup into a device that already has scores, and found the restore replaces everything without warning, so added a confirm step.
body:
The restore button reads a JSON backup and writes it to local storage. I had tested restoring on a clean device, but not on one that already had play data.

On a copy of the tablet data I restored an older backup. The newer scores were overwritten without a message. That is the specified behavior, but it is easy to do by accident, and the user could lose a week of results.

I added a confirm dialog that states what will be replaced, using the counts in the file and the current data: 'Replace 412 attempts with 380?'. A kid cannot get to this page easily, since the parent page is behind a small hold-to-open button, but a parent can still tap wrongly.

The counts come from the same summing function used for the words-practiced line, so there is no duplicate logic. If the backup is newer than the current data, the dialog says so in plain words.

I wrote tests for three cases: restore into empty storage with no dialog needed, restore over data with confirmation, and cancel leaving data untouched. The cancel case matters most and it passes.

The dialog is a native confirm, so no focus handling was needed and screen readers handle it. I tried it on the tablet and it looked fine.

I also made sure the schema number in the backup is checked before the dialog, and a file with a higher number than the app knows is rejected with a message. That already worked and now has a test.

Deployed. The note has a new line about the confirm.

summary: Looked into a console warning about a passive event listener on the keyboard page and found it comes from one old touch handler, then removed it since nothing uses it.
body:
While testing the restore dialog on the tablet, the console showed a warning about a non-passive touch listener slowing scrolling. I had not seen it before because I normally watch for errors.

I searched for touchstart in the code and found one handler on the document, left over from the first weeks when I tried swipe gestures for the score board. The gesture was dropped long ago and the handler did nothing.

I removed it and the helper that it called, 14 lines in all. Then I rebuilt and the warning was gone.

I checked that scrolling the sticker page and the missed-words list still worked on the tablet, and it did.

Tests pass and the bundle is a few hundred bytes smaller. I also searched for other listeners of the same kind and found none.

The lesson is to look at warnings, not only errors, in the next play check. Deployed.

summary: Reviewed every place the game writes to local storage and found two writes that did not handle a full or blocked storage, so wrapped them and show a gentle message.
body:
After the restore work I thought about what happens if local storage fails. That can occur in private browsing or when the quota is full. The game would then lose scores without telling anyone.

I listed all the writes with a search for setItem. There were nine call sites, but most go through the central save function, which already had a try and catch that logs to the console. Two did not: the backup counter and the last-played time were written directly.

I moved both to the central function. Now every write goes the same way.

The central function previously swallowed the error. I changed it to also set a flag, and the start screen shows a one-line note: 'Scores could not be saved on this device'. It uses a status role so it is announced once.

To test, I made a fake storage that throws on write, and checked that the flag is set, the message shows, and the game still lets the kid play the round. A failing save must not stop the game, since the kid still wants to practice.

I wrote four tests. The first is a normal write, the second a throwing write, the third that the flag clears after a later good write, and the fourth that reads still work when writes fail. All pass.

I tried the real case on the laptop by filling storage with junk in a separate site profile. The message appeared. On the tablet I did not simulate it, since the data there is real.

One limit: I cannot tell the difference between a full quota and a blocked storage from the error alone in every browser, so the message is general. That seemed fine.

Deployed after the build. The note has a line about the flag.

summary: Planned and started a simple end-of-term summary page for the parent: for each kid, words practiced, best streak and the five most missed words, built from data the game already stores.
body:
The user said at the weekend that it would be nice to see a short summary at the end of the school term, to share with a teacher. I had the pieces: the words-practiced counter, the streak value and the missed-words list.

I wrote down what the page should show. For each kid: total words practiced, best streak ever, number of stickers, and the five most missed words with their counts. No charts, since the page must be readable in print and on the tablet.

The best streak was the first problem. The game stores the current streak and the freeze count, but not the best ever. I could compute it from the attempt history by walking days in order, which is slow to write but accurate. I wrote that as a function and tested it with a history that has a gap covered by a streak freeze.

The second problem was the missed words. The list cap I added last week is only for display, so the full data is there. I reused the sort but with a count rather than a time.

I built the page as a section on the parent page with a print stylesheet. The first version prints with the buttons hidden and the text in black on white. In portrait on the tablet the two kids' blocks stack, which follows the grid fix from before.

I ran the numbers on real data. The older kid had 412 words earlier and now a little more, and the younger kid 268 plus a few. The page agreed with the console sums.

Tests cover the best streak with a freeze, no history, and a tie in missed counts, which sorts by word alphabetically so the order is stable. All pass.

What is left: labels for screen readers on the blocks, and a check of the print preview on the laptop. I did not deploy yet. I will do those next session and ask the user to read the page for wording.

One decision: the page shows no names of the missed words in any other language or in bold, to keep it plain. If the teacher wants more, the backup file has everything.

summary: Finished the summary page: added screen reader labels, checked the print preview on the laptop, fixed a page break that split a kid's block, and deployed it.
body:
I picked up the summary page from yesterday. Three things remained: labels, print, and a final read.

For labels, each kid's block is a section with an aria-labelledby that points to the kid's name heading. The numbers are in a definition list so a screen reader reads each label with its value, for example 'Words practiced: 440'. The earlier accessibility review had found the same kind of gap in three features, so I did this at the start rather than later.

The print preview on the laptop showed the older kid's block split over two pages, with the missed words on the second. I added a rule to avoid breaking inside a block. After that each kid fits on one page. The preview showed a footer with the page address, which comes from the browser and not from the page, so I left it.

I also found that the print stylesheet hid the 'Backup' and 'Restore' buttons but not the 'Last backup' line. It is harmless but looked odd on paper, so I hid it for print.

The user read the page and asked for one change: show the term's words as 'words practiced since the start' rather than a bare number, because a bare 440 seemed to mean one week. I changed the label.

Tests still pass and I added one for the label text. The build went up by about 1 KB, which is fine.

On the tablet, the page loads quickly and the sections stack in portrait. I checked rotation twice with no layout jump and no repeated live region announcements.

Deployed. The next step is to put a line in the note and see whether the user actually uses the page.

summary: Fixed the best-streak calculation on the summary page, which counted a streak freeze day as a break and showed 6 instead of 9 for the younger kid.
body:
The user printed the summary and noticed that the younger kid's best streak said 6, while they remembered the tablet showing 9 for a while. I checked the data.

The history has a freeze marker on days when the kid used a snowflake. My function walked the days and reset the count when a day had no attempts. A frozen day has no attempts, but it should keep the streak alive without adding to it. The test I wrote for a gap with a freeze passed only because the freeze was at the end of the run, not the middle.

I added a test with a freeze in the middle: days one to four played, day five frozen, days six to nine played. The expected best is 8, since the frozen day does not count. The function returned 4, so the test failed, as it should.

The fix was to treat a frozen day as neither a break nor an addition. After it, the test passed, and the real data gave 9 for the younger kid, hmm, the live streak value had counted the frozen day as well, so the two disagreed by one.

That raised the question of which is right. The game's live streak adds one for a frozen day, which I checked in the streak code written in the earlier weeks. So the summary should be consistent with the live rule. I changed the function again so a frozen day adds one, and the test now expects 9. The real data matched what the tablet had shown.

I rewrote the test name to say what the rule is, so a later reader does not repeat my confusion. I also added a note in the code that the rule must match the live streak.

The older kid's best streak did not change, 14 in both. All tests pass and the build is the same size. Deployed, and I told the user to reprint the page.

summary: Wrapped up the term work: reviewed all changes since the maintenance note, updated it with the summary page, restore confirm and storage warning, and listed nothing further as planned.
body:
I read the full list of changes from the planning session onward and checked each against the note. Several were not in it yet.

The items added were: the exact-10 and duplicate checks on the parent page, the cap on the missed-words display, the numbered backup file name, the voice fallback with the voiceschanged retry, the profile question on the start screen, the restore confirm, the removal of the old touch listener, the storage failure message, and the term summary page with its streak rule.

I wrote them into the note in the same plain style as before, with one or two lines each and the file names, so someone returning after a long break can find the code. For the streak rule I added a sentence that the summary and the live streak must agree on frozen days.

I also updated the list of commands: npm run lint:words checks the word files, and the tests and build are unchanged. The word check found nothing new on the latest lists.

For numbers, the build is about 39 KB compressed and the test suite has just over 100 tests, all passing. The count of practiced words was 440 for the older kid and 281 for the younger on the last check.

I then did a play check on the tablet with the older kid's list. No console errors or warnings, sounds fine, the profile question did not appear since the same kid was playing, and slow replay started quickly.

The open list is empty now. The decision to keep the dependency set frozen stays. The kids use the game less, and the user said the school app covers most of the practice, so I do not plan more features.

If something breaks after a browser update, the places to look first are the voice picker, the cache list plugin and the storage save function. I put that sentence at the top of the note.

Nothing was left uncommitted. The session ended with the site deployed and the note up to date.

summary: Checked the site once more from the tablet after the term wrap-up and found the summary page, restore confirm and storage warning all behave, with no open items.
body:
Opened the live site on the tablet and walked through the start screen, one full list of 10 words and the parent page. Everything loaded from the service worker after one online visit, and the new cache list matched the built files.

On the parent page the summary page printed correctly again, and the page break fix from yesterday held. The restore confirm appeared as expected when a backup was loaded into a profile that already had scores.

I also forced the storage warning by filling local storage in the browser tools, and the gentle message showed instead of an error. The console was clean apart from the usual voice list message on first load, which resolves itself once the voices are reported.

Nothing was changed in the code. The maintenance note is current, so the next step is to leave the project alone until the kids or the user ask for something.

summary: The user asked for the weekly list to be readable aloud twice before the kid types, so I looked at how the speech queue works and planned a small repeat option.
body:
The user said the younger kid often misses the word because the tablet speaks it once and the room is noisy. They asked whether the game could say each word twice. I read through the speak function in the game module to see how it queues utterances.

The function creates one SpeechSynthesisUtterance, sets the saved voice and rate, and calls speak. The replay button calls the same function, so a second kid-initiated reading already exists, but kids do not always notice it. The request was therefore about an automatic repeat.

Two designs came up. The first is to queue two utterances back to back with a short pause between them. The second is to repeat only when the kid has not typed anything for a few seconds. The second is friendlier but needs a timer that must be cancelled on every key press and on every new word, which is where the old lost-letter bug lived.

I chose the first design for its simplicity, with a setting on the parent page, off by default so the older kid is not annoyed. The pause would be about 800 ms, implemented by a short timeout that is cleared if the kid presses replay or moves on.

I did not write code yet. The plan is to add a boolean to the settings object stored in local storage, default it to false when missing so existing profiles keep working, and cover it with two tests: one for the queue length and one for the cancelled timeout. I will build it in the next session and test it on the tablet with the actual voice.

summary: Built the speak-twice option as a pause between two readings of each word, with a setting on the parent page, after the user asked for the list to be read aloud twice.
body:
The user asked yesterday whether each word could be read twice before the kid types, because the younger kid often misses the start of a word. I looked at how the speech code works in src/speech.ts. It creates one utterance per word and waits for the end event before it shows the input field. That made the change small: queue a second utterance after a short pause, and show the input only after the second end event.

I added a setting called repeatCount with the values 1 and 2, stored next to the voice and speed settings in local storage. The default stays at 1, so nothing changes for anyone who does not turn it on. The parent page got one checkbox labelled 'Read each word twice', with a label that screen readers announce correctly. The checkbox writes the setting the same way the speed slider does, through the existing wrapped storage write.

The pause between the two readings is a fixed 800 ms timer for now. On the laptop with the default voice the two readings sounded natural. I also checked that pressing the replay button during the pause cancels the pending second reading, so the words do not overlap. Before this change, the replay button simply spoke the word again, and it kept doing that.

I wrote two tests: one for the order of the utterances and one for the cancel case. Both pass, and the full test run stays green. The build is still small, with the bundle growing by well under 1 KB compressed. I did not deploy it yet, because I want to hear it on the tablet first, and the tablet voice is the one that has caused trouble before.

Next I will try it on the tablet tomorrow with the saved voice and watch for cut-off audio. If the fixed timer misbehaves there, I will switch it to start from the end event. The setting is global at the moment, and the user may want it per kid, so I noted that as a likely follow-up.

summary: Tried the speak-twice option on the tablet and found the second reading cut off the first on one voice, so the pause now starts from the end event instead of a fixed timer.
body:
I deployed the change and tried it on the tablet with the saved voice and the option turned on.

On the first word the second reading started before the first had finished, so the word was spoken over itself. The cause was that I had started the 800 ms timer when the first utterance was queued rather than when it ended. For short words it looked fine on the laptop, but the tablet voice is slower and the longer words overlapped.

The fix was to attach the timer start to the end event of the first utterance. If the end event never fires, which happens on some voices when speech is cancelled, a fallback timer of five seconds clears the state so the game does not wait forever.

I also noticed that cancelling speech with the browser's cancel call fires an error event with the value 'interrupted' on some browsers. The handler had logged this as a console error, so I made it ignore that value and log only real errors.

After the change I listened to all ten words of this week with the option on. Each word was read twice with a clear pause and no overlap, and replay during the pause cancelled the second reading as intended. With the option off, behaviour was identical to before.

I updated the two tests so they fire the end event by hand, and added a third for the fallback timer. All tests pass and the type check is clean. The service worker updated on the tablet after a reload, and the cache list included the new build files.

The maintenance note gets a short line about the option and the end-event timing in the next review.

summary: Heard back that the younger kid likes the double reading, and the user asked to turn it on only for that profile, so the setting became per profile.
body:
The user reported that the younger kid now catches more words on the first try. The older kid, however, found the repeat annoying when the tablet was handed over, because the setting was global.

I checked how settings are stored. The speed and voice are global, and the profile object only holds scores, stickers and the streak. The simplest correct change was to move repeatWord into the profile object and leave speed and voice where they are.

I wrote a small migration that runs on load: if the global settings contain repeatWord, its value is copied to every existing profile and the global key is removed. Profiles that already have the value are left alone, so running it twice changes nothing. The backup format carries profiles, so I checked that a backup made before the change restores correctly and gets the default of false.

The parent page now shows the checkbox once per profile, under each kid's name, with the name in the label so the screen reader says which kid it affects. The profile confirm step from before still works, since it only reads the last-played record.

Tests added: migration from global to profile, migration run twice, restore of an old backup. I also ran the whole suite and the type check, both clean.

On the tablet I switched profiles and confirmed the younger kid hears two readings while the older hears one. The user was told the older kid's setting is off by default and can be changed on the parent page.

summary: Looked at the play logs and saw the younger kid played three lists this week, all with the double reading, and no errors, so the option is considered done.
body:
I went through the local play logs the user exported from the tablet. The younger kid played three lists this week, and the older kid played one. No error entries were recorded.

The average for the younger kid was 8 of 10 on the first try, compared with 6 of 10 in the logs from the weeks before the option. That is a small sample, so I note it only as a good sign and not as proof.

I also checked the time between the end of the first reading and the first key press. It dropped slightly, which fits the idea that the second reading helps the kid decide what to type.

No code was changed. I added a line to the maintenance note about the per-profile setting and the migration so a future reader knows why the global key is gone.

summary: Answered the user's question about whether the double reading slows the game down much, and found it adds about 2 seconds per word at the current speed.
body:
The user asked whether the double reading makes a list take much longer. I measured it on the laptop with the saved speed. A word with the option off takes about 1.2 seconds to speak, and with it on about 3.2 seconds including the pause, so about 2 seconds more per word.

Over a list of 10 words that adds around 20 seconds if every word is heard only once per attempt. The replay button remains available either way, so a kid who needs it can still press it.

I told the user that this seemed small compared with the typing time, and that the pause length is a constant in the code if they want it shorter. They said it was fine as it is.

summary: Checked an evening of play after the per-profile change and saw the right profile settings, a clean console and the service worker up to date on the tablet.
body:
In the evening I watched the younger kid play one list and the older kid play another on the tablet. The younger kid heard each word twice and the older once, so the per-profile setting worked across the switch.

The profile confirm question appeared once when the tablet was handed over, as it should. Scores and stickers were saved to the correct profiles, and the console showed no errors or warnings.

The service worker had updated to the latest build and the cache list matched the built files. I also made a backup and restored it into the same device, and the confirm step appeared and the settings stayed intact.

Nothing is left open from this topic. The next step is to leave the project alone unless the kids ask for something.
